- `hero.math.log-partition.note`: ln Z of a spin chain against inverse temperature, and its tangent, whose slope is the energy
- `hero.math.markov-blanket.label`: a Markov blanket
- `hero.math.markov-blanket.note`: a Markov blanket: sensory states (squares) carry the outside in, active states (triangles) push out, and the inside talks to the outside only through them
- `hero.math.mean-field-free-energy.label`: free energy of a magnet
- `hero.math.mean-field-free-energy.note`: the exact mean-field free energy against magnetisation: one valley above the critical point, two below
- `hero.math.metropolis-acceptance.label`: the Metropolis rule
- `hero.math.metropolis-acceptance.note`: the chance a Metropolis step is taken against the energy it costs, at four temperatures
- `hero.math.onsager-heat.label`: the specific heat peak
- `hero.math.onsager-heat.note`: the exact specific heat of the 2D Ising model: it diverges at the critical temperature
- `hero.math.onsager-magnetisation.label`: the 2D Ising magnet
- `hero.math.onsager-magnetisation.note`: Onsager's exact magnetisation of the square-lattice Ising model: two branches that meet at the critical temperature
- `hero.math.pbit-and-gate.label`: a p-bit AND gate
- `hero.math.pbit-and-gate.note`: the eight states of three p-bits wired as an AND gate: the four that obey AND come up most often
- `hero.math.pbit-samples.label`: p-bit samples
- `hero.math.pbit-samples.note`: a p-bit's chance of +1 against its input, with one real draw at each input along the top and bottom
- `hero.math.phase-diagram.label`: the phase diagram
- `hero.math.phase-diagram.note`: the magnetisation of a mean-field magnet over field and temperature as contours; the bold line is the jump at zero field below the critical point
- `hero.math.quasi-orthogonal.label`: nearly orthogonal
- `hero.math.quasi-orthogonal.note`: the cosine between two random bipolar words in 8, 64, 512 and 10,000 dimensions: the bell narrows toward zero
- `hero.math.replica-exchange.label`: replica exchange
- `hero.math.replica-exchange.note`: one replica climbing and descending a ladder of eight temperatures as neighbours swap
- `hero.math.schottky-anomaly.label`: a two-level bump
- `hero.math.schottky-anomaly.note`: the heat capacity of a two-level system peaks where the temperature matches the gap
- `hero.math.sdm-critical-distance.label`: the critical distance
- `hero.math.sdm-critical-distance.note`: Kanerva's critical distance: reading a sparse distributed memory from a read-address closer than it converges on the stored word; from farther away it drifts off
- `hero.math.sdr-false-match.label`: a false match
- `hero.math.sdr-false-match.note`: the chance that a random sparse code of 40 bits in 2,048 shares at least theta bits with a given one, on a log scale
- `hero.math.sk-overlap.label`: the spin-glass order
- `hero.math.sk-overlap.note`: the Edwards-Anderson order of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass: frozen below T = 1 and gone above with no field; a small field rounds the corner
- `hero.math.variational-free-energy.label`: variational free energy
- `hero.math.variational-free-energy.note`: a true posterior (solid) and a simpler guess (dashed); free energy is surprise (the filled bar) plus their divergence (the open bar above it)
- `hero.paper.bricken-circle-intersection.label`: two access circles
- `hero.paper.bricken-circle-intersection.note`: the intersection of the read circle and a pattern's write circle, at distance d apart (Bricken and Pehlevan 2021, arXiv, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.bricken-critical-distance.label`: SDM critical distance
- `hero.paper.bricken-critical-distance.note`: the critical distance of a sparse distributed memory against the Hamming distance, n = 1,000 (Bricken and Pehlevan 2021, arXiv, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.chowdhury-bits-pbits-qubits.label`: bits, p-bits, qubits
- `hero.paper.chowdhury-bits-pbits-qubits.note`: a bit is 0 or 1, a p-bit fluctuates between them, a qubit holds a superposition (Chowdhury et al. 2023, arXiv, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.fullsack-free-energy.label`: tilting free energy
- `hero.paper.fullsack-free-energy.note`: the free energy of an Ising magnet tilted by a field, and where its valleys disappear (Füllsack and Reisinger 2021, PLOS ONE, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.kim-hopfield-phases.label`: Hopfield phases
- `hero.paper.kim-hopfield-phases.note`: the phase diagram of a Hopfield network in temperature and load: paramagnetic, spin-glass and retrieval (Kim et al. 2017, PLOS ONE, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.loossens-affect-ising.label`: an affective Ising model
- `hero.paper.loossens-affect-ising.note`: two populations of binary units, positive and negative, exciting themselves and inhibiting each other (Loossens et al. 2020, PLOS Computational Biology, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.loossens-free-energy-surface.label`: a free energy surface
- `hero.paper.loossens-free-energy-surface.note`: the free energy surface of the affective Ising model, with its two valleys drawn below it (Loossens et al. 2020, PLOS Computational Biology, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.masuda-basin-graph.label`: a basin graph
- `hero.paper.masuda-basin-graph.note`: a basin graph: each local minimum with the states that settle into it (Masuda et al. 2025, PLOS Complex Systems, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.masuda-energy-landscape.label`: two energy landscapes
- `hero.paper.masuda-energy-landscape.note`: two one-dimensional energy landscapes: local minima, the barrier between them, and the state hopping across it in time (Masuda et al. 2025, PLOS Complex Systems, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.masuda-local-minimum.label`: a local minimum
- `hero.paper.masuda-local-minimum.note`: a local minimum of an Ising energy: one state and the five states one flip away, each with its energy (Masuda et al. 2025, PLOS Complex Systems, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.masuda-sk-phases.label`: spin-glass phases
- `hero.paper.masuda-sk-phases.note`: the phase diagram of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model: paramagnetic, ferromagnetic and spin-glass (Masuda et al. 2025, PLOS Complex Systems, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.melanson-coupled-cells.label`: two coupled cells
- `hero.paper.melanson-coupled-cells.note`: two LC cells coupled through a capacitor: the unit of a thermodynamic computer (Melanson et al. 2023, arXiv, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.morales-ising-configurations.label`: Ising configurations
- `hero.paper.morales-ising-configurations.note`: spin configurations of the 2D Ising model below, near and above the critical temperature (Morales et al. 2015, PLOS ONE, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.paper.morales-variance-peak.label`: the variance at Tc
- `hero.paper.morales-variance-peak.note`: the variance of the magnetisation of the 2D Ising model peaks at the critical temperature (Morales et al. 2015, PLOS ONE, CC BY 4.0)
- `hero.pause`: ❚❚ pause
- `hero.pic.pause`: Pause the picture
- `hero.pic.play`: Play the picture
- `hero.plate.babbage-number-card.label`: Babbage's number card
- `hero.plate.babbage-number-card.note`: Babbage's number card for the Analytical Engine, after Passages from the Life of a Philosopher (Freeman, Automatic Mechanical Punching ... Machines, 1915)
- `hero.plate.cajal-climbing-fibre.label`: a climbing fibre
- `hero.plate.cajal-climbing-fibre.note`: Ramón y Cajal's climbing fibre of the adult human cerebellum (Manual de histología normal, 1921)
- `hero.plate.cajal-purkinje-cell.label`: a Purkinje cell
- `hero.plate.cajal-purkinje-cell.note`: Ramón y Cajal's Purkinje cells of the human cerebellum, Golgi method (Manual de histología normal, 1921)
- `hero.plate.darcy-sunfish-grid.label`: Sunfish transformation grid
- `hero.plate.darcy-sunfish-grid.note`: The porcupine-fish grid deformed into the sunfish, Fig. 382 (D'Arcy Thompson, On growth and form, 1917)
- `hero.plate.dircks-weighted-wheel.label`: Overbalanced weight wheel
- `hero.plate.dircks-weighted-wheel.note`: A perpetual motion wheel with weighted levers, Fig. 52 (Dircks, Perpetuum Mobile, 1861)
- `hero.plate.ewing-magnet-domains.label`: magnets in groups
- `hero.plate.ewing-magnet-domains.note`: Ewing's model of molecular magnets falling into groups (Magnetic Induction in Iron and Other Metals, 1900)
- `hero.plate.galileo-moon.label`: Galileo's moon
- `hero.plate.galileo-moon.note`: Galileo's drawing of the moon at first quarter (Sidereus nuncius, 1610)
- `hero.plate.galton-quincunx.label`: the quincunx
- `hero.plate.galton-quincunx.note`: Galton's quincunx: shot falls through pins into a bell curve (Natural Inheritance, 1889)
- `hero.plate.galton-tumbling-slab.label`: the tumbling slab
- `hero.plate.galton-tumbling-slab.note`: Galton's polygonal slab model of primary and subordinate stability (Natural Inheritance, 1889)
- `hero.plate.ganot-crookes-radiometer.label`: Crookes radiometer
- `hero.plate.ganot-crookes-radiometer.note`: Crookes's radiometer, Fig. 651 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.ganot-gyroscope.label`: Gyroscope on stand
- `hero.plate.ganot-gyroscope.note`: Gyroscope, Fig. 37 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.ganot-herons-fountain.label`: Hero's fountain
- `hero.plate.ganot-herons-fountain.note`: Hero's fountain, Fig. 217 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.ganot-morse-key.label`: Morse telegraph key
- `hero.plate.ganot-morse-key.note`: The Morse key, Fig. 999 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.ganot-phonograph.label`: Edison's phonograph
- `hero.plate.ganot-phonograph.note`: Edison's wax-cylinder phonograph, Fig. 302 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.ganot-ruhmkorff-coil.label`: Ruhmkorff induction coil
- `hero.plate.ganot-ruhmkorff-coil.note`: Ruhmkorff's induction coil, Fig. 1047 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.ganot-wimshurst-machine.label`: Wimshurst machine
- `hero.plate.ganot-wimshurst-machine.note`: Wimshurst's influence machine, Fig. 773 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.gray-hand-bones.label`: Gray's hand bones
- `hero.plate.gray-hand-bones.note`: The bones of the left hand, dorsal surface, Fig. 220 (Gray, Anatomy of the human body, 1918)
- `hero.plate.guillemin-anchor-escapement.label`: Clock escapement wheel
- `hero.plate.guillemin-anchor-escapement.note`: The anchor escapement of a pendulum clock, Fig. 6 (Guillemin, The Applications of Physical Forces, 1877)
- `hero.plate.guillemin-foucault-pendulum.label`: Foucault's pendulum
- `hero.plate.guillemin-foucault-pendulum.note`: Foucault's pendulum experiment, Fig. 8 (Guillemin, The Applications of Physical Forces, 1877)
- `hero.plate.guillemin-foucault-telescope.label`: Foucault's reflecting telescope
- `hero.plate.guillemin-foucault-telescope.note`: Léon Foucault's telescope with silver mirror, Fig. 207 (Guillemin, The Applications of Physical Forces, 1877)
- `hero.plate.guillemin-gregory-telescope.label`: Gregorian telescope
- `hero.plate.guillemin-gregory-telescope.note`: Gregory's telescope on its stand, Fig. 205 (Guillemin, The Applications of Physical Forces, 1877)
- `hero.plate.guillemin-herschel-telescope.label`: Herschel's great telescope
- `hero.plate.guillemin-herschel-telescope.note`: Sir W. Herschel's large telescope at Slough, Fig. 203 (Guillemin, The Applications of Physical Forces, 1877)
- `hero.plate.guillemin-roberval-balance.label`: Roberval's balance
- `hero.plate.guillemin-roberval-balance.note`: Roberval's balance, Fig. 13 (Guillemin, The Applications of Physical Forces, 1877)
- `hero.plate.haeckel-aulosphaera.label`: Haeckel's lattice sphere
- `hero.plate.haeckel-aulosphaera.note`: Aulosphaera, a radiolarian with a geodesic lattice shell (Haeckel, Die Radiolarien vol. 4, 1888)
- `hero.plate.haeckel-cannopilus-cross.label`: Haeckel's cross skeleton
- `hero.plate.haeckel-cannopilus-cross.note`: Cannopilus, a four-armed lattice skeleton (Haeckel, Die Radiolarien vol. 4, 1888)
- `hero.plate.haeckel-cannopilus-disc.label`: Haeckel's radiate disc
- `hero.plate.haeckel-cannopilus-disc.note`: Cannopilus, a shell seen from above (Haeckel, Die Radiolarien vol. 4, 1888)
- `hero.plate.haeckel-haeckeliana.label`: Haeckel's spined radiolarian
- `hero.plate.haeckel-haeckeliana.note`: Haeckeliana, a spined radiolarian (Haeckel, Die Radiolarien vol. 4, 1888)
- `hero.plate.huygens-reflection.label`: Huygens' reflected wave
- `hero.plate.huygens-reflection.note`: A wave front reflected from a plane, built from wavelets (Huygens, Abhandlung über das Licht, 1890 edition of the Traité de la lumière)
- `hero.plate.huygens-wavefront.label`: Huygens' wavelets
- `hero.plate.huygens-wavefront.note`: A wave front built from the small waves of each particle (Huygens, Abhandlung über das Licht, 1890 edition of the Traité de la lumière)
- `hero.plate.kelvin-tide-predictor.label`: the tide predictor
- `hero.plate.kelvin-tide-predictor.note`: Kelvin's tide predictor (Popular Lectures and Addresses, vol. III, 1891)
- `hero.plate.kepler-nested-solids.label`: Kepler's nested solids
- `hero.plate.kepler-nested-solids.note`: The planetary spheres nested between the five regular solids (Kepler, Mysterium cosmographicum, in Opera omnia vol. 1, 1858)
- `hero.plate.kepler-trigon.label`: Kepler's great conjunctions
- `hero.plate.kepler-trigon.note`: The triangles of the great conjunctions of Saturn and Jupiter (Kepler, Mysterium cosmographicum, in Opera omnia vol. 1, 1858)
- `hero.plate.maxwell-lines-of-force-two-charges.label`: Maxwell's lines of force
- `hero.plate.maxwell-lines-of-force-two-charges.note`: Maxwell's lines of force and equipotential surfaces about two charges (Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, 1873)
- `hero.plate.meyer-shot-marks-maxwell-law.label`: Shots at a target
- `hero.plate.meyer-shot-marks-maxwell-law.note`: Shot-marks round a bull's-eye, Meyer's picture of Maxwell's law (Meyer, The Kinetic Theory of Gases, 1899)
- `hero.plate.michelson-harmonic-analyser-curves.label`: the analyser's waves
- `hero.plate.michelson-harmonic-analyser-curves.note`: Curves drawn by Michelson's harmonic analyser (Light Waves and Their Uses, 1903)
- `hero.plate.newton-prism.label`: Newton's prism
- `hero.plate.newton-prism.note`: A ray through a prism to the eye, Fig. 13 (Newton, Opticks, 1704)
- `hero.plate.newton-rainbow.label`: Newton's rainbow
- `hero.plate.newton-rainbow.note`: The two rainbows and the eye, Fig. 15 (Newton, Opticks, 1704)
- `hero.plate.perrin-brownian-tracks.label`: Brownian tracks
- `hero.plate.perrin-brownian-tracks.note`: Perrin's traced paths of three Brownian grains (Atoms, 1916)
- `hero.plate.scoresby-snow-crystal.label`: Scoresby's snow crystal
- `hero.plate.scoresby-snow-crystal.note`: A branched six-rayed snow crystal drawn by Scoresby (An account of the Arctic regions vol. 2, 1820)
- `hero.plate.scoresby-snow-star.label`: Scoresby's stellar crystal
- `hero.plate.scoresby-snow-star.note`: A stellar snow crystal with plated arms (Scoresby, An account of the Arctic regions vol. 2, 1820)
- `hero.plate.thome-water-soldier.label`: Thomé's water soldier
- `hero.plate.thome-water-soldier.note`: The water soldier, Stratiotes aloides (Thomé, Flora von Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz vol. 1, 1903)
- `hero.plate.thompson-iron-filings-bar-magnet.label`: Iron filings
- `hero.plate.thompson-iron-filings-bar-magnet.note`: Iron filings settled around a bar magnet (Thompson, Elementary Lessons in Electricity and Magnetism, 1905)
- `hero.plate.thomson-isotherm-loop.label`: The isotherm loop
- `hero.plate.thomson-isotherm-loop.note`: James Thomson's continuous isothermal with its unstable loop (Maxwell, Theory of Heat, 1899)
- `hero.plate.thurston-hero-aeolipile.label`: Hero's steam engine
- `hero.plate.thurston-hero-aeolipile.note`: Hero's engine, the aeolipile, Fig. 3 (Thurston, History of the Growth of the Steam-Engine, 1901)

- `home.sci`: Settling is sampling: each thing is a p-bit, a coin that comes up +1 (yes) or −1 (no), and the machine keeps re-tossing one thing at a time, so that in the long run every arrangement s turns up with probability proportional to e^(−β E(s)), with β = 1/T. Each toss sets a thing to yes with probability P(yes) = (1 + tanh(β I)) / 2, where I = lean + Σ pull × neighbour is the sum of its lean and its pulls times its neighbours’ values, and the arrangement drifts toward low energy E = −Σ lean·s − Σ pull·s·s′, the quantity Settling lowers.
- `home.start.label`: GETTING STARTED
- `home.start.lede`: From a clone of the SETTLE repository to a question answered with evidence. Each program runs live in your browser under its code.

- `home.step2`: 2 · write a first program
- `home.step2.note`: One thing, named :coin, leaning toward yes with strength 1. Settle it 40,000 times and ask how often it came up yes.
- `home.step3`: 3 · run it
- `home.step3.note`: The output of that program. The exact answer is (1 + tanh 1) / 2 = 88.08%.
- `home.step4`: 4 · ask a question with evidence
- `home.step4.note`: The grass is wet: did it rain? Hold the wet-grass light on and count the rain light. The release binary says {wet}% with the grass held wet, {none}% with nothing held and {dry}% with it held dry.
- `home.surprise`: Also built on a settling machine, outside the statement families: SURPRISE, a small first-person game whose agent acts to keep its observations unsurprising (Friston’s free-energy principle, in toy form).
- `home.weather`: rain, sprinkler and wet grass, settling with the grass held wet

## kanerva

- `kanerva.algebra.label`: THE ALGEBRA IN MOTION · MEASURED
- `kanerva.algebra.lede`: The dollar of Mexico needs two moves, the tie and the vote. The same two moves can hold many ties in one vector and take a product of several words apart again. We ran three small experiments on this and drew fifteen of them for the home page; three are here.
- `kanerva.algebra.p1`: A resonator network takes a vector made by tying three unknown words together and finds all three at once, correcting each guess from the other two. With 64 words a codebook in 256-bit vectors the plain rule found the answer {sign} percent of the time. Setting weak matches to zero and adding a little noise, as an analog memory chip does without trying, found it {noise} percent of the time. The zeroing alone left small searches stuck on wrong answers ({thresh} percent found at 16 words); the noise freed them ({noise16} percent).
- `kanerva.algebra.p2`: One vector of 512 numbers holding 40 tied pairs gave back {fhrr} percent of them when its numbers were phasors, {map} percent as plain sums of plus and minus ones, and {bsc} percent when every sum was rounded to a bit. Reading a crowded sum one member at a time, taking the loudest away each time, found {peel} percent of 80 members where reading them all at once found {plain} percent.
- `kanerva.algebra.p3`: A number can be written as a vector of clocks, each turned by it at its own speed. Two such vectors agree as much as their clocks point the same way, and the shape of that agreement, a sinc, a bell or a sharp peak, is set by how the speeds were spread. With 2,048 clocks the measured shapes stayed within {gap} of theory. These are measurements of a toy algebra, not of our language model.
- `kanerva.algebra.title`: Holding many ties, and taking them apart
- `kanerva.algebra.why.clocks`: Thirty-two clocks, one for each phasor of a query compared with a stored value. As the query comes home the hands turn into line and the curve beneath them, the similarity, climbs to 1. In this algebra, similarity is many independent clocks agreeing.
- `kanerva.algebra.why.noise`: Two grids of the same 48 problems: on the left the plain resonator, on the right the same with a threshold and a little noise; a square fills when its three factors are found. The plain rule settles 14 and leaves the rest circling or stuck, while with the noise all 48 come to agree. A little randomness lets every guess give way until the three fit together.
- `kanerva.algebra.why.peel`: Two curves of the members found in a crowded sum: the lower reads the K loudest at once, the upper reads one, takes it away and reads again. The hatched gap is the members who were there all along but drowned out. Letting the loudest step aside is how every member gets heard.
- `kanerva.analogies.d1.precise`: Each word is {D} random bits. Dollar and peso agree on {pct} of them: unrelated words agree on about half.
- `kanerva.analogies.d1.title`: Every word is a long row of random dots.
- `kanerva.analogies.d2.precise`: bind: c = a XOR b, bit by bit. Tying again with b gives back a, so a tie can be undone.
- `kanerva.analogies.d2.title`: Tie a role to its value: a dot lights where the two rows differ.
- `kanerva.analogies.d3.precise`: bundle: each bit of USA is the majority of the three ties. USA still agrees with MONEY tied to dollar on {pct} of its bits.
- `kanerva.analogies.d3.title`: A country is a vote of its three ties.
- `kanerva.analogies.d4.precise`: USA XOR MEXICO keeps a trace of dollar XOR peso, because MONEY XOR MONEY cancels.
- `kanerva.analogies.d4.title`: Tie the two countries together. The result maps each of one country's values to the other's.
- `kanerva.analogies.d5.precise`: dollar XOR (USA XOR MEXICO): a noisy copy of the word that plays dollar's part in MEXICO.
- `kanerva.analogies.d5.title`: Push dollar through the map.
- `kanerva.analogies.d6.precise`: similarity = 1 - 2 x (differing bits) / {D}. Peso scores {top}, the next word {next}; chance spreads about 0.010.
- `kanerva.analogies.d6.title`: Ask the memory which word the answer looks like. Peso lights up.
- `kanerva.analogies.d7.iq.aria`: the IQ-test form of the dollar of Mexico
- `kanerva.analogies.d7.precise`: MEXICO XOR USA XOR dollar is the word from step 5 again. Cleaned up, it is {name} at {sim}; the next word scores {next}.
- `kanerva.analogies.d7.title`: The same question, as an IQ test.
- `kanerva.analogies.d8.fewer`: fewer than 100%
- `kanerva.analogies.d8.precise`: (SWEDEN XOR USA) XOR (USA XOR MEXICO) agrees with SWEDEN XOR MEXICO on {share} of its bits: the USA in the middle cancels exactly. Krona pushed through it comes back as {answer} at {sim}.
- `kanerva.analogies.d8.title`: Go through a third country. Sweden to the United States, then on to Mexico.
- `kanerva.analogies.d9.precise`: The roles NAME, CAPITAL and MONEY cancel out of the map (MONEY XOR MONEY is all zeros). What is left pairs usa with mexico, washington with mexico city, and dollar with peso.
- `kanerva.analogies.d9.quote`: “The mapping vector has the same form as the holistic record H introduced earlier, except that in place of abstract variables we have an exemplar: the particulars for the United States, USA, WDC, and DOL, play the role of the variables in terms of which the Mexican data are interpreted. This agrees with our common use of language when we refer to the peso as the Mexican dollar, for example. The ‘Mexican dollar’ is immediately understood even if there is no such a thing, literally speaking, and we know that it does not exist.”
- `kanerva.analogies.d9.title`: Why Kanerva calls this a prototype.
- `kanerva.analogies.h.dollar`: The dollar of Mexico, step by step
- `kanerva.analogies.h.king`: King is to queen as man is to woman
- `kanerva.analogies.h.more`: Three more from the same paper
- `kanerva.analogies.k1.precise`: KING = majority(KIND tied to person, RANK tied to royal, SEX tied to male); QUEEN, MAN and WOMAN are built the same way.
- `kanerva.analogies.k1.title`: A person is a vote of three ties: what kind, what rank, what sex.
- `kanerva.analogies.k2.precise`: KING XOR MAN cancels the person and male ties and keeps royal XOR common.
- `kanerva.analogies.k2.title`: Tie KING to MAN. What they share cancels; what makes a king more than a man is left.
- `kanerva.analogies.k3.precise`: KING XOR MAN XOR WOMAN: a woman given what a king has more than a man, that is, a noisy QUEEN.
- `kanerva.analogies.k3.title`: Tie that difference to WOMAN.
- `kanerva.analogies.k4.precise`: The three words we asked with also score high, because the answer is made from them; as in every analogy test they are set aside. Queen scores {top}, the best other word {next}.
- `kanerva.analogies.k4.title`: Ask the memory which word the answer looks like. Queen lights up.
- `kanerva.analogies.king.note`: This one is not in Kanerva’s paper. It is the classic word analogy, built here with the same two moves and roles we chose: KIND, RANK and SEX.
- `kanerva.analogies.label`: THE DOLLAR OF MEXICO, AND KANERVA'S OTHER EXAMPLES
- `kanerva.analogies.lede`: Two moves, the tie and the vote, are enough to ask this and get an answer. A country is a bundle of three ties. Tie two countries together and you get a map between them. Push dollar through the map and peso comes out. Each card shows one step on the first 40 of the 10,000 bits.

- `kanerva.analogies.source`: Source for cards 1 to 9: P. Kanerva, “What We Mean When We Say ‘What’s the Dollar of Mexico?’: Prototypes and Mapping in Concept Space”, AAAI Fall Symposium on Quantum Informatics for Cognitive, Social, and Semantic Processes, 2010 (Technical Report FS-10-08, pp. 2-6; the paper). The paper writes USTATES, MEXICO and SWEDEN with the roles NAM, CAP and MON; the cards spell them out. It also says what a word like this is for: “D can later be retrieved by addressing the memory with A or with a ‘noisy’ version of it that is similar to A. The address A is also called a memory cue.” On this site the word is address, and a damaged one is a noisy address.

- `kanerva.balance.caption`: recall from 10% address-noise, 100 reads a cell (n 256, M 10,000)
- `kanerva.balance.col.dist`: expected distance
- `kanerva.balance.col.load`: {n} words
- `kanerva.balance.col.q`: a bit is +1 with chance
- `kanerva.balance.label`: WHEN THE BITS LEAN
- `kanerva.balance.p`: Words whose bits lean one way sit closer together, crowd each other’s hard locations, and the memory holds far fewer of them. The first row is the control, fair bits. diagnose::balance measures the lean before you write.
- `kanerva.balance.title`: Kanerva’s theory assumes every bit is a fair coin
- `kanerva.deep.fence`: These are small memories of random words, run on a laptop. They show how the mechanism behaves; they do not say that a memory read helps a language model.
- `kanerva.deep.label`: MEASURED HERE
- `kanerva.deep.more`: Every number here comes from these experiments’ own code, kept in the SETTLE repository beside their reports.
- `kanerva.deep.p1`: Every hard-location holds the sum of the words written near it. So a read is a vote of the stored words, each weighted by how many hard-locations its circle shares with the read’s circle. We computed that share exactly: near home it falls as an exponential of the distance, so the read is softmax attention, and the activation-radius sets its temperature.
- `kanerva.deep.p2`: The temperature depends on how much of the space one circle holds, not on the length of the words: at one percent of the space, words of 64, 256 and 1,000 bits give 3.96, 4.19 and 4.16. Our own SDM mixer, whose addresses are product keys and not Hamming circles, follows the same law with 4.05.
- `kanerva.deep.p3`: How far a noisy address can start and still come home, the critical-distance, depends on one number: the words per hard-location, counted with the noise every other word adds through the locations it shares. As the memory grows that edge sharpens into a step. And a memory that wakes a narrow circle keeps its old words while a crowd of new ones arrives: 800 new words, where a wide circle holds them only to 10.
- `kanerva.deep.title`: A read is attention, and every word keeps a home
- `kanerva.deep.why.emerge`: Each bar is how many hard-locations a read shares with one stored word; the dots are the exact share. With a few thousand hard-locations the bars are ragged; as the memory grows to 128,000 they settle onto the curve. The attention is not built in: it emerges from many random locations agreeing.
- `kanerva.deep.why.flow`: Eighty lost addresses in the plane of two stored words, each frame one more read. Most walk home to one word or the other; a few rest between them. The word whose circle holds more hard-locations welcomes from farther away.
- `kanerva.deep.why.lens`: Two activation circles, and the share of hard-locations they hold in common, on a log scale against their distance. Near home the points fall on a straight line, so a read weighs every stored word by an exponential of its closeness: softmax attention, as Bricken and Pehlevan showed. Far away the true share falls faster than the line, so the memory ignores strangers a little more firmly than attention does.
- `kanerva.deeper.algebra`: Holding many ties, and taking them apart
- `kanerva.deeper.label`: GOING DEEPER
- `kanerva.deeper.lede`: Small memories of random words, run on a laptop. They show how the mechanism behaves, with every number from its run. Open the one you want.
- `kanerva.deeper.read`: A read is attention, and every word keeps a home
- `kanerva.deeper.title`: Two studies we ran on the mechanism

- `kanerva.page.how.eq.read`: A read from the address z: the woken locations vote, bit by bit; repeat until z stops changing.
- `kanerva.page.how.eq.wake`: The wake set: every hard location whose address a_i is within r bits of the word z.
- `kanerva.page.how.eq.write`: A write adds the word x (as +1 and −1) to the counters of every woken location.
- `kanerva.page.how.explainer`: New to this? SDM EXPLORE walks through the same memory in Kanerva’s own words, with pictures.
- `kanerva.page.how.intro`: A sparse distributed memory stores long words of bits. It has a few thousand hard locations, each with a fixed random address and a row of bit-counters. To write a word, every hard location near it adds the word to its bit-counters. To read, you give it a read-address, which can be a noisy copy of a word: a read-address with address-noise. The nearby locations add up their bit-counters, and each bit of the answer is the sign of its sum. Kanerva calls the read-address the retrieval address, and also the retrieval cue.
- `kanerva.page.how.label`: HOW AN SDM WORKS
- `kanerva.page.how.name`: The memory is called sparse because its locations are a tiny sample of all possible addresses, and distributed because every word is spread over many hard locations and every hard location holds a blend of many words.
- `kanerva.page.how.sketch`:  the address ──▶ which hard locations lie within r bits of it? │ ┌──────────┼────────── ▼ ▼ ▼ location 17 location 402 location 988 ... each hard location keeps a row of bit-counters +3 -1 +2 .. +1 -4 +2 .. +2 -1 +1 .. (every word ever written near it, added in) └──────────┼────────── ▼ add the rows, bit by bit +6 -6 +5 .. ▼ keep the sign of each sum 1 0 1 .. ──▶ the answer. read again from it until it stops changing
- `kanerva.page.how.sketch.aria`: the memory, drawn as a sketch
- `kanerva.page.how.sources`: Source: P. Kanerva, {book}, MIT Press, 1988. Run the same memory as a machine on SDM explore, or compare three memories on the memory page.
- `kanerva.page.how.title`: A memory is a few thousand hard locations that vote
- `kanerva.page.how.why`: Why it works: a noisy address still wakes most of the locations its word was written to. Their bit-counters agree, so they outvote everything else. Read again and the answer gets closer. Try it on 1,200 hard locations: write a word, damage a copy, read from the copy.
- `kanerva.page.results.label`: RECORDED RESULTS
- `kanerva.page.results.note`: Each number is a recall count from a seeded simulation. None is a timing claim. The reports say “cue” for a noisy address. The full reports are on the results page, and three memories side by side are on the memory page.

- `kanerva.pitch.knife.clamp.body`: Store uses one byte per counter, clamps at ±127, and counts every clamp in overflow.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.clamp.head`: The byte store clamps.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.keys.body`: The key is hashed to 64 bits with FNV-1a and a guessed key can be checked offline against the padding.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.keys.head`: A keyed note is not cryptography.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.noise.body`: At 30% and 40% address-noise the address read does not grow with M, because a 40%-noisy read-address shares about one hard-location with its pattern at every M under that activation-radius.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.noise.head`: Noise above a third of the bits does not get better with a bigger memory.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.rec`: the crate's documentation
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.small.body`: 128 hard-locations (32,768 bit-counters) hold 5 / 0 / 0 / 0 against 25 / 25 / 20 / 0 for a 256-unit Hopfield net with 32,640 pulls. The order reverses at a million hard-locations: 70,000 / 30,000 / 10,000 / 10 against 100 / 70 / 30 / 3.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.small.head`: A small memory loses to a Hopfield net.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.threads.body`: smap::Lazy memoises through RefCell, so one Lazy cannot be shared between threads. store::threads() reads the environment variable SDMSCALE_THREADS (default 8), a name from the SETTLE experiment that wrote it.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.threads.head`: Two of its parts are not thread-safe or thread-clean.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.unstored.body`: At light load every never-stored read-address lands on a stored pattern (500/500), so no signal read off the final state can refuse it. The travel rule refuses it; in crowded stores its refusal falls to 0.044 until it is calibrated on the memory’s own random probes.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.unstored.head`: A never-stored address lands on something anyway.

- `kanerva.pitch.knives.lede`: A sparse distributed memory is a sharp tool. The crate keeps its edges rather than hiding them.

- `kanerva.pitch.why`: SETTLE’s first memories were Hopfield nets. A Hopfield net pulls on every pair of bits, so it grows as the square of the word. A 256-unit net held 25 words at 10% address-noise and none at 40%. We wanted a memory that grows with its number of hard locations, holds thousands of words, and answers a read-address it has never seen with the nearest word it has. Kanerva described that memory in 1988. We built it in SETTLE, measured it against Hopfield at equal memory, and pulled it out into this crate. The numbers are in the crate’s docs on this page and in the measured results.
- `kanerva.predict.caption`: n 256, M 10,000, activation-radius {r}; recall is the share of 100 reads that end on their word
- `kanerva.predict.col.cells`: 300 words: measured, TRACK

- `kanerva.predict.label`: THE PREDICTION, CORRECTED
- `kanerva.predict.p`: The S-map predicts how many words a memory holds before you build it. At 30% address-noise or more it promises too many. TRACK, the crate’s tracking prediction, follows the measured recall. At a million hard locations the S-map predicted 1,648 words at 30% noise where 700 were measured, and 403 at 40% where 3 were.
- `kanerva.predict.title`: The plain map is optimistic once the noise reaches 30%

## lb2

- `lb2.blurry.h`: Recall from a blurred key
- `lb2.blurry.p`: As in the recall puzzle, but each key is several symbols long and some of them are swapped for others before the question. An exact-match memory would fail as soon as one symbol changes. A sparse distributed memory should degrade slowly, because a blurred key still wakes many of the same slots.
- `lb2.chip.fades`: {h} fades
- `lb2.chip.size`: one size at any length
- `lb2.chip.window`: no window
- `lb2.copy.h`: Copy a run of symbols
- `lb2.copy.p`: A run of random symbols is followed by the same run again, and every symbol of the second run is scored. To copy, a model must step back by one and match by content. Here the transformer leads at the shortest length, and every model falls away as the run grows.
- `lb2.cost.label`: THE COST PER TOKEN
- `lb2.cost.p1`: To go on writing, either model keeps only its memory: {mb} MB at the size we train, whether the text so far is ten tokens or ten thousand. A transformer keeps a cache that grows by one entry with every token, so a longer text costs it more memory and more work for every new token.
- `lb2.cost.p2`: The memory is not free, though. On one GPU the same layers with the memory switched off train at {o} tokens a second; PARTIAL trains at {p} and FULL at {fu}. Most of each model’s time goes to its memory.
- `lb2.cost.title`: One size at any length
- `lb2.fades.f0`: Fade {f}: only the token just before survives, so this head is a one-step look back.
- `lb2.fades.f1`: Fade {f}: a write halves in about {h} tokens, so this head holds the last few words.
- `lb2.fades.f2`: Fade {f}: a write halves in about {h} tokens, so this head holds the last few sentences.
- `lb2.fades.f3`: Fade {f}: nothing fades, so this head holds the whole text, blended together.
- `lb2.fades.label`: THE FADES
- `lb2.fades.p1`: Each layer’s memory has {h} heads, and before every new write each head multiplies what it holds by its own fade. A write made some tokens back counts the fade once for every token since.
- `lb2.fades.p2`: The fades are the same in FULL and in PARTIAL. The think step that follows, the table or the MLP, works on the current token alone and holds no past.
- `lb2.fades.title`: One head for the last token, one that never forgets
- `lb2.not.l1`: One run each, one seed. A gap of a few points between two models is inside what a second seed could move.
- `lb2.not.l2`: Small models on puzzles with their own alphabet, where the noise is easy to tell apart from the keys. A model that wins here may still lose on real text.
- `lb2.not.title`: What the puzzles do not show
- `lb2.puzzles.before`: The puzzles were run before FULL was chosen, so FULL has no puzzle scores; the charts below are PARTIAL’s alone.
- `lb2.puzzles.label`: THE PUZZLES
- `lb2.puzzles.p1`: These puzzles test the memory alone, on small versions of the models: {w} wide and {l} layers, each trained for {s} steps on the puzzle itself. Each sequence holds {n} pairs of a key and a value, and then asks for some of the values back. Guessing gives about {c}% right.
- `lb2.puzzles.title`: The memory puzzles, measured
- `lb2.recall.h`: Recall after a gap
- `lb2.recall.p`: A gap of noise sits between the pairs and the questions. The models trained with gaps of up to {g} tokens, so the longer gaps were never seen in training. PARTIAL answers {a}% right at a gap of {g0} and {b}% at {g1}. With the memory off the answers sit at chance. The transformer answers {ta}% at {g0} and falls to {tb}% at {g1}.
- `lb2.top.go`: how it forgets
- `lb2.top.lede`: Neither model has a window of past tokens to look back over. Each reads only the newest token, and everything earlier lives in a memory of fixed size that the text writes into as it goes. This page shows how that memory forgets, why it costs the same at any length, and what the memory puzzles measured.
- `lb2.top.puzzles`: the puzzles
- `lb2.top.sub`: How far back FULL and PARTIAL reach, and what it costs them.
- `lb2.window.label`: NO WINDOW
- `lb2.window.p1`: A transformer keeps every earlier token and looks straight back at any of them. FULL and PARTIAL keep none of them. Each token writes into the memory and reads from it, and later tokens find what it left there by content, through the address.
- `lb2.window.p2`: The memory is lossy, because many tokens write into the same slots and their values mix. What the model keeps is a blend, not a copy. The fades decide how fast the blend forgets.
- `lb2.window.title`: The past is in the memory, nowhere else

## learning

- `learning.boltz.bars`: mean test accuracy over 3 splits (%)
- `learning.boltz.plain`: We fitted settling machines to sklearn’s 8x8 digits, with a pixel on when its value is at least 8, and classified them by Settling. The bars compare their accuracy with the baselines, as a mean over three splits. The live lab fits a fully visible machine in this tab.
- `learning.boltz2.bars`: MMD x1000 against held-out test digits: lower is closer to real digits (means over 3 seeds)
- `learning.boltz2.plain`: We built a chain of small machines that each remove a little noise, and measured how close their samples come to real digits. MMD is a distance between two sets of pictures; lower means closer.

- `learning.common.float.aria`: a 28 by 28 picture

- `learning.digit8.aria`: a handwritten digit, 8 by 8 pixels
- `learning.digitsettle.aria`: 28 by 28 lights settling out of noise into MNIST test digits, one after another
- `learning.draw.centred.aria`: the drawing centred in 28 by 28
- `learning.draw.centred.cap`: centred, 28 x 28 grey
- `learning.draw.clear`: clear the pad
- `learning.draw.empty`: draw a digit
- `learning.draw.exact`: exact readout
- `learning.draw.held.aria`: the drawing as held pixels
- `learning.draw.held.cap`: held lights (grey at least one half)
- `learning.draw.hint`: Draw one digit, large, in the middle. Lift the pen and the machine settles.
- `learning.draw.live`: settles in this tab
- `learning.draw.pad.aria`: drawing pad: draw one digit with the mouse, a pen or a finger
- `learning.draw.settled`: settled answer
- `learning.draw.sweep`: sweep {t} of {total}. Your strokes are not MNIST’s scans, so the machine can fail here on a digit a person reads easily. Its accuracy is measured on the test set.
- `learning.dyn.blend.body`: Two networks trained from different random starts both solve the same problem, yet averaging their weights breaks the answer halfway (left): 17 of 120 points go wrong. Matching their hidden units first, which only relabels them and changes nothing they compute, lets every blend hold (right). Two solutions that looked like strangers agree once each unit meets its partner.
- `learning.dyn.blend.head`: Matched, the blend holds.
- `learning.dyn.lede`: Seven small experiments on how learning moves, run on one laptop and drawn as settles. Three of them, with what each shows.
- `learning.dyn.ring.body`: A small network learns to add numbers that wrap around at 59. The film shows its weights for the 59 numbers, seen through one frequency: a tangle that closes into a ring, each number taking its own place. Each hidden unit settles on one Fourier frequency while weight decay pulls the memorised answer toward the general rule. Nothing is left out: once the rule is learned, every number has a home on the ring.
- `learning.dyn.ring.head`: The numbers make a ring.
- `learning.dyn.table.body`: Stripes of the addition table: on the left only the 40% of sums the network was shown, on the right its answers everywhere after grokking, 2,088 of the 2,089 unseen sums right. A broken pattern made whole by a rule rather than a memory.
- `learning.dyn.table.head`: The table made whole.
- `learning.dyn.taught.decay`: Grokking needs a gentle pressure: without weight decay the same network stays at 4.5% on the unseen sums.
- `learning.dyn.taught.muon`: Muon gives every direction a fair step: all 8 directions of a target reach 90% by step 233, the faintest first, while plain gradient descent leaves the faintest behind.
- `learning.dyn.taught.sdm`: In our SDM language model one batch's gradient reaches only the memory rows its reads woke, 3,038 of 65,536 in the first table. That is how it learns, not a gain: at 20M tokens its reads still score the same as no reads (1.668 against 1.662 bits per byte).
- `learning.dyn.taught.title`: What the experiments taught
- `learning.dyn.taught.tngd`: A settling particle can do the linear algebra of learning: its average position lands within 0.91% of the natural-gradient step, the idea behind thermodynamic natural gradient descent.
- `learning.explain.classic`: The classic route. A second machine learns only the pixels (no labels). Its hidden things' yes-rates become 500 features, and an ordinary logistic regression reads the digit from them. That is how Boltzmann machines were first used on MNIST.
- `learning.explain.coins`: Given the pixels and labels, each hidden thing flips its own coin; given the hidden things, each label does. Doing all hidden then all visible is one exact sweep of the sampler.
- `learning.explain.kinds`: The machine has three kinds of things, each yes or no. 784 pixel things (a pixel is yes when its grey value is at least 128 of 255), ten label things (one per digit), and a layer of hidden things the machine uses however helps it. Every hidden thing pulls on every pixel and every label; nothing else is connected. That shape is a restricted Boltzmann machine.
- `learning.explain.learning`: Learning. Show the machine a digit with its label held on. Let it take one step on its own (settle the hidden things, rebuild the picture, settle the hidden things again). Then move every pull toward what the example did and away from what the machine did by itself.
- `learning.explain.likely`: An arrangement is likely when things agree with their leans and when pulled pairs agree.
- `learning.explain.plain`: The machine is an energy over pixels, labels and hidden things. Learning lowers the energy of real digits with their labels, and reading a digit lets the labels settle against held pixels.
- `learning.explain.reading`: Reading a digit. Hold a new digit's pixels, let the hidden and label things shake, and take the label that is yes most often. That is the settled readout. The exact readout computes, for each of the ten labels, how likely the machine finds that label with these pixels, and takes the best. It draws no coins.
- `learning.explain.rule`: Raise a pull when the examples agree on that pair more often than the machine does after a short settle (contrastive divergence, one step); the last term keeps pulls small. η starts at 0.005 and falls to a tenth over 20 passes.
- `learning.guide.dream.awake`: AWAKE: push the real digit down
- `learning.guide.dream.cap`: The energy over all pictures; lower means more likely. Awake, the valley under a real digit is pushed down; dreaming, the valley the machine wandered into on its own is pushed up, until it is a hill.
- `learning.guide.dream.dream`: a dream
- `learning.guide.dream.dreaming`: DREAMING: push the dream up
- `learning.guide.dream.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 3 · AWAKE AND DREAMING
- `learning.guide.dream.p1`: Learning changes the leans and pulls so that real digits get a low energy. Lowering them alone is not enough, since the machine could make every picture likely. So each step also raises the energy of what the machine imagines on its own.
- `learning.guide.dream.p2`: Awake. The machine is shown a real digit with its label held on. The hidden lights settle against it, and the machine counts how often each pixel and each hidden light agree.
- `learning.guide.dream.p3`: Dreaming. The machine lets go of the digit. From those hidden lights it rebuilds a picture and a label of its own, settles the hidden lights again, and counts the same agreements in its dream.
- `learning.guide.dream.p4`: Each pull then moves by the difference: up where the real digit agreed more than the dream, down where the dream agreed more. Real digits sink into valleys and the dreams are pushed out of them. The method is called contrastive divergence; a dream one step long is CD-1, the rule this page’s machine was trained with.
- `learning.guide.dream.read`: Read it as: the pull between pixel i and hidden light k changes by a small step η times how much more the two agreed awake than in the dream. When the dreams look like the real digits, the difference is zero and learning stops.
- `learning.guide.dream.real`: a real digit
- `learning.guide.dream.title`: Learning: down for real digits, up for dreams
- `learning.guide.filters.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 4 · WHAT A HIDDEN LIGHT COMES TO MEAN
- `learning.guide.filters.p1`: At the start every pull is a little random noise, so a hidden light answers to nothing in particular. As the rounds go by, the pulls from one hidden light to the pixels take on a shape.
- `learning.guide.filters.p2`: The shape is called a filter. The hidden light says yes when ink falls on the pixels it pulls toward lit, and no when ink falls on the pixels it pulls toward dark. Most filters become parts of digits: a bar, a curve, the loop of a 6, the corner of a 7.
- `learning.guide.filters.p3`: Nobody told the machine what a stroke is. Strokes are what let its one-step dreams look like real digits. The INSPECT tool further down draws all 500 filters this machine learned.
- `learning.guide.filters.title`: A hidden light becomes a stroke detector
- `learning.guide.lights.cap`: Pixels on the left, hidden lights in the middle, labels on the right. Every line is a pull. The hidden lights flicker because they are decided again and again.
- `learning.guide.lights.hidden`: hidden
- `learning.guide.lights.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 1 · THE LIGHTS
- `learning.guide.lights.labels`: labels
- `learning.guide.lights.p1`: Picture the machine as a set of lights, each of which says yes or no. The rest of this page calls each light a thing. There are three kinds, and each kind has one job.
- `learning.guide.lights.p2`: The 784 pixel lights hold the picture: a pixel is yes where the ink is. The ten label lights name the digit, one for each of 0 to 9. The hidden lights, 500 of them in the machine on this page, are given no job at all; the machine learns what to use them for.
- `learning.guide.lights.p3`: Every hidden light is joined to every pixel and every label, and no two lights of the same kind are joined. That restriction gives the machine its name, a restricted Boltzmann machine, and it lets all the hidden lights be decided at once.
- `learning.guide.lights.pixels`: pixels
- `learning.guide.lights.title`: A machine made of lights
- `learning.guide.numbers.cap`: Three numbers from this page on one scale from 0 to 100: chance, the plain baseline, and the machine, each the share of the 10,000 test digits read correctly.
- `learning.guide.numbers.chance`: shuffled labels (chance)
- `learning.guide.numbers.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 8 · THE NUMBERS
- `learning.guide.numbers.logistic`: logistic regression
- `learning.guide.numbers.machine`: the machine, settled
- `learning.guide.numbers.p1`: An accuracy is the share of the 10,000 test digits read correctly. The machine never saw those digits while it learned, so the number measures what it learned rather than what it memorised.
- `learning.guide.numbers.p2`: Every result names its readout. Settled means counted from a live settle, coins and all; exact means computed with no coins. The gap between the two is the cost of reading by settling.
- `learning.guide.numbers.p3`: Two fixed points stand beside every result. Logistic regression on the same black and white pixels is the plain baseline a learner should beat. A machine trained on shuffled labels shows chance, about 10 in 100, so a score far above it was not reached by luck.
- `learning.guide.numbers.p4`: A sweep is one look at every hidden and label light. More sweeps give a firmer vote, and the chart under RECORDED · SETTLE TIME shows how fast it firms. A mean of 3 seeds means the machine was trained three times from different random starts and the scores were averaged.
- `learning.guide.numbers.title`: What the numbers on this page mean
- `learning.guide.pair.cap`: Two lights joined by a positive pull, shown in turn in all four arrangements. When they agree the energy is low; when they disagree it is high.
- `learning.guide.pair.energy`: energy
- `learning.guide.pair.high`: disagree: high
- `learning.guide.pair.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 2 · LEANS, PULLS AND THE ENERGY
- `learning.guide.pair.low`: agree: low
- `learning.guide.pair.p1`: Each light has a lean, a number saying which answer it prefers on its own. Each joined pair has a pull, a number saying how much the two want to agree. A positive pull wants them to match; a negative pull wants them to differ.
- `learning.guide.pair.p2`: The energy adds up how unhappy an arrangement is. Every light that goes against its lean adds to it, and every pair that goes against its pull adds to it. The machine finds an arrangement of low energy likely and one of high energy unlikely.
- `learning.guide.pair.pull`: pull
- `learning.guide.pair.read`: Read it as: the energy is minus the leans of the pixels and labels (a), minus the leans of the hidden lights (b), minus the pulls (W) between every hidden and visible pair. The chance of an arrangement falls off exponentially with its energy, and Z only makes all the chances add up to one.
- `learning.guide.pair.title`: Leans, pulls and the energy
- `learning.guide.read.cap`: A held 3. The labels flicker while the hidden lights find their places; then one label keeps saying yes, and its count wins the vote.
- `learning.guide.read.held`: held pixels
- `learning.guide.read.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 5 · READING A DIGIT
- `learning.guide.read.p1`: To read a new digit, the machine holds its pixels on and starts the ten labels at random. Then the two layers take turns: the hidden lights settle against the pixels and the labels, and the labels settle against the hidden lights.
- `learning.guide.read.p2`: At first the labels flicker, because the hidden lights have not agreed yet. Within a few sweeps one label keeps saying yes. The machine counts each label’s yeses over the settle and answers with the one that said yes most often.
- `learning.guide.read.p3`: That answer is the settled readout. The exact readout tosses no coins: it works out how likely each label is with these pixels and takes the best. The two agree on almost every digit.
- `learning.guide.read.title`: Reading is settling with the pixels held
- `learning.guide.read.votes`: votes
- `learning.guide.temp.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 7 · TEMPERATURE
- `learning.guide.temp.p1`: Each light decides by tossing a weighted coin. Its input, its lean plus the pulls of the lights it is joined to, sets the weight: a strong input makes the coin nearly certain, a weak one leaves it nearly fair.
- `learning.guide.temp.p2`: The temperature divides the input before the toss. Hot, every coin is close to fair and the lights jitter. Cold, every coin follows its input and the lights freeze into the arrangement the pulls favour.
- `learning.guide.temp.p3`: This machine was trained and is read at temperature 1, so its learned pulls already say how sure it should be. The live settle above has a temperature slider: heat the machine and its answer wanders, cool it and the answer locks.
- `learning.guide.temp.read`: Read it as: the chance a light says yes rises from 0 to 1 as its input goes from strongly negative to strongly positive, and the temperature T sets how steep the rise is.
- `learning.guide.temp.title`: What the temperature does

Rose is a light that is on and agrees with its lean, orange is heat (on against its lean). The classifier does the same thing with the pixels held and the labels free.

- `learning.inspect.labels.cap`: its pulls onto the ten label things

- `learning.lab8.head`: the 8x8 lab, live
- `learning.lede.pick`: Pick a digit: its pixels are held as lights, and 500 hidden things and ten label things shake until one label keeps saying yes.
- `learning.loading`: loading …
- `learning.loading.machine`: loading the machine …
- `learning.missing.mnist`: public/data/mnist/ ({a} and {b})
- `learning.more.coin.aria`: A digit whose pixels light up in cyan and indigo as a scan line passes; a bar beside it rises and falls with the running sum; a point climbs an S-shaped curve to the chance of yes; then a light flips like a coin, and a mint line of its yes-rate closes on the dashed chance.
- `learning.more.coin.cap`: One hidden light of the trained machine, close up. Cyan pixels push its sum up, indigo ones push it down. The curve turns the sum into a chance, and the coin says yes about that often.
- `learning.more.coin.coins`: the coin, 4 tosses a second
- `learning.more.coin.curve`: chance of yes
- `learning.more.coin.line`: digit {d} · hidden light {k} · input {x} · chance {p} · {y} of {n} coins said yes
- `learning.more.coin.p`: Take one hidden light and watch it decide. It adds up a pull from every pixel, plus its own lean, plus the label held on. A large sum makes its coin nearly certain to say yes; a sum near zero leaves the coin nearly fair. That one rule, repeated for all 500 lights at once, is half of a sweep.
- `learning.more.coin.sum`: sum
- `learning.more.dream.aria`: A band of 500 small lights above three digit pictures. Left, a real digit in pale blue. Middle, the machine’s dream of it in pink, nearly the same. Right, a map that lights cyan where one hidden light’s pulls would rise and indigo where they would fall; some band lights flash orange where they changed their minds.
- `learning.more.dream.awake`: awake
- `learning.more.dream.cap`: One learning step on the trained machine: the real digit, its dream one step later, and how one hidden light’s 784 pulls would move (cyan up, indigo down). A trained machine dreams nearly the real digit, so the change is brightest where the two differ. Before training the dream is noise and the change is large everywhere.
- `learning.more.dream.change`: the change
- `learning.more.dream.dream`: dream
- `learning.more.dream.line`: digit {d} · the dream differs in {c} of 784 pixels · {f} of 500 hidden lights changed their minds · hidden light {k}
- `learning.more.dream.p`: Here is one such step on this page’s trained machine. Its one-step dream of a test digit differs from the digit in {a} of 784 pixels on average; the same step on an untrained machine, with tiny random pulls, changes {b}. That is what training bought: dreams close enough to the truth that each step is a small correction.
- `learning.more.filters.aria`: Twelve small square pictures start as cyan and indigo noise and, as a machine learns live, sharpen into strokes and blobs; beside them a flashing training digit and two lines, a mint one falling and a lime one rising.
- `learning.more.filters.cap`: A small machine of 12 hidden lights learning 600 digits in this tab, one minibatch of 20 a frame. Each square is one hidden light’s pulls to the 784 pixels. Every 20 seconds it forgets and starts again from noise.
- `learning.more.filters.line`: epoch {e} of {E} · {n} digits seen · the dream wrong on {r}% of pixels · stroke shape {s}
- `learning.more.filters.p`: Below, a small machine learns in this tab from nothing. Its twelve filters begin as noise, where a pull has nothing to do with its neighbours, and within 240 minibatches they turn into smooth patches. The lime line measures it: how much each pull agrees with the four around it, {a} at the start and {b} at the end on the recorded run.
- `learning.more.filters.recon`: pixels the dream got wrong
- `learning.more.filters.shape`: how much the pulls look like strokes
- `learning.more.map.1`: the lights
- `learning.more.map.2`: the energy
- `learning.more.map.3`: awake and dreaming
- `learning.more.map.4`: strokes
- `learning.more.map.5`: reading
- `learning.more.map.6`: noise
- `learning.more.map.7`: temperature
- `learning.more.map.8`: the numbers
- `learning.more.map.aria`: The guide in eight steps
- `learning.more.noise.dream`: The redraw starts from a real page. Started from noise alone, with a label held on, this machine seldom dreams a digit of that label: {a} of {b} tries with the averages of its coins and {c} of {b} with the coins themselves. Contrastive divergence one step long teaches a good reader and a poor dreamer.
- `learning.more.noise.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 6 · NOISE
- `learning.more.noise.p1`: A machine that has learned what digits look like can see one through noise. Turn pixels over at random and the page drifts away from the digit, but the hidden lights still answer to the strokes that are left, and from them the machine redraws a clean digit.
- `learning.more.noise.p2`: Measured on {n} test digits: with a fifth of the pixels turned over, the page agrees with the clean digit on {a}% of its pixels and the machine’s redraw on {b}%, and the machine still reads {r} of the {n} correctly. With a third turned over it reads {r2}.
- `learning.more.noise.title`: Reading through noise
- `learning.more.salt.aria`: A digit on the left fills with orange speckles as noise turns its pixels over. Beside it, a pink copy stays clean: what the machine redraws from the noisy page. Ten bars show how likely each label is, and two lines show the noisy page falling away from the clean digit while the redraw stays close.
- `learning.more.salt.cap`: Salt on the page: noise turns over up to a third of the pixels. The page drifts far from the digit; the machine’s redraw stays close, because its hidden lights know what digits look like. The reading holds well into the salt and then gives way.
- `learning.more.salt.line`: {f}% of pixels turned over · the page agrees with the clean digit on {a}% · the redraw on {b}% · read as {r} (true {d})
- `learning.more.salt.page`: the page, salted
- `learning.more.salt.redraw`: what the machine redraws
- `learning.more.trace.aria`: Three strips like a chart recorder, each with ten rows for the labels 0 to 9, scrolling left. In the hot strip pink dots are scattered over every row. In the middle strip one row is nearly solid with a few flickers. In the cold strip one row is solid and nothing else lights.
- `learning.more.trace.cap`: The same digit read three times at once. Hot, every label flickers, yet the count still leans the right way. At temperature 1, where the machine was trained, one label holds with a little doubt. Cold, the first label to win freezes and keeps it.
- `learning.more.trace.cold`: cold, T 1/4
- `learning.more.trace.hot`: hot, T 4
- `learning.more.trace.line`: true digit {d} · sweep {n} · hot leads with {a} · T 1 leads with {b} · cold leads with {c}
- `learning.more.trace.p`: Below, one digit is read three times at once, hot, at temperature 1 and cold, and every sweep of the ten label lights is recorded. Over 96 sweeps on {n} test digits, the leading label was right {a} times hot, {b} times at temperature 1 and {c} times cold. Cold is not better: a cold settle freezes on the first label to win and keeps it, right or wrong.
- `learning.more.trace.warm`: T 1, as trained
- `learning.more.valleys.aria`: A digit beside a cyan line with ten dips, one for each label 0 to 9. The deepest dip, the label the machine finds most likely, glows lime. Pink sparks fall into whichever dip’s label says yes in a live settle, and small pink bars under the labels count them.
- `learning.more.valleys.cap`: Ten valleys, one per label, each as deep as the exact readout’s score for this digit. The settle never sees the valleys; its sparks simply land most often in the deepest one. On a hard digit two valleys compete.
- `learning.more.valleys.line`: true digit {d} · exact readout {x} ({p}%) · settled readout {s} after {n} sweeps
- `learning.more.valleys.p`: The exact readout can be drawn as a landscape of ten valleys, one per label, each as deep as the machine finds that label likely with these pixels held. The settle never sees the landscape. It only tosses coins, and its label lights land most often in the deepest valley, which is why the two readouts agree.
- `learning.next.p1`: This page taught a machine to read by changing its pulls, slowly, over many passes. A sparse distributed memory reads the same digits a different way: it writes each one into the hard-locations near its address, once, and reads by letting those locations vote.
- `learning.next.p2`: SDM tells that memory and its cycle. SDM-UNFOLD takes one write and one read apart, step by step. A vote of the memory is the cold end of a settle like the ones above, so the three pages are one story.

## lsdm2

- `lsdm2.chat.lede`: The chat below runs an earlier SDM model in your browser. FULL, the model this page is about, has had its chat tune, and its score is in the table below; it does not run in this chat. Expect loosely on-topic text, not answers. Type in the box to open the full window.
- `lsdm2.chat.title`: Talk to an SDM language model
- `lsdm2.chip.full`: FULL: SDM in every part
- `lsdm2.chip.noatt`: no attention
- `lsdm2.chip.partial`: PARTIAL: SDM and an MLP
- `lsdm2.differ.label`: HOW THEY DIFFER
- `lsdm2.differ.p1`: Without the word table, FULL has {a} weights and PARTIAL has {b}, almost the same. PARTIAL’s MLP uses all of its weights for every token. FULL’s table reads {r} rows a layer for each token, so most of its weights sit unused on any one token. A larger table would cost more memory and no more work per token.
- `lsdm2.differ.p2`: Today the dense MLP trains faster. On one GPU, PARTIAL trains at about {p} tokens a second and FULL at about {f}. With the memory switched off the same layers run at {o}, so the memory between tokens is most of the cost of both.
- `lsdm2.differ.title`: The same number of weights, spent two ways
- `lsdm2.not.l1`: Neither model has been shown to beat a transformer of its size. Where a score has not landed, the page says no score yet.
- `lsdm2.not.l2`: The pictures show the steps the code takes. A light stands for a part, not for one weight, and the counts in the captions are the real ones.
- `lsdm2.not.l3`: The memory puzzles on the lookback page were run with small versions of these models, not at the size we train them.
- `lsdm2.not.label`: WHAT WE DO NOT CLAIM
- `lsdm2.not.title`: What these pages do not say
- `lsdm2.read.label`: HOW IT READS
- `lsdm2.read.more`: The address itself, a grid searched from two short lists, is drawn on sdm-unfold.
- `lsdm2.read.p1`: Each token also makes a query. The query picks {k} slots the same way the key did, and the read is the weighted mean of what was written there. A slot nobody wrote reads as nothing. A token reads before it writes, so it only ever sees earlier tokens.
- `lsdm2.read.p2`: Then comes the think step. In FULL, a second query picks {k} of the table’s {s} rows in each head, about {p}% of them, and blends those rows with a softmax. In PARTIAL, the MLP widens the vector to {n} numbers, gates it and narrows it back, and every weight takes part.
- `lsdm2.read.title`: A query, a weighted mean, then the think step
- `lsdm2.step.label`: THE NEXT TOKEN
- `lsdm2.step.more`: In more detail: enfold and unfold, and <a2>how far back the memory reaches</a2>.
- `lsdm2.step.s1`: Enfold: the newest token’s row of the word table becomes a vector of {d} numbers.
- `lsdm2.step.s2`: Each of the {n} layers reads its memory, writes the token into it and adds the read to the vector, then adds its think step.
- `lsdm2.step.s3`: Unfold: the last vector is scored against the same word table, one score for each of the {v} words.
- `lsdm2.step.s4`: The scores become chances and one token is drawn. It becomes the next input, and the memory carries everything that came before.
- `lsdm2.step.title`: How either model writes, one token at a time
- `lsdm2.store.label`: WHAT EACH STORES
- `lsdm2.store.p1`: The memory between tokens is written while the model reads. Each layer has {h} heads, each head has {s} slots, and each slot keeps a running sum of the values written into it and how much was written. It starts empty for every new text, and it holds only what this text has put there.
- `lsdm2.store.p2`: FULL’s table and PARTIAL’s MLP are written by training and then frozen. They hold what the model learned from all of its training text. Reading never changes them.
- `lsdm2.store.title`: A memory for this text, and a store for everything learned
- `lsdm2.top.go`: the two models
- `lsdm2.top.history`: the history
- `lsdm2.top.lede`: Both models are built from sparse distributed memories, and neither has attention. FULL is SDM all the way through. PARTIAL keeps one ordinary part, the MLP. This page shows what each one stores, how it writes and reads, how it picks the next word, and why FULL is the one we take forward.
- `lsdm2.top.sub`: Our two SDM language models, FULL and PARTIAL, taken apart.
- `lsdm2.two.label`: THE TWO MODELS
- `lsdm2.two.p1`: Both models read a text one token at a time, through {n} layers. Every layer does two things. First it writes the token into a memory and reads back what earlier tokens wrote there. That memory is the only way one position in the text learns anything about another. Second, it thinks about the current token on its own.
- `lsdm2.two.p2`: The two models differ only in that second step. In PARTIAL it is an ordinary MLP of {n} neurons, every one of them used for every token. In FULL it is a trained SDM table of {s} rows in each of {h} heads, and each token reads {k} of them.
- `lsdm2.two.title`: One memory between tokens, two ways to think
- `lsdm2.why.behind`: PARTIAL did better on the first test, and FULL goes forward anyway. What we want to learn is how far a model built only from SDMs can go.
- `lsdm2.why.full`: FULL asks a second question: can a sparse trained table do the MLP’s job too? The idea comes from the cerebellum, whose wiring Kanerva’s SDM was first modelled on: for each input only a few cells out of very many fire. If it works, a model can grow its table without growing its work per token.
- `lsdm2.why.label`: WHY WE TRY EACH
- `lsdm2.why.off`: Both are measured against a control: the same layers with the memory switched off, so that nothing at all passes between positions. A model that cannot beat it has learned nothing from its memory.
- `lsdm2.why.partial`: PARTIAL keeps the MLP, which nearly every working language model has. So it asks one new question: does a memory written while reading make a better language model?
- `lsdm2.why.ruling`: FULL goes forward. It becomes the base of the next SDM CHAT. We are trying other shapes of it now, in the shape sweep below, and each winning shape is to be compared with a transformer of the same shape. PARTIAL stops after its first test, where it served as the comparison.
- `lsdm2.why.title`: Two questions, a control, and the one we take forward
- `lsdm2.write.label`: HOW IT WRITES
- `lsdm2.write.p1`: From its vector, each token makes a key, a value and a gate. The key picks the best {k} of a head’s {s} slots. The value is added into those slots, weighted by how well each one matched. The gate scales the whole write between nothing and full strength, so a token that matters little can write weakly.
- `lsdm2.write.p2`: Before each new write, every head fades what it already holds by its own factor: {a}, {b}, {c} and {d}. A head with a fade of {a} keeps only the newest token, so it works as a one-step look back. A head with a fade of {d} never forgets.
- `lsdm2.write.p3`: The table and the MLP take no writes while the model reads. Training changes them, a little after every batch of text.
- `lsdm2.write.title`: A key, a value and a gate

## lsl

- `lsl.att.cap`: How to read it: both sides read the same text, one token per step. In the attention panel the lines are the comparisons it makes; their number climbs. In the memory panel the outlined slots are the ones this token uses; brighter slots hold more writes. A drawing: the real grid has {m} slots a head and a token picks {p}.
- `lsl.att.count`: token {n}: {c} comparisons
- `lsl.att.rule`: Sharp: any earlier word can be found exactly. The cost grows with the text, one more comparison for every token read.
- `lsl.att.title`: ATTENTION · EVERY PAST TOKEN, KEPT
- `lsl.bars.axis`: TEST bits per byte · shorter bar is better
- `lsl.bars.best`: ← best
- `lsl.curves.aria`: Five curves, one per fading average, showing how much of a token is left as it gets older. By 300 tokens back even the slowest holds about 5 percent.
- `lsl.curves.cap`: How to read it: the left edge is the newest token, at 100%. Each curve shows how much of a token one average still holds as it gets older. The cyan band on the left is the 8 tokens seen exactly. Lower and further left means forgotten sooner.
- `lsl.curves.key`: fade {d} · half-life {h}
- `lsl.curves.reach`: {n} back: the slowest keeps {p}
- `lsl.curves.x`: tokens back
- `lsl.flow.aria`: The newest model from left to right: the text, the lookback, one map, then 16 hops of a memory read and a small dense step, then the head and the next token.
- `lsl.flow.head`: the head
- `lsl.flow.head.sub`: scores tokens
- `lsl.flow.hops`: these two, {h} times over: the hops
- `lsl.flow.look`: the lookback
- `lsl.flow.look.sub`: {b} exact, {a} fading
- `lsl.flow.loop`: the chosen token joins the text, and it runs again
- `lsl.flow.map`: one map
- `lsl.flow.map.sub`: to width {w}
- `lsl.flow.mlp`: dense step
- `lsl.flow.mlp.sub`: width {f}
- `lsl.flow.next`: next token
- `lsl.flow.next.sub`: one of {v}
- `lsl.flow.read`: memory read
- `lsl.flow.read.sub`: {k} of {m}
- `lsl.flow.text`: the text
- `lsl.flow.text.sub`: so far
- `lsl.loop.cap`: How to read it: the same words go into both loops, one per step. Each chip in a summary is a remembered word; brighter means more of it is left, and the outlined chips are the words that matter. A drawing of the idea with made-up fades, not a measured model.
- `lsl.loop.fade`: fade × {f}
- `lsl.loop.ours`: OURS · A FIXED FADE
- `lsl.loop.ours.rule`: Every word fades the summary by the same {f} and goes in at full strength. After a few words, filler crowds out what mattered.
- `lsl.loop.sel`: SELECTIVE · MAMBA’S IDEA
- `lsl.loop.sel.rule`: The word picks the fade and the write. Filler barely writes and keeps the summary as it is; a word that matters makes room for itself. The words that matter survive.
- `lsl.loop.step`: Step {k} of {n}.
- `lsl.loop.summary`: the summary
- `lsl.loop.write`: write {w}
- `lsl.mix.count`: token {n}: reads 3 slots, writes the same 3
- `lsl.mix.grid`: {n} slots drawn for the real {m} per head
- `lsl.mix.rule`: Each token’s address picks a few slots. It reads what earlier tokens left there, then adds itself. The cost per token stays the same at any length, but tokens that share a slot blur together.
- `lsl.mix.title`: THE RUN-TIME MEMORY · A FIXED GRID
- `lsl.stream.aria`: A row of {n} tokens, the newest on the right. The newest {b} are lit: the model sees those exactly. Under the row, {a} fading averages; each fades its older tokens at its own rate.
- `lsl.stream.band`: fade {d} · half-life {h}
- `lsl.stream.cap`: How to read it: each token slides left as a new one arrives. Brighter means the model still holds more of that token. The top band forgets almost at once; the bottom band still holds the whole row.
- `lsl.stream.exact`: the last {n}: seen exactly
- `lsl.stream.now`: now →
- `lsl.stream.row`: tokens
- `lsl.stream.text`: THE TEXT SO FAR

- `lsl.top.title`: SDM-LOOKBACK

- `magic8.honest.label`: WHAT IT DOES NOT KNOW
- `magic8.honest.p1`: The teacher is a small base language model trained on {tokens} tokens of educational web text. It continues text; it was never taught to answer questions, and it does not know whether Paris is the capital of France.
- `magic8.honest.p2`: Its decision is a property of the words in the question, and magic-8-ball reproduces that property. The table measures the teacher against the true answers: it is at chance, and on BoolQ it is below the score of always answering yes.
- `magic8.honest.title`: This model is not a knowledge source
- `magic8.intro.p1`: The model here is magic-8-ball. It answers a yes or no question with YES, UNSURE or NO. It does not run a language model to do it. It reads one vector, the {d} numbers the teacher (SDMCHAT's best model that reads an SDM) forms for the question before it does anything else, and turns them into a decision with {d} weights and one constant.
- `magic8.intro.p2a`: The idea. JEV is a small head that predicts which experts a large model will route to next. It is trained on that model's own routing traces, so the engine can fetch the experts before the model asks.
- `magic8.intro.p2b`: SDMJEV does the same thing to SDMCHAT. We asked the teacher {rows} questions, recorded how far it leaned towards yes or no on each, and fitted a fast head to that record. The bet is that the decision is already present in the teacher's first vector, before its memory, its readout and its 129,280-way output layer run. On the {test} held-out test questions the head agrees with the teacher on {agree} of them.
- `magic8.intro.p3`: The head was taught to copy the teacher. The teacher is a small base model and is near chance on the truth (see HOW IT WAS TRAINED), so this is a magic 8 ball, no oracle.
- `magic8.intro.riding`: WHAT THIS IS
- `magic8.intro.title`: A decision read in one pass from SDMCHAT's vector space
- `magic8.k.decision`: decision
- `magic8.k.lean`: lean
- `magic8.lean.aria`: The lean axis. NO below {lo}, UNSURE between, YES above {hi}. The student's lean is {s}.
- `magic8.lean.aria.teacher`: The lean axis. NO below {lo}, UNSURE between, YES above {hi}. The student's lean is {s}; the teacher's lean is {tl}.
- `magic8.lean.student`: student {v}
- `magic8.lean.teacher`: teacher {v}
- `magic8.list.aria`: the twenty answers
- `magic8.machine.label`: THE SETTLING MACHINE
- `magic8.machine.p`: Over 500 seeds with these settings, a group given a chance of 0.98 was read {yes}, {unsure} and {no} of the time (yes, unsure, no). With equal leans the groups came out {eyes}, {eunsure} and {eno} over 5,000 seeds, against 50, 25 and 25.
- `magic8.machine.title`: Twenty answers settle into three groups
- `magic8.measured.caption`: TEST split, {n} questions; agreement with the teacher's three-way decision (95% bootstrap interval), and the rank correlation of the leans
- `magic8.measured.label`: WHAT WAS MEASURED
- `magic8.measured.p1a`: Chance agreement for the shipped student, from the class rates alone, is {chance}. A student trained on shuffled leans stays near it, and the same head on a random vector space of the same shape reaches {random}: token identity alone carries part of the teacher's decision, and the teacher's vector space carries the rest.
- `magic8.measured.p1b`: The reference probe on the teacher's own last hidden state reaches {reference}, which is close to the ceiling for any student, since the teacher's lean is nearly a straight line in that state.
- `magic8.measured.p2.now`: The small SDM read (width 256, 20M tokens) leans differently: the rank correlation of the two models' leans on the test split is {rho} and their three-way decisions agree on {agree}. Neither is better against the truth.
- `magic8.measured.p3`: The full teacher spends most of its time in the output layer. A teacher that computes only the 32 answer-word logits gets the same lean (largest difference {diff}) {trimmed} times faster, and against that fair comparison magic-8-ball is still about {shipped} times faster. Other work loaded the machine during the run, so read the ratios; the milliseconds are noisy.

- `magic8.settle.n.locked`: on alone from sweep {s}; the leader changed {c} times
- `magic8.settle.n.other`: two lights of different groups push apart (A)
- `magic8.settle.n.pick`: {w}, one of {n}
- `magic8.settle.n.same`: push apart less (A - tie, tie {tie}), so moves inside a group are cheap
- `magic8.settle.n.schedule`: geometric over {sweeps} sweeps, then {hold} held at {T}
- `magic8.settle.n.self`: every light wants to be on (A / 2)
- `magic8.settle.p1`: Each of the twenty answers is a light that is on or off. Its lean is the log of its group's chance divided by the group's size, shifted so the best is 0. So the ten yes answers share the yes chance, and with equal chances the yes group weighs twice what each other group weighs, as on the real ball.
- `magic8.settle.p2`: Each sweep visits the twenty lights in a random order and sets each one on with probability 1 / (1 + e-u/T), where u is its lean plus the self bias plus the pulls from the lights now on. Hot, many lights flicker. Cold, one light stays on and the rest are pushed off. The seed comes from your question, so the same question gives the same answer; SHAKE AGAIN changes the seed.
