- `magic8.train.caveat`: The caveat. The teacher does not know the answers. On the templated questions with a known answer its YES or NO is right {tpl} of the time. On BoolQ it is right {bq} of the time, while always answering yes scores {always}. magic-8-ball copies that teacher closely, so it is a magic 8 ball, no oracle.
- `magic8.train.choice`: The choice. Four one-pass students were fitted and compared on the validation split only. The rule: {rule}. The test split was used once, after the choice.
- `magic8.train.data`: The data. {templated} questions were written from small fact tables (animals, capitals, numbers, colours, everyday facts, and Magic 8 Ball questions with no answer). {boolq} came from BoolQ. Each question was put in the prompt and run through the teacher once. The label is the teacher's lean, not the true answer.
- `magic8.train.fit`: The fit. A ridge regression from x0 ({d} numbers) to the lean, on the {train} training questions. Each input is standardised first, and the penalty was chosen from {grid} by agreement on the validation split; {param} won. The result is {d} weights and a constant, the whole of magic-8-ball.
- `magic8.train.label`: HOW IT WAS TRAINED
- `magic8.train.memories`: Why the memories lost. A memory can only separate questions that reach different locations. The teacher's own address reaches {locs} of its {m} locations across every question, and two questions share {overlap} of their 64. Every prompt ends {answer}, and the teacher addresses its memory mostly from the last words. Both memory students put every test question in UNSURE.
- `magic8.train.result`: The result. On the {test} test questions magic-8-ball gives the teacher's class {agree} of the time (kappa {kappa}; rank correlation of the leans {rho}). When it disagrees it moves one band, to or from UNSURE: on the test questions where the teacher said YES or NO, it never said the opposite.

That gives {nf} × {d} = {f} numbers. The teacher's first matrix W_x maps them to x0, {d} numbers. The last tokens are the same for almost every question, so the two averages carry most of what is particular to yours.

## memory

- `memory.chip.hop`: Hopfield
- `memory.chip.keys`: notes under a key
- `memory.chip.live`: live in your browser
- `memory.chip.lm`: the memory in our language model
- `memory.chip.sdm`: Kanerva SDM
- `memory.chip.soft`: soft SDM, toward attention
- `memory.dense.label`: MEASURED · DENSE MEMORY
- `memory.dense.p1`: The Hopfield memory above sums its patterns' pulls in pairs. Krotov and Hopfield's dense memory raises each pattern's overlap to a higher power before it votes, which makes the valleys steeper and lets many more of them fit. We measured it on the CPU: at 48 units, recall from 10% noise held 6 patterns with pairs, 76 with the cube, 512 with the fourth power, and at least 8,192 with the exponential.
- `memory.dense.p2`: With the exponential, one update is the read that attention does: the query weighs every stored pattern by a softmax and moves to their average. Its error falls as exp(-beta times separation); the measured slope was -1.018. Lower beta and memories that share parts settle together: twelve memories in three families gave one fixed point below beta 4.0, three family prototypes between 4.6 and 14.7, and all twelve from 24.8.
- `memory.dense.p3`: These are memories of random or drawn patterns read by their own rules, so they show a mechanism, not a result about our SDM language model, whose learned store, every time it trained stably, tied a model without it, up to 2.0 billion tokens. The link is the sharpness: our soft read's cut-off plays the part that beta plays here.
- `memory.dense.pick.dream`: Forty random starts of a Hopfield net, before (left) and after (right) it dreams: a disc ends in a stored memory, a ring in a false one. Hopfield, Feinstein and Palmer let the net settle from noise and gently weaken whatever it settled into; false memories are the ones it falls into most, so they fade first. After 304 dreams 28 starts find a true memory, against 7 before.
- `memory.dense.pick.family`: Twelve memories in three families, drawn on a plane: rings are the memories, discs are where each one settles. Each family shares a part, and the inverse temperature beta works like a zoom: at high beta every memory keeps itself, between 4.6 and 14.7 the members of a family settle together on what they share, and below that all twelve agree on one point. Nothing is lost by agreeing: turn beta up and every memory is back.
- `memory.dense.pick.wells`: The energy of a modern Hopfield net holding two close memories, drawn as contour lines, while beta falls. Two wells become one at beta 6.067 in the run, and 6.014 from a line of algebra: at the midpoint the update has slope beta times sin squared of the half-angle, and the wells part when it reaches one. Two memories near each other can share one home without either being erased.
- `memory.dense.title`: Sharper energies hold more, and close memories can agree
- `memory.equal.addr`: SDM address read, best activation radius
- `memory.equal.hop`: Hopfield (same memory)
- `memory.equal.title`: 30% address-noise, P90 at equal memory (M x 256 bit-counters), log-log
- `memory.equal.topk`: SDM top-k read
- `memory.equal.x`: budget: SDM hard locations M
- `memory.h1`: SDMMEMORY
- `memory.hop.damage`: address-noise to the start
- `memory.hop.figcap`: {k} · mirror
- `memory.hop.from`: start from
- `memory.hop.go`: add noise to the letter and settle
- `memory.hop.how.label`: HOPFIELD · HOW IT RECALLS
- `memory.hop.how.title`: A damaged letter rolls down into its valley
- `memory.hop.idle`: press a button to start the memory
- `memory.hop.label`: LIVE · HOPFIELD MEMORY
- `memory.hop.letters`: stored letters (up to 8)
- `memory.hop.mirrorof`: mirror of {k}
- `memory.hop.noise`: settle from random noise
- `memory.hop.plain`: A Hopfield memory stores each pattern as a valley in its energy. A damaged letter starts on the valley's side, and Settling rolls it down to the stored pattern.
- `memory.hop.rule`: store rule
- `memory.hop.rule.hebb`: Hebbian
- `memory.hop.rule.proj`: projection
- `memory.hop.settling`: settling …
- `memory.hop.small.letters`: The letters show the limit of the simplest rule. With the Hebbian rule and the letters S, E, T and L, recall falls into one blend, because the letters overlap and their backgrounds agree. The projection rule makes each letter an exact fixed point.
- `memory.hop.small.mirror`: The pulls record only which pixels agree with which, so the mirror image of a stored pattern, with every pixel reversed, is a valley as well: E(-s) = E(s). A settle begun from noise often ends in a mirror or in a fake valley: 22.3% fake for 5 random patterns.
- `memory.hop.state`: the memory's current state
- `memory.hop.stored`: stored {k}
- `memory.hop.temp`: temperature
- `memory.hop.title`: Recall a noisy letter
- `memory.how.label`: HOW THESE MEMORIES WORK
- `memory.how.p2`: In Hopfield's memory the patterns are held in the pulls. In Kanerva's sparse distributed memory they are held in the bit-counters of random hard locations, drawn here as lights. The soft version of Kanerva's memory becomes attention in its limit.
- `memory.how.title`: Every memory here carves a valley
- `memory.keys.accepted`: ACCEPTED: the padding checks out
- `memory.keys.engine.js`: the key turn and the keyed read are computed by a JavaScript copy of the KANERVA crate while the crate loads; the Hopfield settle runs in JavaScript
- `memory.keys.engine.kanerva`: the key turn and the keyed read are computed by the KANERVA crate (kanerva::keys), compiled to WebAssembly; the Hopfield settle runs in JavaScript
- `memory.keys.forced`: forced read: “{text}”
- `memory.keys.how.label`: KEYS · WHAT A KEY HIDES
- `memory.keys.how.title`: The text is hidden, the note is not
- `memory.keys.label`: LIVE · KEYS
- `memory.keys.landed`: landed in the note's valley: overlap {q} · note bits right when read with the true key {p}%
- `memory.keys.note`: the note (up to 59 bytes)
- `memory.keys.plain`: A key turns the note before it is stored, so only an address turned by the same key starts near the note's valley. The key hides what the note says. It does not hide that a note is there.
- `memory.keys.pub`: public memories beside it
- `memory.keys.readwith`: read with the key
- `memory.keys.recall`: recall with this key
- `memory.keys.refused`: REFUSED: the padding does not check out
- `memory.keys.saved`: saved under the key
- `memory.keys.small.stranger`: A stranger who lands in the note's valley holds the turned pattern, and this reads as about 50% of bits right, which is chance. The key protects the text of the note and leaves its existence visible. It is not cryptography.
- `memory.keys.small.turn`: A key is a rotation of the cube: a mask of sign flips together with a shuffle of positions. The note is stored in its turned form, and the holder of the key reads the memory from the turned all-yes padding, which the holder knows. A wrong key turns the result into noise.
- `memory.keys.state`: the memory state, 512 things
- `memory.keys.stranger`: read without the key, starting from noise
- `memory.keys.title`: Store a note under a key
- `memory.labscrate.line`: These two labs, the soft SDM above and the keyed notes below, run the KANERVA crate since 2026-10-06 (before that day they ran a JavaScript copy, whose curves and counts differ); the recorded results further down were measured with settle-rs, not with the copy.
- `memory.lights.default`: a pattern of lights
- `memory.lm.answer.full`: Our newest model, FULL, is built another way: its run-time memory is the only path from one token to the next, and it beats the same layers with the memory switched off by more than the noise. It is taken apart on SDM.
- `memory.lm.answer.label`: THE SHORT ANSWER
- `memory.lm.answer.links`: The full story, with every number, is further down. The four memories you can try come first.
- `memory.lm.answer.p1`: Our SDM language model can carry two kinds of memory. The learned store is filled during training and read at every hop. The run-time memory is written while the model reads. We test each one the same way: train the model with it, train it again without it, and compare the test scores.
- `memory.lm.answer.p2b`: On the web test, every time the learned store trained stably, it tied. After a chat tune it came out a hair worse. The run-time memory helped one small early model, then fell behind on every larger one. Our best guess at why: the model looks back only about {reach} tokens, and guessing the next word of web text rarely needs more.
- `memory.lm.answer.p3`: The last big test has finished: this model at full scale, with its store on, beside the same model with it off. Their scores are on the SDM model page.
- `memory.lm.answer.title`: Added memory has not helped our language model yet
- `memory.lm.gap.aria`: Our best memory-off SDM against a transformer of the same width: {words}. The transformer leads at every point.
- `memory.lm.gap.c0`: early runs
- `memory.lm.gap.c1`: after the shape hunt
- `memory.lm.gap.c2`: more data
- `memory.lm.gap.c3`: the full runs
- `memory.lm.gap.fig`: Our SDM against a transformer
- `memory.lm.gap.figsub`: Width {w}, memory off, against a transformer of the same width. Test bits per byte: lower on the chart is better
- `memory.lm.gap.label`: AGAINST A TRANSFORMER
- `memory.lm.gap.lon`: our SDM, memory on
- `memory.lm.gap.lsdm`: our SDM, memory off
- `memory.lm.gap.ltf`: transformer
- `memory.lm.gap.lwide`: our SDM at width {w}
- `memory.lm.gap.p1`: The chart sets our best memory-off SDM beside a transformer of the same width, at each amount of training data we tried. Lower is better. The number between each pair is how far the SDM is behind, in bits per byte.
- `memory.lm.gap.p2`: The gap fell from {g0} in the early runs to {g3} at {tok}B tokens. Most of the early drop came from a better shape, not from more data, and the shape changed between the later points too: the hop block grew from {m1} to {m2} wide. So this is not one clean curve.
- `memory.lm.gap.p3`: Our widest model, at width {w}, reaches {v}: still {g} behind. The transformer leads at every amount of data we have run.
- `memory.lm.gap.p4`: One idea we hold: the SDM may learn more slowly and catch up later, once it has seen more data. It is a fair guess, and it is untested. The test is one fixed shape, memory on and off, and the transformer, each trained on {a}M, {b}M, {c}B and {d}B tokens.
- `memory.lm.gap.title`: The gap has narrowed. It has not closed.
- `memory.lm.gap.tokb`: {tok}B tokens
- `memory.lm.gap.tokm`: {tok}M tokens
- `memory.lm.hops.aria`: Hops against test score, memory off: {words}. Memory on at {a} and {b} hops tied memory off. Memory on at {c} hops and memory off at {d} hops did not fit a {gb} card.
- `memory.lm.hops.card`: {gb} card
- `memory.lm.hops.fig`: More hops, a lower score, then a wall
- `memory.lm.hops.figsub`: Width {w}, {tok}M tokens each, memory off unless marked. Test bits per byte: lower is better
- `memory.lm.hops.label`: MORE HOPS
- `memory.lm.hops.loff`: memory off
- `memory.lm.hops.lon`: memory on
- `memory.lm.hops.onwall`: memory on stops here
- `memory.lm.hops.p1`: Each step down is the same model with more hops: more passes through the same block before it predicts. Lower is better, so every step down is a gain.
- `memory.lm.hops.p2`: More hops still help, by less each time: {d1} from {a} to {b} hops, {d2} from {b} to {c}, {d3} from {c} to {d}. That last step is inside the noise.
- `memory.lm.hops.p3`: Two walls stop the climb, and both are the card, not the idea. With memory off, {h192} hops did not fit a {gb} card: the hop blocks alone hold about {p} billion parameters. With memory on the wall comes sooner. Each hop keeps its own {mb} MB store-sized buffer, so {h64} hops did not fit. At {h16} and {h32} hops, memory on tied memory off.
- `memory.lm.hops.title`: The hop staircase, and two walls
- `memory.lm.hops.wall`: does not fit
- `memory.lm.hops.x`: hops
- `memory.lm.mixer.ahead`: run-time memory ahead
- `memory.lm.mixer.aria`: The control’s training loss minus the run-time memory’s, by step: {words}. It rises above zero, then falls below and keeps falling.
- `memory.lm.mixer.behind`: run-time memory behind
- `memory.lm.mixer.end`: behind by {v} at step {s}
- `memory.lm.mixer.fig`: The run-time memory’s lead, step by step
- `memory.lm.mixer.figsub`: Training loss, width {w}, window {win}. Above zero the run-time memory is ahead; below zero it is behind
- `memory.lm.mixer.flip`: behind by step {s}
- `memory.lm.mixer.label`: THE RUN-TIME MEMORY
- `memory.lm.mixer.p1`: This chart follows one run of the run-time memory against its control, the same model without it, through training. It plots the control’s training loss minus the run-time memory’s. Above zero, the run-time memory is ahead. Below zero, it is behind.
- `memory.lm.mixer.p2`: It led by {lead} at step {s1}. By step {s2} the control was ahead. At step {s3} the run-time memory trailed by {behind}, and its gradients kept growing. The test score agreed: {fade} bits per byte worse than the control. Weight decay cut the damage to {wd} but did not remove it.
- `memory.lm.mixer.p3`: Past run-time memories followed the same shape: ahead early, unstable later. A training loss is not a test score, so this chart shows the shape and the test score gives the verdict. The verdict: leave it out of the base run until it trains stably.
- `memory.lm.mixer.peak`: ahead by {v} at step {s}
- `memory.lm.mixer.title`: A lead that faded
- `memory.lm.mixer.x`: training step
- `memory.lm.next.addr`: An address that learns without blowing up
- `memory.lm.next.addr.t`: Letting the address learn freely diverged. Untried: a small separate loss for the address, normalised queries, or a gradient scaled well below one.
- `memory.lm.next.card`: A bigger card
- `memory.lm.next.card.t`: A {big} card would fit memory on at width {w}, and at {h} hops or more. A {small} card fits neither.
- `memory.lm.next.chat`: A small cousin of this model runs live in your browser on SDMCHAT; every result so far is on the SDM model page.
- `memory.lm.next.fair`: A fair long-context test
- `memory.lm.next.fair.t`: Our model against a transformer that sees {w} tokens or more, on text that needs a long memory.
- `memory.lm.next.label`: FUTURE · NOT IN ANY RUN YET
- `memory.lm.next.later`: Does the SDM catch up later?
- `memory.lm.next.later.t`: Extend the base run’s kept {kept}B-token checkpoint toward {big}B tokens, beside a transformer at {big}B. A gap that keeps shrinking supports a late catch-up. A flat gap does not.
- `memory.lm.next.long`: A long-state query
- `memory.lm.next.long.t`: Build the store’s read address from a long running state, so a memory read can reach past {reach} tokens.
- `memory.lm.next.p1`: None of these has run. Each is an idea, with the reason we think it could work and what we already know.
- `memory.lm.next.recall`: A recall test
- `memory.lm.next.recall.t`: Score the model on facts seen once and needed later. If memory matters, this is where it shows. Bits per byte may simply hide it.
- `memory.lm.next.rest`: Other next steps are not about memory: more hops, more data, extending the base run toward {big}B tokens, and a second seed to settle width {w2} against {w1}, which differ by less than the noise. Learned and selective fade rates for the averages, and a reset at each new document, are on the lookback page.
- `memory.lm.next.select`: Selective writing into the run-time memory
- `memory.lm.next.select.t`: Borrowed from Mamba: a learned gate decides how hard each token writes and how fast each slot forgets, so the memory keeps the important word and drops the filler. It might also calm the unstable gradients.
- `memory.lm.next.stable`: A stable run-time memory
- `memory.lm.next.stable.t`: Plainer fixes for the same instability: clip its gradients on their own, give it a lower learning rate, normalise its output, use fewer layers of it, or put it only in the last hops.
- `memory.lm.next.tag`: future
- `memory.lm.next.title`: What could make memory pay
- `memory.lm.pairs.aria`: Memory on minus memory off, in test bits per byte; below zero the memory helped. {words}.
- `memory.lm.pairs.big`: the store, at full scale
- `memory.lm.pairs.chat`: the store, after a chat tune
- `memory.lm.pairs.div`: diverged: its gradients blew up
- `memory.lm.pairs.fade`: every head fading
- `memory.lm.pairs.fig`: Memory on minus memory off
- `memory.lm.pairs.figsub`: Test bits per byte. The shaded band is our noise, ±{noise}: a dot inside it is a tie
- `memory.lm.pairs.gmix`: the run-time memory
- `memory.lm.pairs.graded`: the same, with graded weights
- `memory.lm.pairs.gstore`: the learned store
- `memory.lm.pairs.h16`: the store, {h} hops
- `memory.lm.pairs.h32`: the store, {h} hops
- `memory.lm.pairs.helps`: ← the memory helps
- `memory.lm.pairs.hurts`: the memory hurts →
- `memory.lm.pairs.k64`: {n} locations awake, not {k}
- `memory.lm.pairs.label`: MEMORY ON AGAINST MEMORY OFF
- `memory.lm.pairs.n400`: width {w} · {tok}M tokens
- `memory.lm.pairs.nbig`: width {w} · {h} hops · {tok}B tokens
- `memory.lm.pairs.nchat`: chat test · width {w} · {tok}B tokens
- `memory.lm.pairs.noise`: Why ±{noise}? The same model run on two different machines scores up to {noise} apart. We call a smaller difference a tie, never a win or a loss.
- `memory.lm.pairs.nold2`: width {w} · an older setup
- `memory.lm.pairs.old`: an early, narrow model
- `memory.lm.pairs.p1`: Each row is one pair of runs: the same model trained twice, once with a memory and once without, everything else equal. The dot is the memory-on score minus the memory-off score. Left of zero means the memory helped. Right of zero means it hurt.
- `memory.lm.pairs.perhop`: one store per hop
- `memory.lm.pairs.qgrad`: the address learns freely
- `memory.lm.pairs.read2`: What we conclude. On the web test the learned store has never moved the score. Seven versions, from {a}M to {b}B tokens of training, all land inside the noise. After a chat tune, the store scored {chat} worse on the chat test, just outside the noise. We had predicted a tie; that prediction missed, by a hair. Letting its address learn freely made training blow up. The run-time memory helped the early narrow model by {old}, and hurt every wider model, by {lo} to {hi}.
- `memory.lm.pairs.score`: Every score here is test bits per byte: the average number of bits the model needs to guess each byte of {n} tokens of text it never trained on. Lower is better.
- `memory.lm.pairs.slr`: the store learning {x} times faster
- `memory.lm.pairs.title`: Every pair, side by side
- `memory.lm.pairs.wd`: fading, plus weight decay
- `memory.lm.pairs.wide`: the wide-block model
- `memory.lm.pairs.win`: the store at window {win}
- `memory.lm.pairs.x`: memory on minus memory off, test bits per byte
- `memory.lm.run.chat`: One more pair has finished: the two {tok}B-token window-{win} models, tuned for chat. On the chat test, memory off went from {a} to {b} and memory on from {c} to {d}: memory on is {gap} worse, just outside the noise. On the web test they still tie ({e} on, {f} off). We had predicted a tie at chat; that missed by a hair.
- `memory.lm.run.done`: Both have finished. Their scores, with every run before them, are on the SDM model page.
- `memory.lm.run.label`: THE LAST BIG TEST
- `memory.lm.run.p1`: The base run is this model at full scale: memory on, width {w}, {h} hops, a hop block {mlp} wide, a {win}-token window, {tok}B tokens, on {g} GPUs. Its twin is the same model with memory off: same data, same order, same code.
- `memory.lm.run.p3`: What we predicted before either finished: the store ties memory off at full scale, within {noise}; the longer window beats the window-{w} model; and the transformer stays ahead.
- `memory.lm.run.p6`: Stopped with no score: a {tok}B-token run at width {w} that asked whether more data still helps the {h}-hop shape ended at step {s} of {n}, so that question is still open.
- `memory.lm.run.title`: Memory on and memory off, at full scale
- `memory.lm.src`: source: each run’s logged test score
- `memory.lm.srctrain`: source: the two runs’ logged training losses
- `memory.lm.two.aria`: Left: the learned store, a grid of locations filled by training. At each hop a few locations wake and are read; nothing is written. Right: the run-time memory. Each token of the text writes into a few slots, the slots fade, and later tokens read them.
- `memory.lm.two.cost`: Memory is not free. At width {w}, the model with its store on trained at {on} thousand tokens a second. The same model with it off ran at {off} thousand. Memory on runs at {x} times the speed.
- `memory.lm.two.fig`: Two kinds of memory, side by side
- `memory.lm.two.figsub`: A drawing of how each one works, not a measurement
- `memory.lm.two.hop`: hop {h}
- `memory.lm.two.l1`: written by training, then fixed
- `memory.lm.two.l2`: read at every hop: about {k} of {m} locations wake
- `memory.lm.two.l3`: never sees the text it is reading
- `memory.lm.two.label`: OUR LANGUAGE MODEL · TWO KINDS OF MEMORY
- `memory.lm.two.lh`: the learned store
- `memory.lm.two.lstat`: in the base run · ties memory off
- `memory.lm.two.p1`: Our SDM language model reads text and predicts the next token. In between, it passes one vector through the same block again and again. Each pass is a hop. A memory is something a hop can look things up in, and the model has room for two.
- `memory.lm.two.p2`: The learned store holds what training taught: {m} locations, written by gradient descent like every other weight. At each hop about {k} of them wake and are read. It never sees the text in front of it. It is in the base run.
- `memory.lm.two.p3`: The run-time memory is written while the model reads. Each token writes into the slots its address picks, and a later token reads what earlier ones left there, faded by each head’s own decay. It is the one part that could let the model reach far back. It is not in the base run, for the reasons below.
- `memory.lm.two.r1`: written while reading, token by token
- `memory.lm.two.r2`: a later token reads what earlier ones wrote
- `memory.lm.two.r3`: old writes fade, at each head’s own rate
- `memory.lm.two.rh`: the run-time memory
- `memory.lm.two.rstat`: not in the base run · fell behind
- `memory.lm.two.text`: the text being read, one token at a time
- `memory.lm.two.title`: A store it learns, and a memory it writes as it reads
- `memory.lm.why.label`: WHY MEMORY MAY NOT PAY ON THIS TEST
- `memory.lm.why.p1`: Our model has no context window in the transformer sense. It sees the last {back} tokens exactly, plus {avg} fading averages of everything before them. The slowest average loses half of what it holds in about {half} tokens, so its real reach is about {reach} tokens. The lookback page tells the full story.
- `memory.lm.why.p2`: Guessing the next token of web text is mostly a local job. The last few words carry most of the answer, and a memory of facts from far back has little to add to that score.
- `memory.lm.why.p3`: Our yardstick shares the blind spot. The transformer we compare against trains on windows of {tw} tokens. Neither model has been asked to remember something from long ago.
- `memory.lm.why.p4`: A recall test would ask exactly that: a fact seen once, needed later. Bits per byte averages over every byte, so it can hide a memory that matters on the few bytes where recall counts. We have not run that test yet.
- `memory.lm.why.p5`: One more clue, with memory off: a longer training window helps up to about {w2} tokens ({a} at {w1}, {b} at {w2}), then goes flat ({c} at {w3}) and then worse ({d} at {w4}). Our reading, untested: at window {w1} many positions sit near the start of their example, where the fading averages have not filled yet. Past {w2}, almost every position already has its full lookback. That fits a reach of a few hundred tokens at most.
- `memory.lm.why.title`: The model looks back about {reach} tokens
- `memory.locM`: hard locations M
- `memory.noise`: noise in the address
- `memory.noisefmt`: {p}% of bits flipped
- `memory.obars.aria`: overlap with each stored pattern
- `memory.of`: {a} of {b}
- `memory.picker.aria`: stored patterns
- `memory.pulls.h`: Reading by content instead of by address
- `memory.pulls.small`: The pulls read wakes a location when its stored counters agree with the current state; the address plays no part. The sealed threshold scaled to the store's density failed, because rows holding one other pattern wake together. Waking exactly the k = p M rows with the largest agreement worked everywhere.
- `memory.race.aria`: the address shares 3 hard locations with its target and 4 with a rival; the rival wins the read
- `memory.race.bars`: reads that failed, by the target's shared hard locations minus the best rival's (M 1e5, r 107, T 5)
- `memory.race.cap`: The stored pattern whose wake set shares the most hard locations with the address wins every bit where it differs.
- `memory.race.ring`: dashed: the address's wake ring
- `memory.race.rival`: rival: shares 4
- `memory.race.smap`: Every S-map variant treats the other patterns as fresh noise on every bit and predicts about 0.1% failure. The RACE predictor, built after the data, treats them as whole patterns and lands close to the measured failures.
- `memory.race.subtitle`: a drawing of the mechanism, not a measurement
- `memory.race.target`: target: shares 3
- `memory.race.title`: The race between whole patterns
- `memory.radius.cap30`: 30% address-noise: P90 capacity against hard locations M, log-log
- `memory.radius.cap40`: 40% address-noise: P90 capacity against hard locations M (cd0.4 activation radius)
- `memory.radius.cd03`: cd0.3 activation radius
- `memory.radius.cd04`: cd0.4 activation radius
- `memory.radius.control`: control · {c}
- `memory.radius.failed`: {a} of {b} failed ({p}%)
- `memory.radius.front10`: P90 at 10% address-noise against the activation radius, log y
- `memory.radius.front30`: P90 at 30% address-noise against the activation radius, log y (zeros left out)
- `memory.radius.full`: Capacity at every activation radius and M (the full tables)
- `memory.radius.h.front`: Capacity against the activation radius, at 10% and 30% address-noise
- `memory.radius.h.race`: Capacity stays near 2 at 40% address-noise because whole patterns compete
- `memory.radius.label`: RECORDED · ACTIVATION RADIUS
- `memory.radius.marks`: The report scores predictions as right, wrong or split; the site's marks read right as hit and wrong as miss.
- `memory.radius.peaks`: The 10% peak sits at the SNR activation radius and the 30% peak at the cd0.3 activation radius, plus or minus 1, at every M. No activation radius lifts 40% above 3.
- `memory.radius.plain`: The activation radius decides how many hard locations a read wakes. A very noisy address needs a wider activation radius to reach its pattern, and a wider radius lets the other patterns' noise in.
- `memory.radius.rx`: activation radius r (bits of 256)
- `memory.radius.small`: A small radius keeps a read clean but wakes few locations; a wide one wakes enough locations to reach an address that is far from its pattern, at the price of more noise from the others. The scale test used one activation radius for every address-noise. This test picks the activation radius that keeps an address D x 256 bits away inside the critical distance, and compares it with the SNR radius.
- `memory.radius.snr`: SNR activation radius
- `memory.rcoded.label`: RECORDED · CODED NOTES
- `memory.rcoded.plain`: A note is stored as bits, so fewer bits per character means more text per memory. The tables measure the compression and how many bytes of text come back from each note.
- `memory.rkeys.label`: RECORDED · CAPACITY AND KEYS
- `memory.rkeys.plain`: Both memories were filled with random patterns and read from noisy addresses. The tables count how often a read lands on the right pattern.
- `memory.room.aria`: {M} hard locations; {n} are activated
- `memory.rscale.eqsrc`: Equations: Bricken and Pehlevan 2021, Eq. 25, as given in the report of SDMSCALE.
- `memory.rscale.label`: RECORDED · SCALE
- `memory.rscale.plain`: Capacity here is P90, the largest stored count at which 90% of reads recall. The chart follows it as the memory grows, and the equations are the prediction we tested it against.
- `memory.rsoft.bars`: largest stored count with recall >= 50% at 10% address-noise (first number of each row)
- `memory.rsoft.label`: RECORDED · SOFT SDM
- `memory.rsoft.plain`: Each bar gives the largest number of stored patterns a memory still recalls at least half the time from a 10% noisy address. A longer bar holds more.
- `memory.scale.measured`: measured P90 (SNR policy)
- `memory.scale.smap`: S-map prediction
- `memory.scale.thumb`: 0.1 M (Kanerva's thumb rule)
- `memory.scale.title`: capacity at 10% address-noise (P90) against hard locations M, log-log
- `memory.sdm.M`: hard locations M
- `memory.sdm.engine.js`: computed by a JavaScript copy of the KANERVA crate
- `memory.sdm.engine.kanerva`: computed by the KANERVA crate itself, compiled to WebAssembly
- `memory.sdm.fire`: activation probability
- `memory.sdm.firefmt`: {p}% (activation radius {r} bits)
- `memory.sdm.how.label`: KANERVA SDM · HOW A READ WORKS
- `memory.sdm.how.title`: The nearby hard locations vote
- `memory.sdm.idle`: read from a noisy address
- `memory.sdm.intro.lead.above`: The live memory uses 256-bit words.
- `memory.sdm.label`: LIVE · KANERVA SDM
- `memory.sdm.letters`: letters
- `memory.sdm.live`: read {i} · {n} of {M} locations awake (expected about {e} at radius {r})
- `memory.sdm.other`: landed on a different pattern, {name}
- `memory.sdm.patterns`: patterns
- `memory.sdm.plain`: A stored pattern with some bits flipped is a read-address with address-noise. Kanerva calls it a retrieval address, or a retrieval cue, and the noise in it simply noise.
- `memory.sdm.plug`: This is the memory behind SETTLE’s sdm statement. KANERVA parses that statement: the settle command mounts KANERVA’s parser as a plug-in, and the kanerva command uses the same one, so a line is read one way by both. The KANERVA page shows the word list and the two commands.
- `memory.sdm.random`: random (the tested setting)
- `memory.sdm.read`: the read
- `memory.sdm.readbtn`: read from a noisy address
- `memory.sdm.recalled`: recalled the pattern the address came from
- `memory.sdm.small`: Each hard location has a fixed random 256-bit address. A write wakes every hard location within the activation radius r of the pattern and adds the pattern to the bit-counters of those hard locations. A read wakes the hard locations near the address and lets them vote, bit by bit. Here there are no mirror images: the bit-counters record the signs of the bits, and they keep no record of how pairs of bits agree.
- `memory.sdm.title`: Hard locations and their bit-counters, drawn as lights
- `memory.sdm.verdict`: {what} · overlap with that pattern {q}
- `memory.sdm.voting`: the woken hard locations vote …
- `memory.soft.T`: stored random patterns
- `memory.soft.busy`: reading …
- `memory.soft.dist`: distance d
- `memory.soft.engine.js`: computed by a JavaScript copy of the KANERVA crate while the crate loads
- `memory.soft.engine.kanerva`: computed by the KANERVA crate itself (kanerva::soft), compiled to WebAssembly
- `memory.soft.firing`: activation probability against distance from the address (bits)
- `memory.soft.how.label`: SOFT SDM · HOW THE DIAL WORKS
- `memory.soft.how.title`: A softer edge, and the read becomes attention
- `memory.soft.kernel`: shared activation K(d)/K(0) of two points d bits apart (log)
- `memory.soft.kseries`: kernel · fitted inverse temperature {b}
- `memory.soft.label`: LIVE · SOFT SDM
- `memory.soft.live.frac`: t re-fitted to {t} so the expected activation stays at {p}% of 2,000, the share the hard activation radius {r} activates
- `memory.soft.plain`: A soft memory wakes each hard location with a probability that falls smoothly with distance. In the limit its read is a softmax vote over the stored patterns, which is attention.
- `memory.soft.run`: run 10 noisy addresses through both reads
- `memory.soft.series`: softness {s}
- `memory.soft.small`: The dial turns the hard cut-off, which wakes a hard location if it lies within the activation radius, into a logistic one. As the cut-off softens, the kernel between two points flattens, and the read becomes a softmax-weighted vote over the stored patterns (Bricken and Pehlevan 2021). The match has a limit: at softness 1 the two reads agree on 99.2% of bits and both recall 0%, because the matching inverse temperature is too low to pick out one pattern.
- `memory.soft.soft`: softness (units of sqrt(n)/2 bits)
- `memory.soft.stat.agree`: bits the two reads agree on
- `memory.soft.stat.att`: attention read with the fitted temperature
- `memory.soft.stat.sdm`: soft SDM read recalls (overlap >= 0.95)
- `memory.soft.title`: From hard SDM to attention
- `memory.sweep`: sweep {n}
- `memory.top.cap`: the stored letters S, E, T, L
- `memory.top.cap.live`: settling live
- `memory.top.explore`: how an SDM works
- `memory.top.foot`: 16 by 16 lights each · projection rule
- `memory.top.go`: recall a noisy letter
- `memory.top.here`: sdmmemory
- `memory.top.lede`: A pattern is stored by carving a valley into an energy landscape, and recalled by starting nearby and settling into it. Hopfield's memory, Kanerva's sparse distributed memory, its soft version and a note kept under a key all run in this tab.
- `memory.top.lm`: what memory did in our language model
- `memory.top.panel`: the four stored letters S, E, T and L, each settling out of noise in turn
- `memory.top.sub`: Four memories you can operate, they settle.
- `memory.verdict.fake`: a FAKE VALLEY: stable, but no stored pattern (best overlap {q} with {name})
- `memory.verdict.mirror`: landed on the MIRROR IMAGE of {name} (overlap {q})
- `memory.verdict.stored`: landed on {name} (overlap {q})

The orange walkers carry temperature: they hop the hill, and their share on the right climbs to the exact Boltzmann share. Press gradient descent (T = 0) and drop the swarm again: every walker stays left. Press anneal: the dial falls to 0 slowly and most walkers end in the deeper well.

- `numbers.gradhow.eq.dist`: Above 0 the walkers settle into this distribution. At T = 1 it is the posterior, exp(-U); hotter flattens it, colder sharpens it. With minibatches this is stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (Welling and Teh 2011).
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.doubt`: Doubt: how much the members disagree. It is the entropy of the averaged prediction minus the average entropy of each member's. One set of parameters has none.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.energy`: The energy is the loss of every example plus a prior that keeps parameters small. Lower energy means the parameters fit the data better.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.predict`: A cloud predicts by averaging its members' predictions, not their parameters.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.step`: The Settling step: move downhill by the step h times the slope, then take a random kick. The temperature T sets the kick's size.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.t0`: At T = 0 the kick is gone and the step is gradient descent. With a minibatch of B of N examples the slope is estimated and scaled by N/B: stochastic gradient descent.
- `numbers.gradhow.label`: HOW GRADIENT DESCENT IS SETTLING
- `numbers.gradhow.lede1`: Training a model is finding parameters that make its loss small. Call the loss an energy and the parameters numbers on springs, and training is Settling: every parameter slides downhill, and a temperature shakes it.
- `numbers.gradhow.lede2`: At temperature 0 nothing shakes, and the slide is gradient descent: it stops in the nearest valley. Above 0 the walkers keep moving, and over time they visit each set of parameters as often as the evidence supports. That cloud is the Bayesian posterior. Where the cloud's members disagree, the model is unsure, and it can say so.
- `numbers.gradrec.label`: RECORDED · GRADIENT DESCENT AS SETTLING
- `numbers.h1`: Numbers
- `numbers.how.label`: HOW THE SPRINGS SOLVE A x = b
- `numbers.how.lede1`: A thing in a settling machine need not be yes or no. It may be a number which slides on a spring. The springs are the matrix A, the pull is the right-hand side b, and the calm point of the whole arrangement is the solution of A x = b.
- `numbers.how.lede2`: Noise of temperature T keeps the numbers moving about the calm point. Their average is then the answer, and their spread gives the inverse of A. The cloud shows both for the first two numbers.
- `numbers.how.lede3`: Every walker starts at 0, so the first steps are a burn-in for the softest spring, and the averages start after it. The burn-in is 3 / (h lambda_min) steps, where lambda_min is the smallest eigenvalue of A.
- `numbers.how.plain`: Each number slides on a spring. Settling with a little noise, the springs gather around the solution of A x = b. The average of the cloud gives x, and the spread of the cloud gives the inverse of A.
- `numbers.how.title`: The average is x, the spread is the inverse

## paper

- `paper.abstract`: Abstract. “We put the lime in the coconut and shake it all about.” The sentence is exact, and this paper does no more than say so at length, which is to say briefly. The coconut is a set of pulls between things that are each yes or no; the lime is a set of leans upon them; to shake is to let each thing in turn take a side with the odds its neighbours give it. What remains when the shaking has gone on long enough is the Boltzmann distribution. Without the lime the coconut has no up, and a tumble lands as readily in the mirror as in the memory; with it, one valley is chosen.

- `paper.s1.h`: The coconut and the lime
- `paper.s1.p1`: The first noticeable fact about a settling machine is that it applies to everything: to horses and to sudoku, to memories and to parity checks, to limes and to coconuts. The nature of the things is perfectly indifferent. Each is a yes or a no, si ∈ '{'−1, +1'}', for i = 1, …, n; and between things there are two relations, and only two. A thing may lean, by hi; a pair may pull, by Jij = Jji, with Jii = 0. We call the leans the lime and the pulls the coconut. The coconut is the structure, and it holds; the lime is the particular, and it tilts. Their conjunction is an energy,
- `paper.s1.p2`: which is low where things agree with their leans and pulled pairs agree with each other. The machine prefers the low places, at temperature T, in exactly the proportion
- `paper.s1.p3`: Z has 2n terms and is never computed. That is the whole reason for shaking.
- `paper.s2.h`: Shaking it all about
- `paper.s2.p1`: It is a profoundly erroneous truism that a machine should think before it answers. The precise opposite is the case. Each thing consults only its local field, the lean it has and the pull it feels,
- `paper.s2.p2`: and takes the side +1 with probability
- `paper.s2.p3`: A sweep redraws every free thing once, in a fresh random order; a held thing is merely left out. Rule (4) is the exact conditional of (2), so (2) is left invariant; and since at T > 0 every arrangement can reach every other, (2) is where the shaking ends [1]. The physicist calls this a heat bath and the engineer a p-bit; it is the same coin. On the three-thing weather model the machine agrees with exact enumeration to 0.0008 in a yes-rate and 0.0005 in a pair average ({n}). To anneal is to shake while cooling [2],
- `paper.s2.p4`: from ten times the temperature to a twentieth of it, keeping the calmest arrangement met on the way. To ask is to count: after a tenth of the sweeps is thrown away, the yes-rate of thing i over K recorded sweeps is

- `paper.s3.p2`: for a pull asks only whether two things agree, and an arrangement turned head over heels agrees with itself exactly as before. The empty coconut has no up. A walk that tumbles lands in a valley exactly as calm as the one it left, and in the long run every thing is yes exactly half the time.
- `paper.s3.p3`: Now the instance which breaks it. Restore the lime: E(−s) − E(s) = 2 Σi hi si, so of each pair of mirror valleys one is lower, and the stumbling walk falls into that one. It does not look; it is held. But a lime is small and a coconut large. In the mean-field reading at T = 1, mi = tanh(hi + Σj Jij mj), on a square grid of z = 4 neighbours, the chosen state is stable only while
- `paper.s3.p4`: Beyond it the neighbours alone hold a region either way up, and the lime is outvoted. The film player shows it: with pulls of 0.4 and 0.6 every arm plays the horse at {value}, its mirror image, where the same frames with no pulls reach 15.60 to 27.71 dB. The memory shows it too.
- `paper.s4.h`: Memory, and the size of the house
- `paper.s4.p1`: A Hopfield memory [3] is a coconut with no lime. It stores a pattern ξ by
- `paper.s4.p2`: recalls by rule (4) with no leans, and holds about 0.138 n patterns [4], which is 35 when n = 256: a small place holds only so many houses. Since (−ξ)(−ξ)T = ξ ξT, every memory is stored with its mirror, and from noise the machine finds the mirror more often than the memory: {value} ({n}).

- `paper.s4.p4`: a write adds the pattern to the counters of every woken location, Cm ← f Cm + ξ, and a read is their vote,

A machine with 64 hidden things, so grown (by contrastive divergence, which estimates the second average by a short shake), reads binarised digits at 93.8%, against 91.2% for logistic regression and 7.8% when the labels are shuffled ({n}).

- `poem.exp.context.note`: a fork is a k-character context the poem continues in more than one way; no memory of k characters can recite past it
- `poem.exp.context.question`: The address hashes the last k characters. How long must k be to recite without forking?
- `poem.exp.context.title`: How much context the address holds
- `poem.exp.damage.note`: the memory is written whole, then hard locations are switched off before reading
- `poem.exp.damage.question`: Kill a fraction of the hard locations. What does the poem lose?
- `poem.exp.damage.title`: Destroy part of the memory
- `poem.exp.firstletter.note`: a deliberately small memory ({m} hard locations) so that it makes mistakes; correct counts include the given letters
- `poem.exp.firstletter.opening`: the opening only
- `poem.exp.firstletter.plus`: plus the first letter of each word ({n})
- `poem.exp.firstletter.question`: Tell the memory just the first letter of each word. Does that keep it on the poem?
- `poem.exp.firstletter.title`: Only the first letters
- `poem.exp.flips.note`: at 50% every counter is a coin flip and the memory holds nothing
- `poem.exp.flips.question`: Flip the sign of a random fraction of every counter. Where does recall break?
- `poem.exp.flips.title`: Flip bit-counters
- `poem.exp.hopfield.note`: each line is {slots} slots x 12 bipolar units ({units} units); a quarter of the characters in each read-address are replaced at random; 16 sweeps of p-bit updates with beta rising from 2 to 12. Lines of a poem share their trailing spaces, so they are correlated patterns: the Hebb rule mixes them, the projection rule keeps each one a fixed point
- `poem.exp.hopfield.projection`: projection
- `poem.exp.hopfield.question`: Store whole lines as patterns and let a corrupted line settle back. How many lines fit?
- `poem.exp.hopfield.title`: Settling recall: lines in a Hopfield net
- `poem.exp.hybrid.greedy`: greedy, one character at a time
- `poem.exp.hybrid.note`: a deliberately overloaded memory ({m} hard locations, one pass) so there are mistakes to fix; windows of 6 re-synced to the poem each time; {n} characters
- `poem.exp.hybrid.question`: Let a short Potts settle over the next six characters overrule the greedy choice. Does lookahead help a struggling memory?
- `poem.exp.hybrid.settle`: settle over 6 characters
- `poem.exp.hybrid.title`: SDM proposes, a settle chooses
- `poem.exp.noisy.four`: four lengths, 12 to 64
- `poem.exp.noisy.note`: {n} starts at line beginnings; the 48 characters before each start are corrupted; "back" means 40 correct characters in a row within 160
- `poem.exp.noisy.one`: one hash of 48
- `poem.exp.noisy.question`: Corrupt some characters of the context the memory is given. How soon does it find the poem again?
- `poem.exp.noisy.title`: A noisy read-address
- `poem.exp.radius.note`: {chars} characters, {m} hard locations, 256-bit addresses: a random point is 128 bits away on average
- `poem.exp.radius.question`: How many hard locations should one context write to?
- `poem.exp.radius.title`: The activation radius
- `poem.exp.randomlines.note`: each run stops at its first wrong character or after 400 characters
- `poem.exp.randomlines.question`: Give the memory the poem up to a random line. How far does it recite from there?
- `poem.exp.randomlines.title`: Start anywhere
- `poem.exp.reverse.back`: backwards
- `poem.exp.reverse.fwd`: forwards
- `poem.exp.reverse.note`: a reversed poem is a different text with the same characters; the memory does not care which way it runs
- `poem.exp.reverse.question`: Write the poem reversed, then recite it from the last line to the first.
- `poem.exp.reverse.title`: Backwards
- `poem.exp.size.note`: {chars} characters ({bytes} bytes of text)
- `poem.exp.size.question`: How small can the memory be before the poem stops fitting?
- `poem.exp.size.title`: How many hard locations
- `poem.exp.temperature.note`: scores near 1 for the remembered character and near 0 for the rest; temperature 0 is the greedy recital
- `poem.exp.temperature.question`: Draw each character from the memory's scores instead of taking the best. How far does it get?
- `poem.exp.temperature.title`: Sampling instead of choosing
- `poem.exp.writes.all`: every pair, once
- `poem.exp.writes.err1`: only mistakes, 1 pass
- `poem.exp.writes.err2`: only mistakes, 2 passes
- `poem.exp.writes.err4`: only mistakes, 4 passes
- `poem.exp.writes.note`: every other card uses "only mistakes, 2 passes"; the full recital uses 4
- `poem.exp.writes.question`: Kanerva writes every pattern. What if the memory writes a character only when it would read it back wrong?
- `poem.exp.writes.title`: Write everything, or write only mistakes

- `poem.page.compose.lede.now`: The epic composer in the poem dropdown is EP12. It is scored against the same network trained on web text in place of the epics (FW12, the web-prose model in the dropdown) and against the network before either (BASE), on epic lines none of them saw and on web text.

- `poem.page.empty`: Give the model a title or a first line and press write. It will write from one of the sample titles as soon as it has loaded.
- `poem.page.epics.label`: THE POEM LAB · THE EPICS
- `poem.page.epics.lede`: Each epic was written into its own memory ahead of time, one character at a time, by the same machine as the recital, then frozen into a file. Load one, choose a line, and the memory says what comes next.
- `poem.page.epics.title`: One Kanerva memory per epic, asked from any line
- `poem.page.error`: error: {message}
- `poem.page.exp.label`: THE POEM LAB · EXPERIMENTS
- `poem.page.exp.lede`: Each card builds its own small memory from an excerpt of the poem and measures one thing. The cards run one after another in a second worker once they come into view: the first results take a few seconds, the last a minute or two.
- `poem.page.exp.title`: Ways to remember a poem, each run live in this tab
- `poem.page.film.label`: THE POEM LAB · THE FILM
- `poem.page.film.title`: A memory remembering the poem, as a silent picture of settles
- `poem.page.how.bind`: Multiplying by the address before storing binds the character to its context. A write made at the same address reads back as its code; writes made far away read back as noise, which sums toward zero. Without that binding a frequent character such as the space drowned every other one.
- `poem.page.how.errdriven`: The memory writes a character only when it would read it back wrong (error-driven), and passes over the poem up to {passes} times. Experiment 4 compares this with writing everything.
- `poem.page.how.greedy`: The recital is greedy: each recalled character joins the context for the next. One error makes a context the memory never saw, so the recital is only as good as its weakest step. The rollout measures that.
- `poem.page.how.hybrid`: The settle hybrid holds the next six characters at once and resamples them with a Gibbs schedule whose temperature falls, scoring each choice by how confidently the memory reads the characters after it.
- `poem.page.how.label`: HOW THE MEMORY WORKS
- `poem.page.how.lede1`: The memory holds {m} hard locations, each a random 256-bit address with 256 counters. To store the poem it walks through it one character at a time.
- `poem.page.how.lede2`: The 48 characters before each position are hashed into a 256-bit address. Every location within Hamming distance {radius} of that address (about 80 of them) adds the next character's random code of +1 and -1 to its counters, multiplied entry by entry by the address read as +1 and -1.
- `poem.page.how.lede3`: To recall, the memory forms the address of the context it has, sums the counters of the locations near it, multiplies by the same address again, and picks the character whose code the sum resembles most.
- `poem.page.how.title`: Kanerva's sparse distributed memory, used as a recitation machine
- `poem.page.howl.missing`: Howl: the dev server did not find the local file, so the page uses a public-domain poem.

- `poem.page.page.mintokens`: the poem cannot end before {n} tokens: until then the end-of-text and special tokens are removed from the draw
- `poem.page.page.newline`: every newline the model writes is a line break here, and a blank line is a stanza break
- `poem.page.page.nudge`: the line-break nudge · once the current line has {n} tokens, +{s} (plus 0.5 per extra token) is added to the newline token's logit{stanza}. It changes which token is drawn, never the model; set it to off to see only the model's own line breaks

- `poem.page.page.stanza`: , and every {k}th line to the blank-line token's instead

## privacy

- `privacy.browser.clear`: You can remove all of it at once by clearing this site’s data in your browser’s settings.
- `privacy.browser.groups`: The site keeps a few small things in your browser so that your choices hold on the next page or the next visit. They fall into the groups below. None of them is used for advertising or to follow you across other sites, and none is sent anywhere by default.
- `privacy.browser.label`: IN YOUR BROWSER
- `privacy.browser.memory`: Some things live only in the page’s memory and are gone when you reload: your ADJUST choices on the home hero, the pointer and key timings the contact page records, and the random visit id a rating carries.
- `privacy.browser.title`: What the site keeps in your browser
- `privacy.check.gate`: A score of 0.6 or more sends the message. A lower score does not end anything: a small puzzle opens, you slide a loose piece until it fits its cut-out, and then the message goes. The server draws the puzzle and keeps its answer. It also turns a message away when the hidden field is filled and the score is under 0.2.
- `privacy.check.h`: How the check tells a hand from a script
- `privacy.check.note`: Our own check, used on this contact page only. In the browser it records pointer positions with times and key timings (never which keys), in memory. Pointer: the trace is cut into strokes at pauses and each stroke is measured for straightness, a rise-and-fall speed profile, smooth speed changes, speed spread, sharp turns, hand tremor, the walk exponent (1 for a random walk, exactly 2 for a ruler line, a hand is neither), sample timing, pauses and slowing before clicks. Keyboard: spread of the gaps between keys, key hold times, corrections and Tab moves, so a keyboard or screen-reader user passes without a mouse. Each measure maps to 0..1 and a weighted mean gives the score; the larger of the two paths counts. A hidden field and a minimum time before sending are cheap extras. Only the score and these reasons are sent; the trace is dropped when the page closes.
- `privacy.contact.intro`: The contact form sends a message only when you press send. A quick check that you are a person runs while you are on that page.
- `privacy.contact.label`: THE CONTACT FORM
- `privacy.contact.mail`: The email is delivered by Resend, a mail delivery service, which handles it under its own terms. Its reply address is yours, so an answer comes back to you.
- `privacy.contact.p1`: The pointer check runs in your browser. It keeps pointer positions with their times, and the time of each key press with its kind (a character, a correction, Tab), never which key.
- `privacy.contact.p2`: Sending the form sends your name, your email, your message, the check score, its verdict and its reason lines. It does not send the pointer path or the key timings.
- `privacy.contact.p3`: Nothing else is stored. The contact page sets no cookie and writes nothing to your browser storage, and the recorded movement is gone when you leave the page.
- `privacy.contact.p4`: The message goes by email to our inbox. To limit how many arrive in ten minutes, the server counts recent messages from each network address: in memory, or, where the site has a members database, as a count under a salted hash of the address.
- `privacy.contact.p5`: If the puzzle opens, the page sends the slider position you chose and nothing else about it. The server keeps a used puzzle and a count of missed tries, in memory, for a few minutes.
- `privacy.contact.title`: What the contact form records and sends
- `privacy.feedback.gate`: Before a rating or a note counts, a check in your browser looks at how the pointer moves, how the page scrolls and how long you stay, to tell a person from a script. It runs in memory and sends nothing.
- `privacy.feedback.holds`: A rating holds its time, the set that was playing (its mode, theme, tune, beat and the other settings of the sound), your rating, the track as text and a random visit id that is new on every page load. A note holds your words in place of the rating. Nothing in either names you.
- `privacy.feedback.label`: RATE THE DJ
- `privacy.feedback.p1`: The rate marks on the home hero let you rate the sound, and WHAT IS THIS? lets you write a note. Both are anonymous and need no account.
- `privacy.feedback.sentlive`: Both are sent to our ratings server, which keeps a salted hash of the sender’s network address, never the address itself.
- `privacy.feedback.sentnone`: This copy of the site sends them nowhere: they stay in your browser.
- `privacy.feedback.title`: Ratings and WHAT IS THIS? notes
- `privacy.here`: privacy
- `privacy.members.ask`: ASK answers questions about SETTLE and KANERVA. Your question and the last six turns of the conversation go to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash through OpenRouter, a model service, which asks only for providers that keep no copy of them and handles them under its own terms. The server records the time of each answer and what it cost against your chat balance, never the question itself.
- `privacy.members.label`: MEMBERS AND ASK
- `privacy.members.limits`: To slow down abuse, the server counts recent requests from each network address and each account under a salted hash rather than the address itself: in memory, or in the members database where the site has one. Clerk applies its own limits to signing in.
- `privacy.members.mail`: Clerk emails you the 6-digit codes that confirm your address, sign you in on a new device and reset a password.
- `privacy.members.p1`: Sign-up and sign-in on the members page are run by Clerk (clerk.com), an account service. Clerk holds your email address, the name you give, your password (as a hash, never the password itself) and your sessions, under its own terms. Its script loads only once you open a page in the members folder. This site keeps your Clerk user id, the day it first saw you, your saved runs and your chat balance with what each answer cost.
- `privacy.members.rights`: From your account page you can download what this site holds about you as one JSON file, change your email and your password, and delete your saved runs, your chat balance and your record here. Deleting your record deletes your Clerk sign-in too, unless that sign-in is shared with another site of ours; then the page tells you it was kept, and we remove it when you write to us.
- `privacy.members.runs`: You can save the models you train in SDMSTUDIO to your account: up to 50 runs and 256 MiB in all. A saved run holds its name, its kind, its record and its weights.
- `privacy.members.store`: The account records and the chat balance are kept in a Postgres database at Neon, and the weights of saved runs in Vercel Blob, private storage that only the site’s server can read or hand you a short link to.
- `privacy.members.title`: Members accounts and the ASK page
- `privacy.other.label`: OTHER PARTS
- `privacy.other.mcp`: settle-mcp runs on your own computer when you install it, and talks only to the program that starts it. It sends nothing to us. Its setup step downloads SETTLE and KANERVA from a source you name, and only when you ask.
- `privacy.other.radiolive`: The home hero can join the live radio: it shares the state of its sound (THE DJ’s settings, the steering and your loops) with the other listeners, and each listener shows as a coloured dot with a colour name and nothing else.
- `privacy.other.radionone`: The home hero’s live radio, which shares the state of its sound with other listeners, is a tool for the site’s makers; this copy of the site opens no such connection.
- `privacy.other.title`: The live radio and settle-mcp
- `privacy.rights.ask`: You can ask what we hold about you, ask us to correct it, and ask us to delete it. Most of what this site keeps sits in your own browser, where you can see it and clear it yourself.
- `privacy.rights.changes`: If this policy changes, the change appears on this page with a new date.
- `privacy.rights.children`: The site is not aimed at children. If you believe a child has made a members account, write to us and we will delete it.
- `privacy.rights.complain`: Raise any privacy concern with us first. If we do not resolve it, you can complain to the data protection authority where you live.
- `privacy.rights.label`: YOUR RIGHTS
- `privacy.rights.title`: Children, your rights and changes
- `privacy.sent.analytics`: The site counts its visits with Vercel Web Analytics, from Vercel, which hosts the site. Each time you open a page, your browser sends Vercel one page view: the page’s name with nothing after it, the time, and, on your first page, the site that sent you here. Vercel records with it your rough location (country, region and city), your browser and operating system, and your kind of device. It sets no cookie and keeps nothing in your browser. Vercel tells visitors apart by a hash made from each request and discards it after 24 hours; by its own description the page views are recorded anonymously, not tied to you or to your network address. We see only totals.
- `privacy.sent.fonts`: Every page loads its typefaces from Google Fonts (fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com). So your browser asks Google’s servers for them, and Google sees your network address and your browser’s details, as it would for any web request. Japanese, Chinese and Hindi each add one more Google Fonts request, only when you choose that language. The site sends Google nothing else.
- `privacy.sent.label`: WHAT LEAVES YOUR BROWSER
- `privacy.sent.models`: The models on SDM CHAT, SDMPOEM, SDM WEIRD LITTLE GUY, SDMJEV and SDMSTUDIO run in your browser. Their files come from this site, and what you type to them never leaves the tab.
- `privacy.sent.none`: The site runs no analytics, no advertising and no trackers. Apart from the hero’s YouTube slides, it embeds no video players, and it embeds no social media buttons from other sites. A link to another site, such as YouTube, GitHub or arXiv, takes you there only when you follow it, and that site’s own policy then applies.
- `privacy.sent.noneva`: Beyond those page counts, the site runs no other analytics, no advertising and no trackers. Apart from the hero’s YouTube slides, it embeds no video players, and it embeds no social media buttons from other sites. A link to another site, such as YouTube, GitHub or arXiv, takes you there only when you follow it, and that site’s own policy then applies.
- `privacy.sent.p1`: By default the site sends nothing about you to any server. Your browser fetches the site’s own files from the site: its pages, its pictures, its data and the small models the demos run.
- `privacy.sent.p1va`: Apart from the page counts below, the site sends nothing about you to any server. Your browser fetches the site’s own files from the site: its pages, its pictures, its data and the small models the demos run.
- `privacy.sent.title`: What leaves your browser, and who sees it
- `privacy.sent.youtube`: The home hero can show a YouTube video as one of its slides. Nothing is fetched from YouTube until a video slide is about to show. Then your browser loads YouTube’s player from www.youtube-nocookie.com, YouTube’s privacy-enhanced address, and the video and its pictures from YouTube’s servers (i.ytimg.com, yt3.ggpht.com and googlevideo.com). YouTube sees your network address, your browser’s details and what you do in its player, under Google’s privacy policy. The site does not load YouTube’s player script from www.youtube.com, and sends YouTube nothing else.
- `privacy.terms.link`: The rules for using the site are in the terms.
- `privacy.title`: Privacy
- `privacy.top.sub`: What this site keeps, where it keeps it, and what it sends.
- `privacy.who.label`: WHO WE ARE
- `privacy.who.p1`: SETTLE is a small language for settling machines. This site shows it: its documents, live demos that run in your browser, and the recorded results of the research behind it. The site is run by {operator}, in Australia. This page says what the site stores, where it stores it, and what it sends.
- `privacy.who.title`: Who runs this site and what this page covers

- `puzzles.how.check`: A low energy is not a proof that an answer is right, so the decoded answer is always checked by the puzzle's own rules. Each puzzle writes its rules as costs, with y = (1 + s) / 2 a thing that is 1 when yes:
- `puzzles.how.constants`: In the factoring cost z_ij stands for the product p_i q_j and λ = 2. Sudoku, the nonogram, colouring and n queens use A = B = C = 1; the given reward G is a slider on the sudoku bench. Factoring cools with T = the largest lean or pull / 10.
- `puzzles.how.intro`: Every broken rule costs energy, so the arrangement that breaks no rule is the calmest one. The machine is cooled slowly, and the calmest arrangement it passes is read back and checked in plain code.
- `puzzles.how.label`: HOW A PUZZLE IS SOLVED

- `puzzles.nonohow.fig`: One run of 3 in a line of 8, written as a domain wall
- `puzzles.nonohow.h`: The encoding decides the nonogram
- `puzzles.nonohow.p1`: A nonogram gives each row and column its runs: "3 1" means a run of 3, a gap, then a run of 1. The machine has a thing per cell, and a few more things per run that say where the run starts.
- `puzzles.nonohow.p1b`: The first way to write a start is one thing per possible start, with exactly one of them yes. Moving a run one cell then takes two flips, the old start off and the new one on, and the step between them costs energy, so the cooling machine freezes with runs in the wrong places.
- `puzzles.nonohow.p2`: The domain wall writes a start as a row of "past here" bits that read 1 1 0 0 0: the start is where the ones stop. Moving a run one cell is one flip, and every rule stays a sum over pairs. On the survey's 50 seeds the 10x10 duck went from 0 of 50 solved to 50 of 50 at the same 4,000 sweeps.
- `puzzles.quantum.label`: QUANTUM COUSINS
- `puzzles.quantum.p1`: A max-cut puzzle is an energy, so it can be handed to more than one kind of machine. We wrote one max-cut on 10 nodes and 15 edges as SETTLE pulls and solved it four ways in a seeded simulation: SETTLE's own Gibbs anneal, sixteen copies of the p-bits tied together along imaginary time (simulated quantum annealing), quantum annealing by Schrödinger's equation, and QAOA, a quantum circuit built in layers.
- `puzzles.quantum.p2`: Given enough effort, all four reached the best cut, 13 of the 15 edges: quantum annealing with probability 0.999 over the longest time tried, QAOA with 0.987 at twelve layers, the Gibbs anneal with 0.86 in 64 sweeps, and the sixteen copies with 0.64 in 64 sweeps. A guess would hit it with probability 0.002.
- `puzzles.quantum.p3`: The four efforts are in four different units, measured on a laptop that simulates every quantum amplitude, so the numbers say that each road works on this small puzzle, not that one is faster. The copies of p-bits are ordinary p-bits, so a SETTLE program could write them; what no network of p-bits can do is a Bell test, and that is the line between the two families.
- `puzzles.quantum.pick.landscape`: On the left, the expected energy of a one-layer quantum circuit over its two angles, the best pair ringed; on the right, the puzzle it solves, split so that 13 of its 15 edges join opposite sides. An ordinary optimiser walks the landscape to find the angles, so the classical machine and the quantum one share the work.
- `puzzles.quantum.pick.lz`: Each frame sweeps one spin through an avoided crossing, more slowly than the last, and the line traces its energy. Fast, it is left on its old level; slow, it follows the lower level all the way, as Landau and Zener's formula says. This is why annealing, quantum or SETTLE's own, is done gently: given time, the state keeps pace with its guide.
- `puzzles.quantum.pick.qaoa`: Each frame adds one layer of a quantum circuit to a 10-node max-cut, and the bars show how likely each cut is. A layer is a phase set by the puzzle's own energy, then a gentle mix; with twelve layers 0.987 of the probability rests on the best cut. A puzzle whose pulls cannot all be kept finds the split that keeps the most of them.
- `puzzles.quantum.title`: One puzzle, four roads to its calmest answer

- `puzzles.sudoku.notes.p1`: The puzzle is written as n x n x n yes-or-no things (4,096 for 16x16), one for each combination of row, column and digit. Each cell, and each digit in each row, column and box, is pushed toward exactly one yes, and each given earns a reward G. The machine is then cooled, and the calmest arrangement it passes is read back as a grid and checked by the rules in plain code.
- `puzzles.sudoku.notes.p2`: The 4x4 and 9x9 puzzles come from the sudoku example in settle-rs. The 9x9 easy puzzle solves in 94% of 50 seeds at 50,000 sweeps, and in 32% at 10,000. The larger puzzles are made here: a solved grid by the standard pattern, relabelled and shuffled by the puzzle seed, then emptied down to the chosen share of givens. They are not checked for a single solution, so a puzzle may have several. The check accepts any grid that keeps every rule and every given.

- `relax.dyn.label`: FALLING INTO STEP · MEASURED
- `relax.dyn.lede`: A settle is many small parts, each following its own rule, ending in one shared state. Physics has studied this kind of agreement for a long time. We ran five small experiments on it and made ten short films about it for the home page; three are below.
- `relax.dyn.p1`: Oscillators with different natural rates stay apart until their coupling passes a critical value, then gather into one rhythm. Above that point the share in step follows a known law (Ott and Antonsen) to within {gap}.
- `relax.dyn.p2`: A ring of cells that each see only a few neighbours never agrees under a plain majority vote ({maj} percent of rings): its borders freeze. The GKL rule moves the borders until they meet, and brings the whole ring to the right answer {gkl} percent of the time.
- `relax.dyn.p3`: A network of oscillators that stores six patterns as phases recalled them {none} percent of the time on its own, and {pull} percent once each phase was gently pulled toward 0 or pi. That pull is what makes an oscillator network an Ising machine, and the machine found the calmest arrangement {fast} percent of the time when the pull rose fast and {slow} percent when it rose slowly, as a settle does when it cools slowly.
- `relax.dyn.title`: How many parts come to agree
- `relax.dyn.why.fern`: Two different starts, the words you and me, are both mapped again and again by the same four shrinking maps. Each step brings them closer, and both end as one fern: whatever you begin as, the same shape takes you in.
- `relax.dyn.why.kuramoto`: Oscillators with different natural rates sit on a circle at their phases. As the coupling rises past a critical value they stop drifting apart and gather into one rhythm, and the arrow, the share in step, grows along the dotted law. It is the simplest case of many parts settling into one shared state.
- `relax.dyn.why.memory`: Each cell is an oscillator; a lit block is in phase with a stored arch. From a third of the arch, the coupling pulls the rest into place until the whole pattern returns, as an SDM read completes a word from part of it. It needed a gentle pull toward 0 or pi to work.
- `relax.here`: relax
- `relax.hold.aria`: The side stretch at temperature 3, with Richard's half held when you press the button.
- `relax.hold.body`: The field sits at temperature 3, the workout's heat, so the pose only just shows through the noise. Hold Richard's half and every light there keeps its value through every sweep, drawn in ice, the colour for held; DHH's half goes on boiling. This is SETTLE's hold.
- `relax.hold.head`: Holding: Richard clamped, DHH free
- `relax.hold.hold`: hold Richard
- `relax.hold.release`: release Richard
- `relax.lede`: Each picture is a field of p-bits settling out of noise into two cartoon figures: Richard Simmons, the aerobics instructor, and David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH), the creator of Ruby on Rails. Nothing is drawn as a vector; each figure appears because thousands of lights lean toward it and pull on their neighbours. The workout is noise, the cool-down is annealing (lowering the temperature on a schedule), and relaxing is Settling.

The right one drops to 0.45 at once. In this picture the pose is the only valley, so both arrive; watch how differently they get there.
