- `relax.script.again.dhh.1`: Same four moves, new pose. That is a convention.
- `relax.script.again.m.1`: The heat climbs from {from} back to {to} over {frames} sweeps, the hold is released, and the next pose is stored. The home room reheats from 0.45 to 3.0 over 20 frames the same way.
- `relax.script.again.rich.1`: And when the song ends? We warm up and we do it AGAIN, with a new pose. Every class the same four moves: jiggle, work, cool, settle.
- `relax.script.again.rich.2`: I love you all. Drink some water. Settle petal.
- `relax.script.again.term`: the reheat
- `relax.script.ask.dhh.1`: So the answer is a rate, not a yes. I can live with that.
- `relax.script.ask.m.1`: ask :rain reports the share of recorded samples with rain yes. Held wet grass, 40,000 samples at temperature 1: rain 63.9%, rain and sprinkler 31.6%, rain or sprinkler 95.7%.
- `relax.script.ask.m.2`: The live class asks the lights the pose wants off, in the row beside the held band and in a row far from it, and counts how often each says yes over the stretch's sweeps.
- `relax.script.ask.m.3`: An asked answer carries sampling noise that shrinks with more sweeps; the exact answer is shown beside the live one for the weather model.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.1`: Last stretch, and it's a QUESTION. You don't ask a class "are you tired?" ONCE. You watch them for a whole song and you COUNT.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.2`: How many counts was that light on? Out of how many? THAT'S your answer. Not yes, not no, honey: HOW OFTEN.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.3`: The row next to the held ones says yes more often than the row way over there. Nobody told them to. They felt it.
- `relax.script.ask.term`: reading a marginal
- `relax.script.cooldown.dhh.1`: I like a slow cool-down. Fewer surprises at the end.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.1`: The live class cools geometrically from T = {hot} to {calm} over {frames} sweeps, the same ratio every sweep. The home room does the same over about eight seconds.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.2`: settle-rs anneal: T(t) = 10 T x 0.005t/(S-1). "The core anneal cools from 10T to T/20 and keeps the calmest arrangement visited; the range is fixed at 200x."
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.3`: Slow cool-downs solve more. 4x4 sudoku, share of 50 anneals that found a valid grid: 28% at 100 sweeps, 88% at 500, 100% at 2,000; random guessing 0%. 9x9 easy: 4% / 32% / 94% at 2,000 / 10,000 / 50,000 sweeps.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.4`: For decoding codes, the schedule itself is the lever: "What seems to matter is the schedule of the effective odd-check price: soft while hot, hard while cold."
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.5`: In this little class the picture is the only valley, so dropping the heat at once also settles. A slow cool-down pays where there are many valleys, as in sudoku.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.1`: Okay. Okay, babies. Now we come down. Not all at once! You never stop a class dead, you'll CRASH. We bring the heat down a little... and a little... and a little. Every count a bit cooler than the one before.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.2`: Three... two and a half... two... one and a half... Let the picture come up out of the noise. Don't grab it. Let it come to you, honey.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.3`: You know why I take my time here? Because the people who rush the cool-down end up in the wrong position and they STAY there. The slow ones find the right one. Every time I have ever watched.
- `relax.script.cooldown.term`: annealing
- `relax.script.head.instructor`: THE INSTRUCTOR AND DHH
- `relax.script.head.machine`: THE MACHINE
- `relax.script.hold.dhh.1`: Holding a row is like pinning a version. Everything else moves around it.
- `relax.script.hold.m.1`: hold :wet_grass, :yes fixes a thing. A held thing is left out of the sweep's list of free things, so it never moves.
- `relax.script.hold.m.2`: The live class holds a two-row band yes and raises the heat to T = {T}, so the free lights visibly move and the held ones cannot.
- `relax.script.hold.m.3`: Holding changes the answers: in the weather model, rain is yes 9.0% of the time with nothing held and 63.8% with wet grass held yes.
- `relax.script.hold.rich.1`: Stretch time!! Partners!! You two rows in the middle: somebody HOLDS you. You are ON and you STAY on, no matter what. Everybody else, warm up a touch and feel who's being held.
- `relax.script.hold.rich.2`: See that? The held ones don't twitch. Not once. And everybody near them leans in a little. That's what holding does, honey: you don't move the held ones, the held ones move the ROOM.
- `relax.script.hold.rich.3`: And it works on a question too! You see the grass is wet? HOLD that. Now ask the room about the rain.
- `relax.script.hold.term`: clamping
- `relax.script.nowtag`:  · the class is here
- `relax.script.relax.dhh.1`: It settled. Ship it.
- `relax.script.relax.m.1`: Temperature T = {calm}, beta = {b}. The same fully agreeing light now says yes with chance {p}.
- `relax.script.relax.m.2`: Overlap q = (1/n) sum of ti si: +1 is the picture exactly, -1 its mirror, 0 unrelated. It is the live overlap percentage.
- `relax.script.relax.m.3`: A valley is an arrangement where every single flip costs energy: dEi = 2 si (hi + sumj Jij sj) > 0 for every i.
- `relax.script.relax.m.4`: Settled is not frozen. The machine keeps sampling; a light still flips now and then, and that is what the next stretch reads.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.1`: ...and here we are. Temperature under a half. Nobody's pushing anybody.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.2`: Every light is doing what its lean says and what its neighbours say, and for once they all say the SAME thing, so it just... stays. Look at the two of us, babies. Nobody switched those lights on by hand. You settled into it.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.3`: You can still wiggle a toe. Once in a while somebody wiggles. That's fine. That's alive. Breathe in, breathe out. Settle petal.
- `relax.script.relax.term`: settling
- `relax.script.src.exact`: computed by exact enumeration in this browser; {path}
- `relax.script.src.release`: {path}, run with the release binary
- `relax.script.src.rule`: computed from the rule
- `relax.script.src.rule_relaxjs`: computed from the rule; {path}
- `relax.script.src.sampler`: {path} checks sampled against exact within 0.01
- `relax.script.warmup.dhh.1`: I start wherever the room starts. Convention over configuration.
- `relax.script.warmup.m.1`: In the live class the warm-up runs at beta 0 (infinite temperature), so every light says yes with chance {p} whatever its lean and neighbours say.
- `relax.script.warmup.m.2`: settle-rs starts every free thing at a coin flip.
- `relax.script.warmup.m.3`: A settle burns in a tenth of its sweeps and records nothing from them: "Burn in a tenth of sweeps, then record one arrangement per sweep."
- `relax.script.warmup.m.4`: The start hardly matters: "a p-bit forgets its start in about one sweep", and a warm start bought at most about 1.4 dB on the film grid.
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.1`: OKAY BABIES, ON YOUR FEET!! Nobody knows the routine yet and THAT IS FINE, honey!! Every one of you is a little light going on, off, on, off, like a coin in a tumble dryer!! Flip! Flop! Flip!
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.2`: And listen to me, sweetheart: I do NOT care where you start. Start on, start off, start in the wrong corner of the room. One good sweep and your body forgets it anyway!!
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.3`: And the first few reps DON'T COUNT!! We are loosening up!! Nobody is keeping score in the warm-up, not even me, and I keep score of EVERYTHING!!
- `relax.script.warmup.term`: every light a fair coin
- `relax.script.who.dhh`: DHH:
- `relax.script.who.richard`: RICHARD:
- `relax.script.workout.dhh.1`: Lean 0.9, pull 0.3. Sensible defaults, Richard. I would not change them.
- `relax.script.workout.m.1`: Temperature T = {T}, so beta = 1/T = {b}. The home room's hot phase uses the same {T}.
- `relax.script.workout.m.2`: The update rule: P(si = yes) = (1 + tanh(beta Ii)) / 2, with Ii = hi + J times the sum of the neighbours. Lean h = {lean} toward the picture, pull J = {pull} to four neighbours.
- `relax.script.workout.m.3`: One sweep updates every free light once, in a fresh random order. That is exact Gibbs sampling.
- `relax.script.workout.m.4`: A light whose lean and all four neighbours agree has input {agree}; at T {T} it says yes with chance {p}.
- `relax.script.workout.m.5`: Counting reps: with no pulls, each doubling of sweeps buys 3.01 dB. Measured on the Muybridge horse, 150x100: 15.60 / 18.59 / 21.68 / 24.72 / 27.71 dB at 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 / 80 sweeps.
- `relax.script.workout.m.6`: Form check: the film grid is stable only while J z (1 - m2) < 1; with z = 4, that is J < 0.25 at m = 0. Above it the grid flipped to its mirror image, scoring 1.9 to 4.1 dB.
- `relax.script.workout.rich.1`: NOW WE MOVE!! Temperature THREE, babies!! AND ONE, two, three, four, five, six, seven, EIGHT!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.2`: Every light gets two voices in its ear: its own lean, "I think I belong in the picture," and its four NEIGHBOURS, "come with us, honey!" At this heat the voices are small and the jiggle is BIG. Do you see the two of us in there? A little? A LITTLE!! That's a workout!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.3`: Count your reps!! Every time you DOUBLE the reps you get three more decibels of picture. Three! Every time! I have never had a class that consistent in my LIFE!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.4`: And form check, sweetheart: hold your neighbour's hand, don't CRUSH it!! Pull too hard and the whole row flips into the MIRROR, everybody doing the move backwards, very committed, very wrong!!
- `relax.script.workout.term`: sweeps at T = {T}

## repo

- `repo.kanerva.head`: It’s like Redis! But for Sparse Distributed Memory!
- `repo.kanerva.install`: test KANERVA from its repository
- `repo.kanerva.kicker`: KANERVA · SPARSE DISTRIBUTED MEMORY
- `repo.kanerva.line`: Sparse Distributed Memory: write patterns, read them back from a read-address, a copy with some of its bits flipped.
- `repo.kanerva.note`: A Rust crate with no dependencies. Its home is the {label} .
- `repo.kanerva.para`: KANERVA is a Sparse Distributed Memory toolbox, and it stands alone: its own kanerva command and its own .kanerva program files. You write long patterns of bits into a few thousand hard locations, each pattern spread over the locations whose addresses lie near it. Then you read one back from a read-address, a copy with some of its bits flipped. The nearby locations vote bit by bit, and the stored pattern comes back. It is named for Pentti Kanerva, who described the memory in 1988. SETTLE mounts its sdm family as a plug-in.
- `repo.kanerva.sub`: It’s so awesome!! Wow!
- `repo.kanerva.who`: the navigator, on KANERVA
- `repo.mcp.head`: This is absurd! People will need an MCP to explain or use this nonsense!
- `repo.mcp.install`: install settle-mcp and add it to Claude Code
- `repo.mcp.kicker`: MCP · THE SETTLE MCP SERVER
- `repo.mcp.line`: A Model Context Protocol server: docs and help, setup, and tools for SETTLE and KANERVA.
- `repo.mcp.note`: Node 18 or newer, two dependencies, MIT. Its home is the {label} .
- `repo.mcp.para`: settle-mcp lets an assistant work with SETTLE and KANERVA, in three parts. Docs and help say what everything is named and how it works, with nothing installed. Setup fetches, builds and verifies SETTLE and KANERVA in a folder you choose, and usage runs programs and stores and recalls with a sparse distributed memory.
- `repo.mcp.sub`: Imagine we want to use it from scratch.
- `repo.mcp.who`: the navigator, on settle-mcp
- `repo.note.access`: While it is private, a clone needs access: ask for it.
- `repo.private`: private repository
- `repo.public`: public repository
- `repo.settle.head`: It’s like Ruby on Rails! But for Settling - p‑bits annealing downhill!
- `repo.settle.install`: build SETTLE from its repository
- `repo.settle.kicker`: SETTLE · THE PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE
- `repo.settle.line`: A small language for settling machines.
- `repo.settle.note`: The binary is target/release/settle. The code is the {label} . SETTLE needs KANERVA only for its sdm statements (the sdm feature, on by default), and the first build fetches it from its own repository.
- `repo.settle.para`: SETTLE is a small language for settling machines. You name a few yes-or-no things, say how much each one leans toward yes and how much pairs of them pull toward agreeing, then let the machine settle: every thing keeps flipping like a weighted coin until the whole arrangement calms down. You ask a question by counting how often a thing came up yes. The same few words answer probability questions, clean up pictures, recall memories, solve puzzles and learn from examples.
- `repo.settle.sub`: It’s awesome!
- `repo.settle.who`: the navigator, on SETTLE
- `repo.settlesee.head`: It needs its own colourful neon package page like the others now!
- `repo.settlesee.install`: test settle-see from its repository
- `repo.settlesee.kicker`: SETTLE SEE · THE DRAWING LIBRARY
- `repo.settlesee.line`: Words, shapes, photos and films as a grid of neon lights that settles out of noise. One function for a canvas, one component for React.
- `repo.settlesee.note`: No dependencies, React 18 or newer as an optional peer, MIT. Its home is the {label} .
- `repo.settlesee.para`: settle-see draws every picture on this site. You give it something to settle into: a word, a shape, an SVG, a photo, a list of them, or a small film. It lays a grid of lights over the canvas, each one a p-bit that leans toward your picture and is pulled by its four neighbours, and it cools the grid from noise into the picture, then keeps it alive. Settle is the React component, settle() the same thing for any canvas. A film plays in true time, a new word morphs out of the old one, and every settle on a page shares one loop that pauses when nobody is looking.
- `repo.settlesee.who`: the navigator, on settle-see
- `repo.settletext.head`: Let people not give a whit about the theory and just render text, and render backgrounds, using this effect.
- `repo.settletext.install`: test settle-text from its repository
- `repo.settletext.kicker`: SETTLE TEXT · THE REACT COMPONENT LIBRARY
- `repo.settletext.line`: React components that render text, images and vectors as a live settle of lights. You supply the words and the font.
- `repo.settletext.note`: React 18 or newer as a peer, settle-see as its one dependency, MIT. Its home is the {label} .
- `repo.settletext.para`: settle-text is a set of React components. SettleText takes your words and your font and renders them as a grid of neon lights that comes out of noise, keeps flickering, and shimmers on its own clock. SettleImage does the same for a picture, by brightness, with a dither for photos and the picture’s own colours per light if you want them. SettleVector takes an SVG, by ink. SettleBackground puts any of them behind your content, alive on a slower schedule, or drawn once and still. You choose the colour, size, resolution and glow. The physics is settle-see’s, and you never meet it.
- `repo.settletext.sub`: This is a way in for the visual designers, or programmers who do not care about theory.
- `repo.settletext.who`: the navigator, on settle-text

- `sdm2.cost.cap.partial`: To go on writing, PARTIAL keeps its memory and nothing else: {mb} MB at this size, the same after ten tokens or ten thousand. It trains at about {tps} tokens a second on one GPU, against {off} with the memory off.

- `sdm2.cost.ours`: what {m} keeps to go on: {mb} MB at any length
- `sdm2.cost.theirs`: a transformer’s cache: one entry more for every token

- `sdm2.enf.add`: then the first layer adds
- `sdm2.enf.aria`: {m}: a word picks its row of the word table, the row becomes the vector, and the first layer adds its memory read and its {think} to it.
- `sdm2.enf.cap`: Every word owns one row of the word table, {d} numbers wide. Enfold copies the row out. From then on each layer only adds to it: the memory read in violet, the {think} in the colour of its kind.
- `sdm2.enf.l1`: the token picks its own row of the word table
- `sdm2.enf.l2`: the row is copied out: that is the vector the layers work on
- `sdm2.enf.l3`: the first layer adds to the vector; it never overwrites it
- `sdm2.enf.table`: the word table: {v} rows
- `sdm2.enf.title`: Enfold: a word becomes a vector
- `sdm2.enf.vec`: the vector: {d} numbers
- `sdm2.fades.aria`: {m}: {h} rows, one per memory head; each light is an older token, bright while its write still counts; the head that never fades keeps every light.
- `sdm2.fades.back`: older
- `sdm2.fades.cap.full`: The memory is the only part of FULL that sees the past. Each head fades its writes at its own rate: one keeps only the last token, one halves in about {a} tokens, one in about {b}, and one never fades. The table after it works on the current token alone.
- `sdm2.fades.cap.partial`: The memory is the only part of PARTIAL that sees the past. Each head fades its writes at its own rate: one keeps only the last token, one halves in about {a} tokens, one in about {b}, and one never fades. The MLP after it works on the current token alone.
- `sdm2.fades.head`: head {i} · fade {f}
- `sdm2.fades.line`: token {n}: each light is an older token; how bright it still reads depends on the head
- `sdm2.fades.now`: now
- `sdm2.fades.then.full`: then the table, which holds no past
- `sdm2.fades.then.partial`: then the MLP, which holds no past
- `sdm2.fades.title`: {h} ways to remember the past
- `sdm2.held.base`: a transformer in the next FULL base’s shape and token count, trained on the same text in the same order
- `sdm2.held.depth`: a transformer in the deeper winning shape on {tok} tokens, so the deeper FULL shapes have a yardstick of their own shape
- `sdm2.held.depthnotok`: a transformer in the deeper winning shape, so the deeper FULL shapes have a yardstick of their own shape
- `sdm2.held.finish`: the transformer in the table above, from step {step} to the end of its run, then its final TEST
- `sdm2.held.lead`: Held for later, not cancelled.
- `sdm2.held.why`: Every side-by-side transformer run waits until the SDM work is done: the shape sweep, then the next FULL base in the winning shape and its chat model. Then they run in this order:
- `sdm2.history`: Before these two models we tried other shapes. What each one was and what it found is on the history page.
- `sdm2.keys.aria`: {m}: a grid of {s} by {s} slots, with the scores of the query’s two halves along two sides; the best of each cross, and the best {k} slots light.
- `sdm2.keys.cap.full`: FULL uses this address twice in every layer: in its memory ({ms} by {ms} slots, {mk} picked) and in its table ({s} by {s} rows, {k} picked). Shown here: the table. The search scores {two} sub-keys, not all {m} slots, and still finds the exact best.
- `sdm2.keys.cap.partial`: PARTIAL uses this address once in every layer, in its memory ({s} by {s} slots, {k} picked). Its MLP has no address: every neuron fires. The search scores {two} sub-keys, not all {m} slots, and still finds the exact best.
- `sdm2.keys.cols`: second half: {s} scores
- `sdm2.keys.l1`: each half of the query is scored against {s} sub-keys
- `sdm2.keys.l2`: the best {c} of each half are kept
- `sdm2.keys.l3`: they cross into {x} candidate slots, each scored by the mean of its two halves
- `sdm2.keys.l4`: the best {k} of all {m} slots wake
- `sdm2.keys.rows`: first half: {s} scores
- `sdm2.keys.title.full`: The table’s address: {k} of {m}
- `sdm2.keys.title.partial`: The memory’s address: {k} of {m}
- `sdm2.noscore`: no score yet
- `sdm2.read.aria.full`: FULL: above, a query wakes a few slots of the memory and averages them; below, a second query picks a few rows of the trained table and blends them.
- `sdm2.read.aria.partial`: PARTIAL: above, a query wakes a few slots of the memory and averages them; below, every neuron of the MLP fires.
- `sdm2.read.cap.full`: Above, the read: {k} slots wake (cyan) and their values are averaged by how well each matched. Below, the table: {tk} rows of {slots} wake, about {pct}% of the head, and their rows are blended.
- `sdm2.read.cap.partial`: Above, the read: {k} slots wake (cyan) and their values are averaged by how well each matched. Below, the MLP: each light stands for a group of its {n} neurons, and every one fires for every token.
- `sdm2.read.l1`: the query picks {k} slots; their values are averaged by weight
- `sdm2.read.l2.full`: a second query picks {k} table rows; a softmax blends them
- `sdm2.read.l2.partial`: every neuron fires: gate times up, then down to the width
- `sdm2.read.l3`: both results are added to the vector, and the next layer begins
- `sdm2.read.mean`: their weighted mean
- `sdm2.read.mem`: memory, one head: {k} slots wake
- `sdm2.read.out`: added back to the vector
- `sdm2.read.think.full`: table, one head: {k} of {slots} rows
- `sdm2.read.think.partial`: MLP: all {n} neurons
- `sdm2.read.title`: A read, then the think step
- `sdm2.score.beatoff`: Both FULL and PARTIAL beat the memory-off control by more than the noise, so the memory between tokens does real work.
- `sdm2.score.cap`: TEST bits per byte on held-out web text, lower is better
- `sdm2.score.cap.tok`: TEST bits per byte on held-out web text, lower is better; the first test trains each model on {tok} tokens
- `sdm2.score.chatnote`: The chat column is FULL after its chat tune, scored on held-out chat turns rather than web text.
- `sdm2.score.col.base`: full run
- `sdm2.score.col.chat`: chat
- `sdm2.score.col.first`: first test
- `sdm2.score.col.model`: model
- `sdm2.score.off`: memory off (the control)
- `sdm2.score.ruling`: FULL is the model we take forward: it goes on to the full run and then to chat, and PARTIAL stops after its first test. The transformer is a yardstick of the same size on the same tokens, not one of our models. A gap under {noise} between two scores is not called.
- `sdm2.score.sweep`: Since the first test, the shape sweep found a better FULL on the same {tok} tokens: {best}, against the {first} above. The shape sweep has every run.
- `sdm2.score.tf`: a transformer (the yardstick)
- `sdm2.score.tfahead`: The transformer did better than both on the first test. FULL has ground to make up, and we measure it against a transformer at every step.
- `sdm2.sources`: Every number about FULL and PARTIAL on this page is read from the training records by one script, and is rebuilt whenever a new record lands.
- `sdm2.stack.aria.full`: FULL: a token climbs {n} layers; in each, a few memory slots light, then a few table rows light; the scores for every word form at the top.
- `sdm2.stack.aria.partial`: PARTIAL: a token climbs {n} layers; in each, a few memory slots light, then the whole MLP lights; the scores for every word form at the top.
- `sdm2.stack.cap.full`: Each row is a layer. Left, the memory: {mh} heads, a few slots woken in each. Right, the table: a token reads {k} of {slots} rows in each of {h} heads, so only a few lights come on.
- `sdm2.stack.cap.partial`: Each row is a layer. Left, the memory: {mh} heads, a few slots woken in each. Right, the MLP: all {hidden} of its neurons fire for every token, so the whole strip comes on.
- `sdm2.stack.line.full`: layer {k} of {n}: the memory writes and reads, then a few table rows are read
- `sdm2.stack.line.in`: a token arrives and becomes a vector
- `sdm2.stack.line.out`: the last vector scores every word; the best is the guess
- `sdm2.stack.line.partial`: layer {k} of {n}: the memory writes and reads, then every MLP neuron fires
- `sdm2.stack.scores`: a score for every word
- `sdm2.stack.title`: One token through {n} layers
- `sdm2.stack.token`: a token
- `sdm2.step.aria`: {m}: the text grows by one token a step; the model reads the newest token, scores every word, picks one, and its memory changes but stays the same size.
- `sdm2.step.cap.full`: Each step reads only the newest token. What came before lives in the memory, which keeps one size however long the reply grows. Then the {n} layers think with their tables and score all {v} words.
- `sdm2.step.cap.partial`: Each step reads only the newest token. What came before lives in the memory, which keeps one size however long the reply grows. Then the {n} layers think with their MLPs and score all {v} words.
- `sdm2.step.line`: step {n}: read the newest token, score every word, pick one, write it into the memory
- `sdm2.step.mem`: the memory: one size, rewritten every step
- `sdm2.step.model.full`: {n} layers: memory, then table
- `sdm2.step.model.partial`: {n} layers: memory, then MLP
- `sdm2.step.scores`: scores for all {v} words
- `sdm2.step.text`: the text so far
- `sdm2.step.title`: Writing a reply, one token at a time
- `sdm2.store.a`: written while reading · {slots} slots, one head
- `sdm2.store.aria.full`: FULL: above, one head of the run-time memory fills as tokens are read and fades; below, one head of the trained table holds still, and each token lights the few rows it reads.
- `sdm2.store.aria.partial`: PARTIAL: above, one head of the run-time memory fills as tokens are read and fades; below, the MLP holds still and lights whole for every token.
- `sdm2.store.b.full`: written in training, then frozen · {slots} rows, one head
- `sdm2.store.b.partial`: written in training, then frozen · the MLP
- `sdm2.store.cap.full`: Above: one head of the memory (the head whose fade is {f}), filling as the text is read. Below: one head of the table, a grid of {side} by {side} rows. Training wrote it and reading never does. Each token lights the {k} rows it reads, in cyan.
- `sdm2.store.cap.partial`: Above: one head of the memory (the head whose fade is {f}), filling as the text is read. Below: the MLP’s weights, a light for a group of them. Training wrote them and reading never does. Every token uses all of them, so the whole block lights.
- `sdm2.store.line`: token {n}: its value goes into {k} slots; older writes fade
- `sdm2.store.title`: Two stores, written at two times
- `sdm2.stream.aria`: {m}: the vector drawn after each of {n} layers, each layer adding its memory read and its {think}.
- `sdm2.stream.cap`: Each column is the vector after one layer, a light for a group of its {d} numbers. The two thin bars beside it are what that layer added: its memory read (violet) and its {think}. Nothing is ever replaced, only added to.
- `sdm2.stream.end`: to unfold
- `sdm2.stream.l.full`: layer {k}: + memory read + table read
- `sdm2.stream.l.partial`: layer {k}: + memory read + MLP
- `sdm2.stream.start`: enfold
- `sdm2.stream.title`: The one vector, layer by layer
- `sdm2.sweep.best`: The best FULL so far, at {test}, is the one with {setting}, against {first} for the first test. It trains at {speed} tokens a second, {x} times the first test’s speed.
- `sdm2.sweep.bestTag`: best so far
- `sdm2.sweep.both`: {s} slots a head, {l} layers, {d} wide
- `sdm2.sweep.call.better`: better
- `sdm2.sweep.call.tie`: tie
- `sdm2.sweep.call.worse`: worse
- `sdm2.sweep.cap.depth`: The depth line: layers and width, with each shape’s weights beside it
- `sdm2.sweep.cap.memory`: The memory line: the slots each head of the memory between tokens has, at the first test’s width and depth
- `sdm2.sweep.cap.others`: The other changes, each against the first test
- `sdm2.sweep.col.call`: call
- `sdm2.sweep.col.delta`: against the first test
- `sdm2.sweep.col.setting`: setting
- `sdm2.sweep.col.speed`: training speed, tokens a second
- `sdm2.sweep.col.test`: TEST bits per byte, shorter bar is better
- `sdm2.sweep.col.weights`: weights, millions
- `sdm2.sweep.first`: the first test
- `sdm2.sweep.gap`: A transformer of the same shape, trained on the same {tok} tokens, scored {tf}. The gap to it has narrowed from {first} at the first test to {best}.
- `sdm2.sweep.heads`: {h} table heads
- `sdm2.sweep.label`: THE SHAPE SWEEP
- `sdm2.sweep.layers`: {l} layers, {d} wide
- `sdm2.sweep.mark.high`: UNBRACKETED: the best is the largest setting tried, so this line has not turned yet.
- `sdm2.sweep.mark.in`: BRACKETED: the best setting lies inside the range tried, with a worse one on each side.
- `sdm2.sweep.mark.low`: UNBRACKETED: the best is the smallest setting tried, so this line has not turned yet.
- `sdm2.sweep.memtrend`: Along the memory line, every smaller memory between tokens scored better.
- `sdm2.sweep.memtrend.fast`: Along the memory line, every smaller memory between tokens scored better and trained faster.
- `sdm2.sweep.next`: The FULL base, trained on {tok} tokens, has the first test’s shape. The next FULL base will be trained in the shape this sweep picks.
- `sdm2.sweep.other`: another change
- `sdm2.sweep.others.tie`: A bigger trained table, more rows read a token and more table heads all tied with the first test: the table’s size is not what FULL is short of. The seed row is the same shape trained again; it sets the noise line.
- `sdm2.sweep.p1`: After the first test we swept the shape of FULL: the same recipe on the same {tok} tokens, one change at a time, every run scored on the same held-out web text. Two runs of one shape on different seeds differed by {noise}, so a change counts as better or worse only beyond {line}.
- `sdm2.sweep.pending.many`: {n} more settings on this line have no score yet; their rows fill in when they are scored.
- `sdm2.sweep.pending.one`: One more setting on this line has no score yet; its row fills in when it is scored.
- `sdm2.sweep.reads`: {k} table rows read a token
- `sdm2.sweep.sealed`: sealed, not run yet
- `sdm2.sweep.seed`: the first test’s shape, another seed
- `sdm2.sweep.slots`: {s} slots a head
- `sdm2.sweep.speednote`: Training speed is the median over each run’s logged steps, on one GPU. Weights count everything trained, the word table included.
- `sdm2.sweep.tablesize`: {x} times the table’s rows
- `sdm2.sweep.title`: Which shape of FULL learns best
- `sdm2.sweep.top`: the shape sweep
- `sdm2.sweep.training`: being trained, no score yet
- `sdm2.sweep.twin`: its twin’s
- `sdm2.sweep.twinnote`: The first test kept no log of its own, so its speed is its twin’s: the same shape on another seed.
- `sdm2.tag.full`: FULL
- `sdm2.tag.partial`: PARTIAL
- `sdm2.unf.aria`: {m}: the last vector is matched against every row of the word table; one bar per word; the longest is the guess.
- `sdm2.unf.cap`: Unfold reuses the word table that enfold read, so a word’s row is both how it goes in and how it is scored on the way out. All {v} words get a score; the scores become chances, and the next token is drawn from them.
- `sdm2.unf.l1`: the last vector is normalised
- `sdm2.unf.l2`: it is matched against every row of the word table
- `sdm2.unf.l3`: the best match is the guess for the next word
- `sdm2.unf.scores`: one score per word
- `sdm2.unf.table`: the same word table
- `sdm2.unf.title`: Unfold: a vector becomes a word
- `sdm2.unf.vec.full`: the vector after the last table
- `sdm2.unf.vec.partial`: the vector after the last MLP
- `sdm2.w.memory`: memory
- `sdm2.w.mlp`: MLP
- `sdm2.w.table`: table
- `sdm2.write.aria`: {m}: each new token writes into a few slots of all {h} heads; the gate sets how strongly; each head fades its older writes at its own rate. The {think} below is not written while reading.
- `sdm2.write.cap.full`: Every token writes into {k} of the {slots} slots in each head. The gate scales the write, so a filler token can write weakly. The fade decides how long a write lasts. The table below takes no write at all while the model reads.
- `sdm2.write.cap.partial`: Every token writes into {k} of the {slots} slots in each head. The gate scales the write, so a filler token can write weakly. The fade decides how long a write lasts. The MLP below takes no write at all while the model reads.
- `sdm2.write.fade`: fade {f}
- `sdm2.write.frozen.full`: the table: written in training only
- `sdm2.write.frozen.partial`: the MLP: written in training only
- `sdm2.write.gate`: write gate
- `sdm2.write.halflife`: half-life {h} tokens
- `sdm2.write.life0`: the last token only
- `sdm2.write.life1`: never fades
- `sdm2.write.line`: token {n}: the gate opens to {g}%, and {k} slots in each head take its value
- `sdm2.write.title`: One write, {h} heads, {h} fades

## sdmexplore

- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.aria`: Test bits per byte of every recorded arm, one dot per seed. Lower is better.
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.axis`: TEST bits per byte (lower is better)
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.first`: The first rounds: every arm we measured
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.frozen`: store values frozen random
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.mlp`: store replaced by a dense MLP
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.nostore`: SDM model, store removed
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.qstop`: store fixed (query gradient stopped)
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.qwen3`: transformer (qwen), 3 seeds
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.qwen5`: transformer (qwen), 5 seeds
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.ringed`: ringed: SDM read, small, one of the models on SDMCHAT ({chat}, seed 2)
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.s0`: SDM model, S0 store
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.subtitle`: TEST bits per byte, one dot per seed; lower is better
- `sdmexplore.chat.precise.from`: From the report of {src}, section 4:
- `sdmexplore.chat.precise.p`: n is RMS normalisation, BN a batch norm on the query, k_m_hat a unit-length key, v_m a value row, k = 32. The working vector x then passes a SwiGLU block, and the logits are n(x) against the tied embedding E, one row per token. Bits per byte is the summed negative log probability of each next token, in bits, divided by the bytes of text: it does not depend on the tokenizer. The vocabulary, from the model's own file: {vocab} The embedding table holds {embed}
- `sdmexplore.chat.precise.tag`: THE PRECISE VERSION
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.aria`: The soft top-k read on 128 illustrative scores: the best 64 are kept and fire with weight sigmoid((s - theta) / {soft}).
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.below`: below here: not considered
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.cap`: An illustration of the rule, computed here on made-up scores. A small softness makes the read a hard top 32; a large one gives all 64 nearly weight one half. The model itself runs on SDMCHAT.
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.scores`: SCORES s_m, sorted (illustration: 128 random scores, not the model's)
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.softness`: softness
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.subtitle`: the store's activation rule, drawn on 128 random scores
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.sum`: sum of weights {sum}, divided by k = 32 in the update
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.theta`: theta = the 32nd best score
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.title`: The soft top-k read
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.weight`: FIRING WEIGHT w_m = sigmoid((s_m - theta) / softness)
- `sdmexplore.chat.v2.first`: The first rounds measured the first of those small models: 3,600 locations, 2 hops. There the store first cost 0.017 to 0.025 bits per byte against the same model without it. Once its query gradient was stopped, it tied.
- `sdmexplore.chat.v2.flow`: The hop model, left to right. The memory read and the small dense step repeat once per hop.
- `sdmexplore.chat.v2.how`: Our hop model, the one the memory tests ran on, works like this. Each step it sums up the text so far, turns that into a query, wakes the {k} best of the memory’s locations, and adds what they hold. It does that {h} times, then scores every token and picks one. The picked token joins the text and it runs again. Our newest model, FULL, is taken apart on SDM.
- `sdmexplore.chat.v2.lede`: SDM CHAT is a language model with no attention. Where a transformer would attend, it reads a learned Kanerva-style memory.
- `sdmexplore.chat.v2.look`: It sees the last {b} tokens exactly and the rest as {a} fading averages: a short, blurry lookback, not a context window. SDM-LOOKBACK shows what that means and how it matches Mamba.
- `sdmexplore.chat.v2.result`: So far the memory ties. At {tok} billion tokens, memory on scored {on} and memory off {off}: inside the {noise} noise. The chat in your browser runs smaller models of the same family, each reading a 3,600-location store twice per token.
- `sdmexplore.chip.exp`: six live experiments
- `sdmexplore.chip.locations`: 64 hard locations
- `sdmexplore.chip.radius`: activation radius 12
- `sdmexplore.chip.words`: 32-bit words
- `sdmexplore.ex.close.p`: Kanerva’s two comparisons. A computer’s random access memory: one address wakes one location; here one address wakes several, and the several share what they hold. And the cerebellum: he reads its granule cells as the hard locations and the synapses on its Purkinje cells as the bit-counters, a memory nature built.
- `sdmexplore.ex.kicker`: the explainer · in Kanerva’s words
- `sdmexplore.ex.lecture.neural`: his Neural Computation lecture
- `sdmexplore.ex.lecture.redwood`: his lecture at the Redwood Center, Berkeley
- `sdmexplore.ex.lecture.stanford`: his Stanford seminar, 2017
- `sdmexplore.ex.lede`: Pentti Kanerva published this memory in 1988. {n}-bit words, {M} hard locations, three stored patterns, :cat :dog :owl.
- `sdmexplore.ex.quote.ref`: Kanerva, {lecture}, at {time}
- `sdmexplore.ex.s1.p`: Everything the memory stores or reads is a pattern of bits, here the {n} bits of :cat, drawn as lights: lit for +1, dark for -1. Kanerva’s own examples use a thousand or ten thousand bits. A thousand-bit word has 2 to the power 1,000 possible values, far too many for a memory to keep one location for each.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s1.title`: A word is a long row of bits
- `sdmexplore.ex.s2.p`: An ordinary memory has one location for every address. This one has {M} hard locations. Each has a random {n}-bit address, chosen once and kept, and a row of {n} bit-counters that start at zero. The stars are the three stored patterns; each dot is one hard location, drawn near the patterns its address resembles.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s2.title`: The memory builds a few hard locations, at random addresses, and never moves them
- `sdmexplore.ex.s3.p`: No hard location has exactly the word’s address. So the word wakes every hard location within the activation radius, {r} bits here, and is added to their bit-counters: +1 where the word has a lit bit, -1 where it has a dark one. Writing :cat woke {k} of the {M}; the other patterns went to other hard locations.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s3.title`: A write spreads the word over the hard locations near it
- `sdmexplore.ex.s4.p`: Give the memory an address. The hard locations within {r} bits of it wake, their rows of bit-counters are added up bit by bit, and each bit of the answer is the sign of its column. Shown: the {k} rows woken by a noisy copy of :cat (rose +, indigo -), the column sums, and the answer underneath.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s4.title`: A read lets the nearby hard locations vote
- `sdmexplore.ex.s5.p`: That copy of :cat had {flipped} of {n} bits flipped. It woke {shared} of the {k} hard locations :cat was written to, and their votes outweighed the rest: one read left {off} bits wrong, and reading again from each answer reached :cat in {rounds} reads and then stopped changing. The chart counts the bits that differ from :cat after each read. An address far from every stored word wakes hard locations that agree on nothing, and the answer is noise, which is the memory’s way of saying it does not know.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s5.title`: A noisy address still finds the word, read by read
- `sdmexplore.ex.src`: Each quote is a line of YouTube’s auto-caption, unpunctuated, with the lecture and the time it was said; each one links to that moment of the lecture.
- `sdmexplore.ex.title`: What a sparse distributed memory is
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.busy`: writing and reading… {n} of {total} checkpoints
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.cap`: S-map capacity {cap}
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.chart`: recall (final overlap >= 0.95) from {pct}% address-noise, against the number of patterns stored
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.damage`: damage
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.live`: live: this tab, 48 addresses per point
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.ninety`: 90% recall
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.one`: one memory, written as it goes
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.p90`: recorded P90 {keys} and {scale}
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.smap`: S-map: converges up to {cap}
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.x`: patterns stored
- `sdmexplore.exp.capacity.y`: recall
- `sdmexplore.exp.done`: done
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.before.aria`: The note before the key turns it: a length byte, {bits} text bits, and {pad} padding bits that are all +1.
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.before.legend`: length byte (amber) · the text's bits · padding, all +1 (ice): before the key turns it
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.before.subtitle`: a length byte, the text bits, and padding that is all +1
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.before.title`: The note before the key turns it
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.cap`: The program is the one above; a test replays its five recorded lines. A key is not encryption: it is hashed to 64 bits.
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.dist`: the key's address is {d} bits from the stored note ({pad} padding bits agree by construction)
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.far.aria`: For each note length, how far the key's address sits from the stored note, and whether the read found it.
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.far.axis`: note length in bytes (lime: the key read the note back · red: nothing readable)
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.far.head`: THE NOTE CUT TO EACH LENGTH: bits from the key's address (dashed: the wake radius 112)
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.far.subtitle`: by note length; lime when the key read the note back
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.far.title`: How far the key's address sits from the stored note
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.live`: written and read in this tab
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.long`: the note is longer than {cap} bytes; a keyed note must leave room for its length byte
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.note`: the note ({n} of {cap} bytes)
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.read`: read with the key
- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.saved`: saved under the key
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.cap`: dashed: the sealed measurement X8, recorded in {ledger}.
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.chains`: chains per temperature
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.chart`: share of reads 21 to 30 on the address's own pattern, starting 10% noisy
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.computing`: computing…
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.per`: {n} chains per point
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.plain`: live: tie is a fair coin
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.sealed`: sealed X8, 300 chains (test)
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.self`: live: tie leans to keep (self-pull 0.5)
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.x`: temperature T
- `sdmexplore.exp.melt.y`: share on the pattern
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.aria`: 64 hard location p-bits above 32 data p-bits, joined by pulls equal to the bit-counters. {on} hard locations are on; the data are {pct}% like :{k}.
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.cap`: a test checks that at T = 0 this model gives the release binary's {via} line for the page program.
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.data`: 32 DATA THINGS · lean = the sum of their pulls
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.energy`: energy {e}
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.gibbs`: one round of Gibbs per frame: hard locations, then data
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.locs`: 64 LOCATION THINGS · lean -0.8 each
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.overlap`: overlap with :{k} {v}
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.round`: round {r} · {on} hard locations on
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.start`: start from a 10% noisy address
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.subtitle`: 64 hard location p-bits above 32 data p-bits, joined by pulls equal to the bit-counters
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.temp`: temperature T (0 is the via: :pulls read)
- `sdmexplore.exp.pulls.title`: The hard locations as p-bits
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.again`: START THE COUNT AGAIN
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.aria`: How far each read travels from its address. Noisy addresses of stored patterns travel little; never-stored addresses travel far. The travel rule refuses anything past {h} bits.
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.axis`: bits the read travelled from its address
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.counting`: counting
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.h`: h = {h}: an answer farther than this from its address is refused
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.never`: never-stored random addresses: land on one {land}, accepted {acc} (the rule allows 1%)
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.reads`: {n} reads
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.rule`: h(T) is the largest h with 1 - (1 - P[Bin(32, 1/2) <= h])^3 <= 0.01, so h = {h}.
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.stored`: 10% noisy addresses of stored patterns: land on one {land}, accepted {acc}
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.subtitle`: violet: noisy addresses of stored patterns · red: addresses never stored · dashed: the refusal distance h
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.title`: How far each read travels from its address
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.aria`: The chance a hard location is activated against its distance from the address, at softness {soft}. Expected hard locations activated for this address: {e}.
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.axis`: distance d from the address (bars: where the 64 locations sit for a 10% noisy :cat)
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.exact`: exact, computed here
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.expected`: expected firing for this address {e} (hard: {h})
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.hard`: softness 0 is the hard ball: {n} hard locations wake
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.radius`: activation radius 12, hard
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.softness`: softness s
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.subtitle`: the soft ball of one hard location, at the chosen softness
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.title`: Firing chance against distance
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.tw`: t {tv} · w {wv} · temperature 2w {tw}
- `sdmexplore.exp.still`: still, reduced motion
- `sdmexplore.page.cap.line`: The critical-distance is a second prediction, and it is not settled. At Kanerva’s point (1,000 bits, a million hard locations, radius 451, 10,000 words) KANERVA’s S-map gives 165 bits, Bricken and Pehlevan report 188, and a real store measured 204.3. Nobody has explained the gap. Radius 451 activates 1,072 of the million hard locations; Kanerva 1993’s own sample memory uses radius 447, which activates 445.
- `sdmexplore.page.cap.p`: Kanerva 1993 gives the capacity as a share of the hard locations, where φ is the chance a stored bit is read back right from its exact address. At φ = 0.999 it is 0.105 words per hard location as the memory grows without end, and 0.096 for his million-location sample memory. KANERVA’s theory module reproduces both numbers in its tests. A noisy address holds fewer.
- `sdmexplore.page.cap.title`: How much a memory holds, by Kanerva’s theory
- `sdmexplore.page.chat.title`: How the SDM language model works
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.label`: EXPERIMENTS · SETTLE × KANERVA
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.p`: Each one runs the memory here and sets its result beside a recorded or sealed number. They show where the memory holds, where it melts, and what a key or a refusal rule does to a read.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.title`: Experiments you can run in this tab
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.track`: Experiment 2 sets the S-map’s prediction beside the count. The plain map is optimistic once the address-noise reaches 30%: at a million hard locations it predicted 1,648 words at 30% noise where 700 were measured. KANERVA’s TRACK prediction follows the measured recall (the KANERVA page shows both).
- `sdmexplore.page.exp1.p`: Start from a 10% noisy address, read 30 times at one temperature, and count how many of the last ten reads sit on the pattern. A tied bit (sum exactly 0) is a fair coin at any heat. With a self-pull of 0.5 it leans to keep its value, which is the T = 0 tie rule written as a lean.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp1.title`: The memory melts as it warms
- `sdmexplore.page.exp2.p`: Kanerva's size: 256 bits, 2,000 locations, radius 112. Random patterns are written one at a time. After each, 48 stored patterns are read back from noisy addresses. The S-map (Bricken and Pehlevan's signal-to-noise map, ported from KANERVA) predicts the largest count that still converges. We recorded where recall first fell under 90%.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp2.title`: How many patterns fit, against the S-map's prediction
- `sdmexplore.page.exp3.p`: In the small memory almost every address falls into some stored pattern, so landing on one proves nothing. The travel rule asks how far the answer moved from its address. A stored pattern within h bits of a random address is unlikely, so an answer farther than h is refused.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp3.title`: Refusing an address that was never stored
- `sdmexplore.page.exp4.p`: settle-rs keeps the bit-counters as pulls between 64 hard location things and 32 data things. Settle that model and each hard location is itself a p-bit: it switches on when the data agree with what it holds, and the data take the vote of the hard locations that are on. At temperature 0 this is the {via} read.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp4.title`: The hard locations as settling p-bits
- `sdmexplore.page.exp5.p`: A soft SDM lets a hard location fire with a chance that falls with its distance d. That chance is the p-bit rule with lean t minus d at temperature 2w. As the softness grows the edge of the ball blurs, and t is re-fitted so the expected number of active locations stays the same. At the soft end the read approaches attention.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp5.title`: In a soft SDM a hard location is a p-bit leaning by its distance
- `sdmexplore.page.exp6.p`: A key names a turn of the cube: a sign flip on every bit and a shuffle of positions. The note, its length byte and a padding of +1s are turned and stored; nothing else of the text is kept. The key's address is the turned all-+1 list, which agrees with the note on the padding only. So a short note is found, and a long one leaves the address too far away for an SDM's narrow basins.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp6.title`: A note only its key can find
- `sdmexplore.page.hero.aria`: the three stored 32-bit patterns, :cat :dog :owl, settling out of noise one after another
- `sdmexplore.page.how.label`: HOW IT WORKS · ONE IDEA AT A TIME
- `sdmexplore.page.how.title`: How a read works
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.label`: 1 · LIVE · THE MACHINE
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.line`: Each hard-location has a fixed random 32-bit address and 32 bit-counters. The three stars are the stored patterns, :cat :dog :owl, drawn at their distance from the address.
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.p`: Pick a start on the left: a stored pattern with some of its bits flipped (a noisy address), a word that was never stored, or pure noise. The hard locations within 12 bits of the address wake and vote, and the answer appears on the right. Press RUN and the answer becomes the next address, until the read gives back what it was given. Press an address bit to flip it, or hold it.
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.title`: Pick an address and watch it answer
- `sdmexplore.page.output.line`: The machine in this tab prints the same six lines. A test checks it, and runs the binary again whenever one is built.
- `sdmexplore.page.output.p`: Look at the last two lines: an address that was never written (:zebra) and pure noise both come back as :cat. In a memory this small the basins cover most of the cube. Experiment 3 refuses such reads.
- `sdmexplore.page.output.title`: What the binary prints
- `sdmexplore.page.prog.label`: THE PROGRAM · SETTLE
- `sdmexplore.page.prog.title`: Write it in SETTLE
- `sdmexplore.page.program.line`: The addresses come from the memory's name and seed (FNV-1a of {name}), each pattern from its name, and each noisy address from its seed. So the program and the machine hold the same 64 addresses, the same patterns and the same bit-counters.
- `sdmexplore.page.program.p`: Sixteen lines of SETTLE build the machine. The program calls the read-address {ra}; Kanerva calls it the retrieval address, or the retrieval cue. {an} flips a tenth of its bits.
- `sdmexplore.page.program.title`: The same memory, as a SETTLE program
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.line`: A write adds the pattern, as +1 and -1, to every woken hard-location's bit-counters. A read adds the woken bit-counters bit by bit; a sum of exactly 0 keeps the bit it had.
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.p`: THE VOTE panel under the diagram shows it. Each woken hard-location is a row of 32 bit-counters, rose for positive and indigo for negative. The sums are the bars; the sign of each bar is one bit of the answer. The amber ring marks a tie.
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.title`: Add the bit-counters, keep the sign
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.line`: The dashed circle in the diagram is this set. Move the address and the circle keeps its size while the hard locations slide in and out of it.
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.p`: The distance between two words is the number of bits where they differ. A hard location wakes when its address is within the activation radius. With 64 random addresses and activation radius 12, about five wake for any address.
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.title`: Every hard location within 12 bits wakes
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.line`: Given the address, the 32 bits are independent, so the chance that one read lands on a pattern is the product of the 32 chances. The diagram prints it and counts 400 reads beside it. This read picks hard locations by address and votes with bit-counters, so it is not a settle of one energy. Experiment 4 is.
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.p`: Turn the temperature up in the diagram. At T = 0 a bit takes the sign of its sum. Warm, it is a weighted coin, SETTLE's p-bit: a big sum still almost always wins, a small sum is a near toss-up. The memory holds its pattern when warm and melts when hot.
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.title`: Warm, each bit becomes a p-bit
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l1`: Two random codes of 40 bits in 2,048 share 0.78 bits on average; in 200,000 draws none shared more than 7.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l2`: Keep 3 of the 40 bits and the fragment still shares more with its code than the best of 10,000 strangers does.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l3`: One union of codes held to one false match in a billion fits 3 codes at 4 active bits, 47 at 28 and 14 at 400: there is a best sparsity.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l4`: Read as a sparse code, our SDM language model's first read wakes 32 of 65,536 locations a token and a quarter of all wakes go to 32 locations. That describes the code, not its worth: every time the trained reads trained stably, they tied a model with no reads, up to 2.0 billion tokens.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.label`: SPARSE CODES · WHAT MANY BITS AGREE ON
- `sdmexplore.sparse.p`: The memory above reads with dense addresses. A sparse distributed representation uses very few active bits, 40 of 2,048 here, and two codes are alike when they share bits. Three small experiments, run in a few minutes on a laptop, show why so few bits are enough.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick1.p`: Four columns each touch a different part of one object among 1,000. Alone, each keeps 322 to 350 objects that fit what it felt. They vote, and after two touches all four hold the same one. Pooled evidence settles a question no single column could settle so soon.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick1.title`: Columns that agree
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick2.p`: Each of a code's 40 bits is moved at random with a growing probability. A match needs only 20 shared bits, so the code still knows itself 56.55% of the time when half its bits are moved, just as the binomial law says, while a stranger matches with probability 2.5e-26. A sparse code forgives a great deal and still refuses a stranger.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick2.title`: Noise forgiven
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick3.p`: A spatial pooler of 64 columns learns from random bars, 4 winners for each input. Boosting raises a quiet column and lowers a busy one, so the busiest wins 1.30 times its fair share instead of 2.32. Its fields sharpen into single bars, 53 of 64 clean, and all 16 bars are taken.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick3.title`: Each finds its own part
- `sdmexplore.sparse.title`: Sparse codes that agree
- `sdmexplore.src.refuse`: the refusal experiment
- `sdmexplore.top.cap`: $ settle 01_sdm_state.settle
- `sdmexplore.top.cap.live`: settling live
- `sdmexplore.top.docs`: the KANERVA docs
- `sdmexplore.top.foot`: :cat · :dog · :owl, each 8 by 4
- `sdmexplore.top.go`: operate the machine
- `sdmexplore.top.here`: sdm-explore
- `sdmexplore.top.lede`: The memory here is tiny on purpose: 32-bit words, 64 hard locations, three stored patterns. Small enough to draw every part, big enough to recall a pattern from a noisy address.
- `sdmexplore.top.sub`: A sparse distributed memory, drawn as a machine you operate.
- `sdmexplore.top.title`: SDM EXPLORE

## sdmintro

- `sdmintro.p`: A sparse distributed memory is Kanerva’s memory for long words of bits. It has a few thousand hard locations, each at a fixed random address with a row of bit-counters. A write adds a word to the hard locations near its address. A read wakes the hard locations near the read-address and lets their bit-counters vote, bit by bit, so a noisy address still finds the stored word. The five-step explainer, with pictures, is at the top of SDM EXPLORE.

- `sdmm.g.data.what`: The same shape trained on more web text.
- `sdmm.g.hops.found`: More hops kept helping, each doubling by less: {a} hops scored {av}, {b} scored {bv}, {c} scored {cv}. The curve never turned, so its best sits at the edge we tried. The next step, {wall} hops, did not fit the card.
- `sdmm.g.hops.what`: At width {w} with the memory off, from {lo} to {hi} hops.
- `sdmm.g.hopswide.found`: The same shape of answer, better scores: {a} hops {av}, {b} hops {bv}. The best is at the top edge again.
- `sdmm.g.hopswide.what`: The same hop sweep at width {w}, memory off.
- `sdmm.g.mixer.found`: It led early in training loss, then fell behind as its gradients climbed, and on TEST it was {gap} worse than its control ({fade} against {ctl}); with weight decay, {gap2} worse ({wd}). So the mixer is not in any scored model.
- `sdmm.g.mixer.what`: A Kanerva memory written and read while reading, {layers} layers with fading heads, against the same body without it.
- `sdmm.g.onoff.found`: Every pair tied inside the noise: at {d} width, {on} against {off}; at full scale, {base} against {twin}. Reading a trained store does not change the next-token odds. That is the finding that sent us to a memory written while reading.
- `sdmm.g.onoff.what`: The memory on against the same body with the memory off, at every size we trained.
- `sdmm.g.store.found`: Every one tied its pair inside the {noise} noise: the default store {a}, one store per hop {b}, more locations awake {c}, a hotter learning rate {d}. Letting the read address learn made training diverge ({e}). So the store’s settings did not matter; the store itself did not help.
- `sdmm.g.store.what`: Every setting of the trained store, against the same shape with the memory off.
- `sdmm.g.width.found`: Wider kept helping, less each time: {a} scored {av}, {b} scored {bv}, {c} scored {cv}. The best is the widest we ran, so this is unbracketed too.
- `sdmm.g.width.what`: How wide the working vector is, at {tok} tokens, memory off, {h} hops.
- `sdmm.g.window.found`: This one is settled: the best window, {best}, sits inside the range tried, and the scores either side of it are inside the {noise} noise. Window {a} scored {av}, window {best} scored {bv}, window {e} scored {ev}. So a longer example adds nothing past about {best}.
- `sdmm.g.window.what`: How long each training example is, memory off, {w} hops at width {d}.
- `sdmm.g.yardstick.found`: It set the bar: {a} at {tok1}, {b} at {tok2}. Our best SDM model never beat it, but the race is short-context: the transformer trains at window {w} with {l} layers.
- `sdmm.g.yardstick.what`: A small transformer, the yardstick only, at the same data.
- `sdmm.here`: sdmchat-model
- `sdmm.law.label`: THE LAW
- `sdmm.law.p1`: Every model on this page is built from one part: a sparse distributed memory, Kanerva’s store of hard locations read by an address. The only step that lets one position in the text affect another is an SDM read or write. There is no attention, no softmax over the window, no transformer anywhere in a model we score. The transformer below is a yardstick only, there to say how far the SDM trails.
- `sdmm.law.title`: All SDM, no transformer, from scratch
- `sdmm.mem.mixer`: run-time mixer
- `sdmm.mem.off`: memory off
- `sdmm.mem.on`: memory on
- `sdmm.mem.transformer`: transformer
- `sdmm.part.found`: WHAT WE FOUND
- `sdmm.part.how`: HOW IT PREDICTS THE NEXT TOKEN
- `sdmm.part.why`: WHY WE TRIED IT
- `sdmm.shape.mid.how`: Each layer adds a run-time Kanerva memory: the vector addresses {loc} locations per head, wakes {k}, reads what earlier tokens wrote there, faded per head, and writes itself in; a small dense layer follows, and the head scores the next token.
- `sdmm.shape.mid.m`: a run-time SDM
- `sdmm.shape.mid.r`: read the same grid
- `sdmm.shape.mid.w`: write while reading
- `sdmm.shape.mid.why`: The two findings point one way: a store written in training adds nothing, and a mixer bolted onto the old body would not hold. So make the memory the body. A residual stack where every layer adds a run-time Kanerva memory, written and read as the text goes by, and no attention anywhere.
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.found`: It led early in training loss and then fell behind: {fade} against its control’s {ctl}, {gap} worse, and {wd} with weight decay. Its gradients climbed as it went, and it is in no scored model. The idea was right; this body could not hold it.
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.h`: 3 · THE RUN-TIME MIXER (written while reading)
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.how`: Each token writes a value into the locations its address wakes; a later token reads what earlier ones wrote, faded per head; a small dense layer follows, and the head scores the next token.
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.m`: a Kanerva grid
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.r`: later tokens read
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.w`: each token writes
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.why`: If a trained store adds nothing, let the text itself write into the memory as it is read. Each token writes a value into the locations its address wakes; later tokens read what earlier ones wrote. That is attention’s job, by content, at a fixed cost per token at any length.
- `sdmm.shape.none.found`: It is our best SDM score and the store never beat it. The memory-off twin scored {twin}, and the widest memory-off run {wide} at {tok} tokens; both are the numbers every memory-on run is measured against.
- `sdmm.shape.none.h`: 2 · NO MEMORY (memory off)
- `sdmm.shape.none.how`: The same summary and one map to the working vector, then straight to the tied head: no memory is read at all.
- `sdmm.shape.none.why`: The campaign’s rule: every SDM part must beat a control of the same shape with that part removed. With no store, the body is the lookback features, one map to the working vector and the tied head. This is the floor the store has to beat.
- `sdmm.shape.store.found`: It ties the same body with no store, at every size: the early {w}-wide models cost {lo} to {hi} bpb for the learned store, and at full scale the base run scored {base} against its memory-off twin’s {twin}, {gap} apart, inside the {noise} noise. The store holds what training learned; your text is never written into it, so it adds nothing to what the model can see. That is the finding the rest of this page is about.
- `sdmm.shape.store.h`: 1 · THE TRAINED STORE (memory on)
- `sdmm.shape.store.how`: The tokens so far become a summary; one map makes the working vector; at each of its hops the vector addresses the trained store, a few locations fire and their values join it; the tied head scores the next token. The store is read, not written at run time.
- `sdmm.shape.store.m`: the trained store
- `sdmm.shape.store.r`: a few locations fire
- `sdmm.shape.store.why`: Kanerva’s memory is the whole point: a store of hard locations read by an address, cheap and the same at any text length. Put it where attention would be and see if the body learns to use it.
- `sdmm.shape.tf.found`: It sets the bar: {a} at {tok1} and {b} at {tok2}. It leads our base run by {gap}, and it is a short-context race: the transformer trains at window {w} with {l} layers, and a long-window transformer has never been in it.
- `sdmm.shape.tf.h`: 4 · THE TRANSFORMER (the yardstick)
- `sdmm.shape.tf.how`: Softmax attention compares the current position with every token in the window and mixes their values; a small MLP follows, and the head scores the next token.
- `sdmm.shape.tf.r`: attention over the window
- `sdmm.shape.tf.why`: Not an SDM and never scored as one: a small transformer at the same data, to say how far behind the SDM sits and whether the gap closes with more data.

- `sdmm.shapes.note`: One shared store of {m} locations, {k} awake at each read, is the shape the memory-on runs use; the transformer’s hop column holds its layers and its hop block is its own MLP. GPUs: every sweep run took one card; the base run and its twin each took two.

- `sdmm.walls.h`: The walls: what did not fit a card
- `sdmm.walls.p`: Two shapes stopped against the hardware, and both walls are measured. With the memory off, {wall} hops did not fit a {card} GB card: the hop blocks alone are about {wallParams} parameters. With the memory on the wall comes sooner, because each hop keeps its own store-sized buffer of {buf} MB, so {onWall} hops did not fit (about {bufGb} GB of buffers before any activations), and the store at width {w2048} did not fit either. At {t16} and {t32} hops the memory on tied the memory off; above that the card, not the model, ended the sweep.
- `sdmm.where.aria`: TEST bits per byte: base {a}, memory-off twin {b}, transformer {c}. Lower is better.
- `sdmm.where.base`: the base run, memory on, {tok} tokens
- `sdmm.where.chart`: TEST bits per byte at {tok} tokens, lower is better
- `sdmm.where.chat`: SDM CHAT, on held-out chat turns
- `sdmm.where.p1`: The base run, memory on, scored {base}. Its memory-off twin scored {twin}, {gap} better. That gap is inside the {noise} noise, so the honest reading is a tie: the memory neither helps nor hurts. The transformer scored {tf}, ahead of the base by {gapTf}: a small lead, but a real one, and the transformer still leads.
- `sdmm.where.p2`: One model has beaten a baseline on something that matters. SDM CHAT is the base run chat-tuned on {tok} tokens of conversation: on held-out chat turns it went from {before} to {after} bits per byte, at a cost of {cost} on web text. It is a small model and its replies drift, but on its own test it learned the shape of an answer.
- `sdmm.where.src`: Source: the training records, as of {when}.
- `sdmm.where.tf`: the transformer yardstick, still ahead
- `sdmm.where.twin`: its memory-off twin, the best SDM score
- `sdmm.wip.line`: Small and early; we are building the next one.
- `sdmm.wip.link`: What we tried and what we found
- `sdmm.wip.tag`: EARLY MODEL
- `sdmm.worked.label`: WHAT WORKED, WHAT DIDN’T
- `sdmm.worked.lede`: We swept one thing at a time, and each sweep gets one mark: BRACKETED when its best value lies inside the range tried, UNBRACKETED when the best is at the edge, TIE when nothing moved the score past the noise, and WORSE when every setting lost. Three things worked: more hops, more data, and a wider body. Nothing about the memory worked.
- `sdmm.worked.title`: The sweeps, in plain words

## sdmm2

- `sdmm2.hist.banner`: From here down is the history: the shapes we tried before FULL and PARTIAL, what each one found, and the scores that sent us to the two models above. Every picture below is of an older shape and is marked HISTORY.
- `sdmm2.hist.tag`: HISTORY
- `sdmm2.law.p2`: They are trained from scratch, on web text, with next-token cross-entropy. Every score is TEST bits per byte on held-out text, lower is better, and a gap under {noise} between two runs is not called. Every number in the history is read from the training records, and the site’s tests check each one again against those records and the model code.
- `sdmm2.lede`: We are exploring the shapes an SDM can take, and where it might fit in LLM land. The newest two are FULL and PARTIAL, and FULL is the one we take forward. Below them is the history of every shape that led there.
- `sdmm2.now.label`: NOW · FULL AND PARTIAL
- `sdmm2.now.more`: How each one stores, writes, reads and picks the next word: sdm.
- `sdmm2.now.p1`: Both models put a memory written while reading in every layer, the one part that passes anything between positions. After it, PARTIAL uses an ordinary MLP of {n} neurons. FULL uses a trained SDM table instead, of which each token reads {k} rows in each head. They are trained at {l} layers and a width of {d}.
- `sdmm2.now.title`: The two newest models, and the one we take forward
- `sdmm2.shape.mid.found`: On puzzles it does what no earlier shape could: its recall holds flat out to a gap of {gap} tokens, where the transformer falls to {tf}. It copies in range worse than the transformer does. It became PARTIAL, tested beside FULL in the section above.
- `sdmm2.shape.mid.h`: 5 · THE RUN-TIME SDM (it became PARTIAL)

- `sdmm2.top.now`: the two models now

- `sdmm2.where.title`: The last scores before FULL and PARTIAL, and the honest reading

## sdmtruth

- `sdmtruth.drawers.p1`: The drawers are filled during training, by gradient descent, and are only read while the model writes. They do not remember what you typed a thousand words ago.
- `sdmtruth.drawers.p2`: A memory that is written and read inside the text itself (SdmMix in our code) is built and tested, but it is not part of these runs.

- `sdmtruth.kind.chat.text`: A smaller, older family that runs live in the chat on this site. Its store has 3,600 locations; it scores every key, keeps the best 64 and reads twice per token. Its scores are on its own card and are not compared with the rows here.
- `sdmtruth.kind.dense`: MATCHED COMPUTE
- `sdmtruth.kind.dense.tag`: the fair-cost control
- `sdmtruth.kind.dense.text`: Each look-up is swapped for a dense layer that does the same amount of arithmetic. If this one wins, the look-up was only paying for compute.
- `sdmtruth.kind.off`: MEMORY OFF

- `sdmtruth.kind.off.text`: The same stack with every look-up removed. It answers one question: what does the memory add? Today it holds our best scores.

- `sdmtruth.kind.on.text`: The SDM model. Every hop looks up the shelf of {m} drawers, then runs its MLP. This is the model the project is about.

- `sdmtruth.kind.tf.text`: A standard transformer with attention, trained with the Muon optimiser (mq in run names). We train it only as a yardstick, on the same data and the same test.
- `sdmtruth.kinds.label`: THE KINDS OF MODEL

We change one setting at a time and keep every other: how many hops, how wide the model is, how much data it sees, the batch size, the optimiser, and a second seed to check a result repeats. Each sweep goes on until the score turns, as the next section explains.

- `sdmtruth.ladder.tf2b`: transformer (yardstick)

- `sdmtruth.ladder.trueOff`: memory off

- `sdmtruth.ladder.trueOffSmall.sub`: width {w} · {h} hops · {tok}B tokens
