- `sdmtruth.latest.best`: Best: memory off, width {w3}, {h} hops, {tok}B tokens: {v3}. At width {w}: {v}; at width {w2}: {v2}. Width {w3} beats width {w} by {gap}, inside the noise, so width is undecided at this budget.
- `sdmtruth.latest.hops`: More hops still help: at width {w1}, {h} hops scored {v1}; at width {w2}, 32 hops scored {v2}, the best {tok}M score. The gain per step keeps shrinking and has not turned, so both sweeps are UNBRACKETED. {h128} hops was still training at the time. Width and data are unbracketed too.
- `sdmtruth.latest.label`: THE LATEST RESULTS
- `sdmtruth.latest.lede`: Our best scores come from the memory-off model. It reads no SDM. So they are results for a deep stack of MLPs over a fixed set of context features, not results for the memory. The test that decides it is done: with the memory on, the same model ties.
- `sdmtruth.latest.limit`: A limit: memory on at {h} hops does not fit a {gb} GB RTX 5090 as built, because each hop keeps a {mb} MB store-sized buffer.
- `sdmtruth.latest.more`: The model kinds, the scoring and every sweep are on SDM CHAT.
- `sdmtruth.latest.tf`: The yardstick: a transformer at width {w} on the same {big}B tokens scored {v}. It leads memory off at that width by {lead} and the best memory-off run by {lead2}. At equal data the transformer leads every SDM-family run, so we make no claim that the SDM line beats a transformer.
- `sdmtruth.latest.title`: Where the SDM language model stands today
- `sdmtruth.latest.twin`: The decider is in: the memory-on twin, the same shape at width {w} plus the look-up, scored {on} against {off} for memory off, {gap} apart, inside the noise. It reads its memory and matches memory off; it does not beat it, as in every smaller test.
- `sdmtruth.level.drawers`: WHAT THE DRAWERS ARE, AND ARE NOT
- `sdmtruth.level.line`: IN ONE LINE
- `sdmtruth.level.para`: IN A PARAGRAPH
- `sdmtruth.level.tech`: THE TECHNICAL DETAIL, FOR ML PEOPLE
- `sdmtruth.onoff.cross`: The same question for the smaller models this chat runs, what has been measured and what is still open: what we know, and what we do not.
- `sdmtruth.onoff.label`: MEMORY ON, MEMORY OFF
- `sdmtruth.onoff.line`: Memory on: at every step of its thinking the model also looks something up in a shelf of {m} learned drawers. Memory off: the same model with the look-up taken out.
- `sdmtruth.onoff.para1`: Both models read the text so far and predict the next token. They turn the recent text into one long list of numbers, then pass that list through the same block {h} times. We call each pass a hop.
- `sdmtruth.onoff.para2`: With memory on, each hop first makes a question from the list. The question wakes the {k} drawers whose labels fit it best, out of {m}, and the hop adds what those drawers hold. Then a small network (an MLP) adds its own part. With memory off, each hop is only the MLP.
- `sdmtruth.onoff.para3`: Everything else is the same: the same data, the same test, the same training. So the difference in score is what the memory adds.
- `sdmtruth.onoff.title`: The same model, with and without its memory
- `sdmtruth.pair.figcap`: The same stack twice. The only difference is the LOOK UP box in each hop. The shelf shows 96 drawers to stand for all {m}.
- `sdmtruth.pair.off`: MEMORY OFF
- `sdmtruth.pair.on`: MEMORY ON
- `sdmtruth.score.bracket`: Bracketed or unbracketed. A sweep changes one setting. If the best score sits inside the range tried, the sweep is BRACKETED and the best value is found. If the best is at the edge, it is UNBRACKETED, and the next sweep tries further out.
- `sdmtruth.score.label`: HOW WE SCORE
- `sdmtruth.score.line`: The score is how many bits, on average, the model needs to predict each byte of text it has never seen. Lower is better.
- `sdmtruth.score.noise`: The noise rule. The same setting run on two machines scores up to about {n} apart. So a difference smaller than {n} is not called a win; it is rerun on more data first.
- `sdmtruth.score.p1`: Every run is scored on the same held-out test set from FineWeb-Edu: {tokens} tokens, {bytes} bytes, never used in training. A guess spread evenly over all {vals} byte values would cost {eight} bits a byte. Because the score counts bytes rather than tokens, models with different vocabularies can be compared.
- `sdmtruth.score.tech`: bits per byte = (the sum over the test tokens of -ln p(token)) / (ln 2 × the test bytes). The best run averages {nats} nats per token over {tokens} tokens and {bytes} bytes, which gives {bpb}.
- `sdmtruth.score.title`: Bits per byte, on text the model has never seen
- `sdmtruth.stack.f.avg`: {n} fading
- `sdmtruth.stack.f.back`: {n} past tokens
- `sdmtruth.stack.f.pair`: pair
- `sdmtruth.stack.head`: norm, then the head
- `sdmtruth.stack.hop`: one hop
- `sdmtruth.stack.hopn`: hop {n} of {total}
- `sdmtruth.stack.look`: LOOK UP
- `sdmtruth.stack.look.sub`: wake {k} of {m}
- `sdmtruth.stack.look.sub2`: add what they hold
- `sdmtruth.stack.map`: one linear map to width d
- `sdmtruth.stack.mlp`: small MLP
- `sdmtruth.stack.mlp.sub`: SwiGLU, its own weights
- `sdmtruth.stack.next`: the next token
- `sdmtruth.stack.nolook`: no look-up
- `sdmtruth.stack.nolook.sub`: the drawers are not there
- `sdmtruth.stack.off.desc`: The same stack with the LOOK UP taken out: each hop is only the small MLP. Everything else is the same.
- `sdmtruth.stack.off.title`: Memory off
- `sdmtruth.stack.on.desc`: Read from the bottom up: the text so far becomes 14 feature vectors, one linear map joins them, then a hop repeated {hops} times. In each hop a LOOK UP wakes about {k} of {m} learned drawers and adds what they hold, then a small MLP adds its part. The head picks the next token.
- `sdmtruth.stack.on.title`: Memory on
- `sdmtruth.stack.text`: the text so far
- `sdmtruth.stack.times`: × {n}
- `sdmtruth.tech.cost`: A measured limit: the memory-on path keeps one store-sized buffer per hop ({m} by 1,024 float32 at width 1,024, {mb} MB), so memory on at {hops} hops did not fit a {gb} GB RTX 5090.
- `sdmtruth.tech.features`: Features: the embeddings of the last {back} tokens (t to t-7), {avg} causal moving averages of every earlier embedding (decays 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.97, 0.99) and {pairs} element-wise product of the embeddings of t and t-1. Each is RMS-normalised; the {n} vectors are joined and one linear map takes them to the working width d. The input table is untied; the output head has its own table.
- `sdmtruth.tech.hop`: A hop: x ← x + read(x) when memory is on, then x ← x + SwiGLU(x). After the last hop, an RMS norm and the head. There is no attention: positions meet only through the fixed features, over a window of {w} tokens.
- `sdmtruth.tech.read`: The read is a product-key memory (Lample et al., 2019). A query of 256 numbers, batch-normalised, splits in half; each half scores 256 sub-keys, so a drawer (i, j) of the 256 by 256 grid scores s1[i] + s2[j]. The top 64 drawers are found exactly, each is weighed by sigmoid((s - θ) / 0.25) with θ the {k}nd best score, and their value rows are summed with gain 1/{k}. The values start at zero, so at step one memory on equals memory off.
- `sdmtruth.tech.share`: With --share-store, one shelf of {m} drawers is read by every hop; the 2.0B memory-on twin runs that way. Without it, each hop has a shelf of its own.

## settlesee

- `settlesee.claim`: A grid of lights that settles out of noise into your picture. One line of React.
- `settlesee.code.label`: lights settling into a word
- `settlesee.code.note`: That is the whole call. The lights start as noise, cool into the word, hold it, and heat up again, on a loop that pauses when nobody is looking.
- `settlesee.code.word`: see
- `settlesee.contents.label`: ON THIS PAGE
- `settlesee.contents.lead`: Every picture below is settle-see, live in your browser. The headings and links are settle-text, which is built on it.
- `settlesee.contents.title`: A drawing library, drawn by itself
- `settlesee.copied`: copied
- `settlesee.copy`: copy
- `settlesee.copy.label`: copy the code
- `settlesee.cost.idle`: After five minutes with nobody there, the loop stops until you move.
- `settlesee.cost.label`: WHAT IT COSTS
- `settlesee.cost.loop`: Every settle on a page shares one animation loop.
- `settlesee.cost.m.draw`: ms of drawing a frame, on average
- `settlesee.cost.m.phys`: ms of physics a frame, on average
- `settlesee.cost.m.ran`: have drawn a frame
- `settlesee.cost.m.settles`: settles on this page
- `settlesee.cost.measured`: The numbers above are this page on this machine, read from settle-see’s own meter every two seconds since the page opened.
- `settlesee.cost.off`: A settle off screen, or in a hidden tab, does no work at all.
- `settlesee.cost.reduced`: Ask your system for less motion and every picture is drawn once, still.
- `settlesee.cost.title`: One loop for the whole page, and it stops when you look away
- `settlesee.opt.clear`: No plate: the lights alone, over whatever is behind the canvas.
- `settlesee.opt.cool`: Cool once and stay settled, instead of heating up again.
- `settlesee.opt.dim`: Light the dark lights a little, so the whole grid shows.
- `settlesee.opt.duo`: Two neons: the dark lights glow faintly in the second.
- `settlesee.opt.gl`: Draw in one WebGL2 pass, for a large picture.
- `settlesee.opt.glow`: More bloom, for a sign.
- `settlesee.opt.kicker`: THE OPTIONS, ONE EACH
- `settlesee.opt.label`: a heart in lights: {name}
- `settlesee.opt.lead`: Every option is a prop of Settle and an option of settle().
- `settlesee.opt.lean`: A weak lean: the lights want the picture less, so it stays fuzzy.
- `settlesee.opt.meaning`: The default: the SETTLE colour code. Rose where a light agrees with the picture, orange where it fights it.
- `settlesee.opt.pull`: A strong pull: neighbours agree, so the picture sets in blobs.
- `settlesee.opt.res`: Fewer, larger lights: 24 across.
- `settlesee.opt.single`: One neon for every lit light.
- `settlesee.opt.still`: Start settled and hold still. The pointer still plays on it.

- `settlesee.parts.badge.label`: a {shape} in lights
- `settlesee.parts.badge.say`: A small square settle of one shape in one neon, for a card, a credit or a list.
- `settlesee.parts.hook.label`: lights settling into a {shape}
- `settlesee.parts.hook.next`: next shape
- `settlesee.parts.hook.say`: Build your own component: the hook hands you a canvas ref and the live handle, and the handle re-targets the lights without starting over.

## settletext

- `settletext.access.p1`: Every settled word on this page is also real text. A screen reader hears the words, and the canvas of lights is hidden from it.
- `settletext.access.p2`: Ask your system for less motion and every settle is drawn once, still. On a slow machine this page draws its prose with fewer lights.
- `settletext.access.title`: Who it serves
- `settletext.claim`: Your words, your font, as a settle of lights. One line of React.
- `settletext.code.note`: That is the whole call. The words come out of noise in about a second and a half, keep flickering, shimmer every few seconds, and now and then settle again.
- `settletext.code.words`: What?
- `settletext.contents.alive`: And every one of them is alive. Its lights flicker, and every few seconds it shimmers on its own clock: a glint, a few lights blinking, a soft breath. About one shimmer in ten is a full re-settle. One example near the end holds still on purpose.
- `settletext.contents.label`: ON THIS PAGE
- `settletext.contents.lead`: Every heading, sentence and link below this line is settle-text. The plain parts are the package itself: its install, its steps and its docs.
- `settletext.contents.title2`: A page drawn in its own lights
- `settletext.cost.count`: This page holds {n} settles. The ones you cannot see are paused.
- `settletext.cost.label`: WHAT IT COSTS
- `settletext.cost.link`: the Performance table
- `settletext.cost.measured`: Measured on 2026-10-03 on an M5 Max in headless Chromium with settle-see’s own meter, the minimum over three rounds. The table and its stamp are in the package’s docs on this page.
- `settletext.cost.p1`: The physics is under a fifth of a millisecond a frame at every resolution preset, and the draw one to two and a half. A still picture drew zero frames in five seconds.
- `settletext.cost.p2b`: Alive, a settle keeps sweeping at twelve frames a second between re-settles and at twenty-four while it settles. Off screen, and in a hidden tab, it pauses.
- `settletext.cost.p3`: When many are on screen at once the page thins itself: the flicker slows, at most six shimmers and four re-settles run together, and the rest wait their turn. It never turns static.
- `settletext.cost.title`: A few milliseconds a frame, and the page thins itself
- `settletext.fit`: SETTLE is the language, KANERVA its memory, the MCP the door from an editor, and settle-text is the look of all of it, handed to anyone with a React page.
- `settletext.manifesto`: Give it text. Get the effect.
- `settletext.opt.count`: re-settles so far: {n}
- `settletext.opt.counter`: A callback at each re-settle. This one counts them.
- `settletext.opt.defaults`: Sets the defaults once for a whole part of a page. Every component inside takes them.
- `settletext.opt.dim`: Lights the dark lights a little, so the whole grid shows, as in the hero.
- `settletext.opt.duo`: Two neons: the dark lights glow faintly in the second.
- `settletext.opt.fast`: Settles again every two seconds.
- `settletext.opt.glow`: More bloom, for a sign.
- `settletext.opt.gradient`: A gradient across the words: sunset, aurora, neon, ice, fire, or a list of your own.
- `settletext.opt.intro`: No noise at the start: the words are there at once, then alive.
- `settletext.opt.kicker`: THE OPTIONS, ONE EACH
- `settletext.opt.lead`: Each card sets one prop on the same word. Leave them all out and you get the alive default: a warm simmer, a small shimmer every few seconds, and a full re-settle about one time in ten. A card that sets the re-settle's own clock keeps that clock.
- `settletext.opt.meaning`: The hero’s own colour code: a light that fights its lean flares orange while it settles.
- `settletext.opt.none`: No re-settles. It simmers and shimmers, and never scatters.
- `settletext.opt.rate`: A slower flicker: four sweeps a second between re-settles. fps sets the rate while it settles.
- `settletext.opt.rest`: Settles on its schedule but draws nothing in between: the cheapest live mode.
- `settletext.opt.shake`: Shakes the lights loose instead of heating them.
- `settletext.opt.slow`: A long, uneven wait, and a bigger scatter when it comes.
- `settletext.opt.still`: One flag, and the lights are drawn once and never move again. Everything else on this page is alive.
- `settletext.opt.still.caption`: you can do static things too
- `settletext.opt.temp`: The simmer is a temperature: calm at 0.45, wild at 0.8.
- `settletext.opt.title`: Every default is alive. Every default can change.
- `settletext.opt.word`: Settle
- `settletext.parts.bg.say`: Any of the three behind your content, full bleed. Like everything else it is alive, on a slower schedule than a text.
- `settletext.parts.heading.level`: Heading level {n}
- `settletext.parts.heading.note`: Every heading on this page is one. A screen reader hears the words and the page outline stays whole.
- `settletext.parts.heading.say`: A real heading, level 1 to level 6, each with its own size. The size is CSS, so it follows the window like any heading.
- `settletext.parts.heading.sr`: Six heading sizes, level 1 to level 6, drawn as lights.

- `settletext.shimmer.fx.flurry`: A light flurry of noise across the piece, gone in a second.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.glint`: A thin bright band slides across the letters, left to right.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.glow`: The whole piece brightens once, softly, and fades.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.haze`: The glow softens and smears for a moment, then sharpens.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.line`: One line scatters and settles back.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.resettle`: The full re-settle: the words heat up, scatter and settle back.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.ripple`: A faint ring of light rolls out through the words.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.sparks`: A few sparks flicker just off the edges.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.tilt`: The letters loosen for a moment and pull back into shape.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.twinkle`: A few lights blink brighter, here and there.
- `settletext.shimmer.fx.word`: One word scatters and settles back while the rest hold.
- `settletext.shimmer.how`: One prop chooses the range: a preset, one effect by name, or a list. Each effect is drawn by the settle itself, never by a CSS animation, and at most six run on a page at once.
- `settletext.shimmer.kicker`: THE AMBIENT SHIMMER
- `settletext.shimmer.lead`: Every piece of text on this page shimmers on its own clock, at its own moment. Most shimmers are small: a glint, a few lights blinking, a soft breath. About one in ten is a full re-settle.
- `settletext.shimmer.preset.gentle`: The default: nine small effects about every three and a half seconds, a full re-settle one time in ten.
- `settletext.shimmer.preset.lively`: All twelve small effects, closer together and a little stronger.
- `settletext.shimmer.preset.whisper`: The quietest four: twinkles, a glint, a ripple, a breath, about every five seconds.
- `settletext.shimmer.presets`: Three presets
- `settletext.shimmer.range`: The range, from the faintest to the boldest
- `settletext.shimmer.range.say`: Each card runs only its own effect, every two to three seconds, so you can watch it. Pass the name to deal only that one.
- `settletext.shimmer.title`: Every piece of text keeps its own small schedule

- `settletext.show.lead`: Each recipe is the component itself, imported by name as your page would import it, with the code that made it. Scroll away and it pauses. Come back and it continues. Ask your system for less motion and the words are simply there.

- `settletext.why.body`: Everything on this site is a settle, and until now the only way to have one was to learn how it works. A visual designer wants the look: a title in their own font that settles out of noise and glows, a photo as lights behind a page, a logo drawn in dots. They should get that from a component with a text prop and a font prop, and never meet a lean, a pull or a temperature unless they go looking. settle-text wraps settle-see, the drawing library every picture here runs on. Its components have plain names, and their defaults are the tuning of this site’s own titles.

- `studio.how.p1a`: Every base model here is an SDM read: a network whose next token comes from reading a sparse distributed memory of 3,600 locations, addressed by its last tokens. The width-512 models have 74.7M trainable parameters and the small one 36.0M.
- `studio.how.p1b`: A run keeps the 129,280-token table fixed (it is int8) and trains the rest: the memory’s values and keys, the readout, and the address weights, by AdamW on the next-token loss over your dataset, in plain JavaScript in a Web Worker.
- `studio.how.p2`: The loss is in bits per byte, the unit the recorded results use. The train curve is the loss of each batch; the eval curve is the model’s loss on the last five percent of the dataset, which it never trains on. A sample is drawn every hundred steps from the same prompt, so you can read the model change. Speed is timed on this machine.

## surprise

- `surprise.bits.label`: SURPRISE · IN BITS
- `surprise.bits.p1`: Surprise has a unit. A sight the model gave probability p costs -log2 p bits: one bit for a fair coin, about ten for a one-in-a-thousand sight. The agent above adds this up over its 42 sense bits every step. The average surprise is the entropy, and it is also the length an ideal coder would write, which is why our SDM language model is scored in bits per byte of text it has not seen.
- `surprise.bits.p2`: A learner that reads the first 60,001 bytes of Pride and Prejudice once, paying -log2 p for each byte before counting it, shows the score in motion: a letter model of order 3 ends at 2.743 bits per byte, between gzip (2.970) and bz2 (2.481).
- `surprise.bits.p3`: Settling can also take back surprise that noise put in. We sent a code through a channel that flips 10% of its bits and let p-bits running SETTLE’s own rule read it back. Held at the temperature that matches the noise, their averaged read left 0.0499 of the bits wrong (from 0.1032), as good as belief propagation (0.0490); the same machine cooled to one state left 0.0601.
- `surprise.bits.p4`: A memory can be counted the same way. A Kanerva SDM that hands back each stored bit right or wrong is itself a noisy channel, and the bits it returns rise toward a ceiling as it fills: at most 0.327 bits a counter with 500 hard-locations. Written so that each pattern is its own address, the same memory reads an address it was never given back as itself, so its bits must be counted beside that control.
- `surprise.bits.p5`: These are seeded simulations on a laptop. The decoder is not fast, the code is far from Shannon’s limit, and none of it is a claim about our language model’s store. The three pictures below come from that experiment, drawn live.
- `surprise.bits.pick.decode`: Two linked rings arrive with 77 of their 1,344 bits flipped by a noisy channel. Each bit is a p-bit, coupled to the others by the code the rings were sent in; held at the temperature that matches the noise, their running average settles, and 15 wrong bits remain after 48 sweeps. The decoder is exactly as unsure as the channel was noisy, and it trusts the average of many gentle guesses over one cold verdict.
- `surprise.bits.pick.perfect`: Sixteen flowers: each is a codeword of the Hamming(7,4) code at the centre, with the seven words one bit away as petals; beside them, the Fano plane, whose lines are the code’s words of weight 3. The sixteen balls of eight words cover all 128 words of seven bits with no overlap, so every word has exactly one home and any single flipped bit is forgiven.
- `surprise.bits.pick.sdm`: A Kanerva memory of 2,000 hard-locations is given more pairs to hold, from 1 to 7,500, and one stored ring is read back each time. The ring blurs until 95 of its 256 bits are wrong, yet the information the memory returns climbs to about 96,000 bits. Each memory is held a little less sharply so that many more can be held at all.
- `surprise.bits.title`: Surprise, counted in bits

- `surprise.control.label`: SURPRISE · SDM OR SETTLE?
- `surprise.control.note`: These numbers are live, from the model and the step on screen now. In LEARNING mode the leans and pulls move, so ln Z moves too.
- `surprise.control.p1`: The agent's control is SETTLE-based. Its model is a settling machine: a chain Ising model (a Boltzmann machine whose links form a chain) over the {n} p-bits it senses, with a lean on every bit and pulls between linked bits. Because the links form a chain, ln Z is summed exactly by a transfer matrix, so the surprise of any observation, −ln p(o) = E(o) + ln Z, is exact. To act, the agent steps an imagined copy of the game forward under each of {plans} plans of {horizon} steps, scores every predicted observation by its surprise under the machine, and takes the first move of the plan with the lowest total. Surprise here means how unlikely a sight is under a model fitted to calm wandering: an enemy in view, a hit, a bump or the alarm all make it rise.
- `surprise.control.p2`: It is not SDM. A sparse distributed memory stores patterns at random hard addresses and recalls them by Hamming distance; this agent has no hard locations, no addresses, no counters and no recall. Nothing here uses the Kanerva memory. The settle-drawn picture is SETTLE too: the same p-bit rule, run on the picture’s lights.

- `surprise.controls.help.basics`: A new level is generated from the next seed. Switching the model or starting a new level resets the model to the comfort prior. Nothing here is saved; reloading starts again. The share of one core is the frame time times the frame rate plus the planning time times the step rate. The game stops while the view is off screen.
- `surprise.controls.help.picture`: EVERY FRAME A SETTLE: every frame the raycaster draws a small picture, and a grid of p-bits takes a few sweeps of the SETTLE rule toward it. NEON BY CLASS: each light shines in a neon chosen by what its pixel shows (sky, sun, cloud, skyline, wall, neon trim, floor, enemy, rain), four tones per class from dark to bright. THE PIXEL'S OWN: each light shines in its pixel's colour. THREE: three grids (red, green, blue) settle each colour on its own. SOFT READ draws each light's running average; RAW BITS draws every light fully on or off. A DAY LASTS sets the length of the day; HOLD stops the sky at the time of day chosen. WEATHER: CYCLE brings rain and night sparks on their own clocks.
- `surprise.controls.help.truetime`: TRUE TIME SETTLE: the game films a frame on a fixed grid and keeps the last {ring}; the settle works toward the frame it was given as fast as this machine allows, and once the lights that frame asked to change agree with it to the threshold, it takes the frame the game is at now. The strip under the view marks each filmed frame SHOWN, SKIPPED, NOW (being settled toward) or FILMED (waiting its turn). MACHINE SPEED: 60 or 15 SWEEPS/S hold the settle to that rate, to show what a slower machine does; the game keeps its time either way.

- `surprise.enemies.label`: SURPRISE · THE ENEMIES
- `surprise.enemies.live`: live, this level: {alive} alive · {killed} killed · {hits} hits on the player
- `surprise.enemies.note`: The level holds six enemies at a time: a spiker, a runner, a brute and a swarm of three mites. A killed enemy comes back 120 to 239 steps later. All of them follow fixed rules with no learning, and the agent's imagined copies of the world run the same rules. Each type has its own neon and four frames: two that alternate while it moves, one while it attacks, one when it is hit.
- `surprise.enemies.title`: Four kinds of enemy, each with its own look and rules
- `surprise.fep.choice`: Plans are chosen with probability falling with their expected free energy; γ, the precision, sets how strongly. E(π) is a prior over plans, which in active inference carries habits.
- `surprise.fep.expected`: Expected free energy of a plan π: how far the outcomes the plan is predicted to bring are from the preferred outcomes p̃ (risk), plus how uncertain those outcomes are (ambiguity).
- `surprise.fep.free`: Free energy is surprise plus how far the beliefs q about hidden causes x are from the correct ones. It is never smaller than surprise, and equals it when the beliefs are exact.
- `surprise.fep.intro1`: Karl Friston's free-energy principle says that a living system stays in the small set of states that keep it alive, and that it does this by minimising surprise: how unlikely its sensations are under its own model of the world. Surprise itself cannot be computed directly by the system, so the principle uses an upper bound on it, variational free energy, which can be computed.
- `surprise.fep.intro2`: Perception lowers free energy by changing beliefs. Action lowers it by changing the sensations. Learning lowers it over a longer time by changing the model. Active inference is the name for the action half: the agent chooses actions whose predicted outcomes have low expected free energy.
- `surprise.fep.label`: SURPRISE · THE FREE-ENERGY PRINCIPLE
- `surprise.fep.surprise`: Surprise is the negative log probability of an observation o under the model. Rare observations have high surprise.
- `surprise.fep.title`: Friston's free-energy principle and active inference

- `surprise.map.enemy`: {type} {mode}
- `surprise.measured.arms`: FIXED: the prior never changes. LEARNING: one Boltzmann step per observation at rate 0.02, body preferences held. LEARNING-ALL: the same, with the body preferences learning too. WANDER: the route every step, with no planning: the habit alone. UNTRAINED: the planner with an untrained model, whose every plan predicts the same surprise, so only the habit separates them. RANDOM: a uniformly random move of the nine each step. "enemies" counts every enemy that appeared, including the six present at the start; "seen" counts those the player saw.

- `surprise.measured.classic`: the CLASSIC roster (three spikers, a simpler world), the same engine and seeds: the comparison the mixed roster is measured against
- `surprise.measured.intro`: Measured headless in Node with the same engine: {n} seeds ({first} to {last}), each its own level, {steps} steps each, planning over {horizon} steps with {plans} plans, habit {habit} nats per route step and alarm tail {tail}. Every run is deterministic from its seed; the site's tests re-run seed 1 of FIXED and compare. Measured {date} UTC.
- `surprise.measured.label`: SURPRISE · RECORDED
- `surprise.measured.mixed`: the MIXED roster (a spiker, a runner, a brute and three mites): totals over all seeds per arm; fractions are means over the runs
- `surprise.measured.onsets`: the mixed roster: surprise at the first sight of the k-th enemy, mean over seeds (n = seeds that reached that enemy)
- `surprise.measured.title`: Every mode, run headless against its controls
- `surprise.mode.duck`: duck
- `surprise.mode.hunt`: hunt
- `surprise.mode.lunge`: lunge
- `surprise.mode.recoil`: recoil
- `surprise.mode.retreat`: retreat
- `surprise.mode.wander`: wander
- `surprise.model.fixed`: FIXED
- `surprise.model.learning`: LEARNING
- `surprise.modes.closer`: Which is closer to Friston. LEARNING with the body preferences held. In active inference the parameters of the generative model are learned by the same free-energy minimisation that drives perception and action, on a slower time scale, while the prior preferences over outcomes belong to the kind of creature the agent is and are not rewritten by experience. FIXED is the special case with a learning rate of zero. Letting the preferences learn is the version the principle warns about: an agent that learns to prefer whatever happens to it stops acting to change anything.
- `surprise.modes.fixed`: FIXED. The prior is set once and never changes. An enemy stays exactly as surprising the hundredth time as the first, so the agent reacts to every enemy the same way. Surprise drives action only.
- `surprise.modes.label`: SURPRISE · THE MODES
- `surprise.modes.learning`: LEARNING. After every step the model takes one Boltzmann learning step on what it saw. Views of enemies can become more expected, so the first sight of later enemies can become less surprising (habituation; the measured table shows how much). With the body preferences held (the default), habituation touches only what views look like; being hurt and being alarmed stay exactly as unwelcome. With the checkbox on, the preferences learn too, and the agent learns to expect being hurt and alarmed; the table measures what that does.
- `surprise.modes.title`: FIXED and LEARNING, and which is closer to Friston
- `surprise.pad.aria`: move buttons
- `surprise.pad.help`: Click the view first, then use the arrow keys or W A S D, space to shoot, E to follow the route, F to face the nearest known enemy, C to take cover. Each button takes one step.
- `surprise.page.label`: SURPRISE · WHAT IT IS
- `surprise.page.p1a`: It is a small first-person game. Its level is generated from a seed: rooms of different styles joined by doors and two-cell corridors, lit by neon trim. The whole level is open to the sky: over the walls lies a painted outside, a sun or a moon on its arc, drifting clouds, a skyline of hills and lit towers, and weather.
- `surprise.page.p1b`: Six enemies of four kinds move about the level: a spiker that keeps its distance and fires, a runner that lunges, a swarm of three mites, and a slow brute that fires orbs in a fan. By default the picture is drawn as a settle in true time: the game runs at its own pace, and a grid of p-bits catches up with it, frame by frame, as fast as this machine allows.
- `surprise.page.p2a`: The player is a settling machine with one goal: keep what it senses unsurprising. Its model was fitted to calm wandering through other levels. It has no score and no reward. It has a habit, which is to follow its route from room to room, so wandering is what it does when nothing happens.
- `surprise.page.p2b`: Seeing an enemy, being hurt and being alarmed are all surprising under its model, so in a fight it picks the moves it predicts will lead back to calm, and a dead enemy ends the alarm. You can take the controls at any time; the meter keeps measuring the surprise of what you see.
- `surprise.page.title`: A game agent that acts to keep its observations unsurprising
- `surprise.raybit.door`: door
- `surprise.raybit.enemy`: enemy
- `surprise.raybit.wall`: near wall
- `surprise.reading.asmany`: as many
- `surprise.reading.classic`: {verdict} On the classic roster FIXED took {chpk} hits per 1,000 steps and died {cdeaths} times; on the mixed roster {hpk} and {deaths}, {ratio} times the rate. It still killed {kps} of the enemies it saw ({ckps} on the classic roster), and it took {wratio} times fewer hits than WANDER and {rratio} times fewer than RANDOM on the same levels.
- `surprise.reading.cost`: The mixed roster costs the agent more.
- `surprise.reading.fewer`: fewer
- `surprise.reading.fixed`: FIXED spent {explore} of its steps on the route and visited {rooms} of each level's rooms. It saw {seen} enemies and killed {killed}, {tokill} steps after first sight on average, and took {hits} hits ({hpk} per 1,000 steps) with {deaths} deaths. WANDER, the same route with no planning, took {whits} hits and died {wdeaths} times; RANDOM took {rhits} and died {rdeaths} times.
- `surprise.reading.learning`: LEARNING (preferences held) took {hits} hits ({more} than FIXED), killed {killed} and died {deaths} times. Its first sight of the first enemy measured {l1} nats against FIXED's {f1}, and of the fifth {l5} against {f5}; its mean surprise over the run was {ls} against {fs}.
- `surprise.reading.learningall`: LEARNING-ALL (preferences learning too) had a mean surprise of {s} nats, took {hits} hits, killed {killed} and died {deaths} times. Low surprise is not good play: a model that learns to expect being hurt no longer prefers any outcome.
- `surprise.reading.more`: more
- `surprise.reading.nocost`: The mixed roster did not cost the agent more hits.
- `surprise.reading.notsame`: did not match WANDER on every seed
- `surprise.reading.same`: made exactly the same moves as WANDER on every seed (the per-seed counts are identical)
- `surprise.reading.untrained`: UNTRAINED {verb}: with no model, active inference reduces to its habit. Its mean surprise is {s} nats, {n} times ln 2, the same for every observation.
- `surprise.related.cl1`: Neurons and DOOM. News reports in 2026 describe Cortical Labs' CL1, a computer built on living human neurons, being shown running DOOM: TechSpot, 28 February 2026 and Military.com, March 2026. The Military.com report says the neurons "spin in circles, wander through levels and often die quickly" and that the demo "has not yet appeared in a peer-reviewed scientific paper". We cite these as reports, not as results.
- `surprise.related.darkroom`: The dark room problem. Friston, Thornton and Clark (2012), "Free-energy minimization and the dark-room problem", Frontiers in Psychology 3. {doi}.
- `surprise.related.dishbrain`: DishBrain and Pong. Kagan et al. (2022), "In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world", Neuron. {doi}. Cultured neurons, in a system the paper calls DishBrain, played Pong. The abstract says: "Applying implications from the theory of active inference via the free energy principle, we find apparent learning within five minutes of real-time gameplay not observed in control conditions." The feedback followed the principle: when the paddle hit the ball, "a predictable stimulus was delivered across all electrodes simultaneously"; when it missed, "an unpredictable stimulus was delivered". The paper gives the reasoning: "it should be possible to shape BNN behavior by simply presenting unpredictable feedback following 'incorrect' behavior." The alarm in this game follows the same logic: a live enemy keeps the input unpredictable, and removing it makes the input calm again.
- `surprise.related.gym`: Active inference and Doom. Cullen, Davey, Friston and Moran (2018), "Active Inference in OpenAI Gym: A Paradigm for Computational Investigations Into Psychiatric Illness", Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging 3(9):809-818. {doi}. The abstract names Doom among the OpenAI Gym tasks used.
- `surprise.related.habits`: Habits as a prior over plans. Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, O'Doherty and Pezzulo (2016), "Active inference and learning", Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 68:862-879. {doi}.
- `surprise.related.label`: SURPRISE · RELATED WORK
- `surprise.related.principle`: The principle. Friston (2010), "The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?", Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11(2):127-138. {doi1}. Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck and Pezzulo (2017), "Active Inference: A Process Theory", Neural Computation 29(1):1-49. {doi2}. Parr, Pezzulo and Friston (2022), "Active Inference: The Free Energy Principle in Mind, Brain, and Behavior", The MIT Press, open access. {doi3}.
- `surprise.related.response`: A response to it. Balci et al. (2023), "A response to claims of emergent intelligence and sentience in a dish", Neuron 111(5):604-605. {doi}. A letter from many researchers responding to the paper's claims, as its title says.
- `surprise.related.title`: DishBrain, DOOM and active inference
- `surprise.related.vizdoom`: The research platform. Kempka et al. (2016), "ViZDoom: A Doom-based AI Research Platform for Visual Reinforcement Learning", IEEE CIG 2016. {arxiv}.
- `surprise.rules.brute`: Slow (0.055 cells a step) and takes four hits, twice a spiker. It walks in to 4 cells and keeps coming slowly, and fires three slow orbs in a fan every 40 steps from up to 10 cells. It never ducks or retreats; with 2 points left it rages, 1.7 times faster, firing every 26 steps.
- `surprise.rules.mite`: Comes in a swarm of three. One hit kills a mite, and it is small, so it is a narrow target. While wandering it follows the swarm's first mite. Seeing you, it calls every mite within 8 cells, closes in, and weaves from side to side for the last 3 cells. A dead mite returns beside a live one.
- `surprise.rules.runner`: Chases along the shortest walk at 0.15 cells a step (two thirds of your speed). From 1.4 cells it lunges straight in at 0.24 for up to 8 steps; after a bite or a spent lunge it springs back for 14 steps, then comes again. Sees 13 cells.
- `surprise.rules.spiker`: Wanders between rooms until it sees you (11 cells, a 140 degree view). Then it approaches beyond 6 cells, backs off inside 2.5, strafes between, and fires a shot every 22 steps. After a shot it ducks round a corner; at its last point of health it retreats to cover and comes back. The original enemy, unchanged.
- `surprise.scope.choices`: The alarm-tail term in G, the plan family (one move for 8 steps, or one move for 1, 2 or 4 steps and then another), the fast "face" turn and the habit's size are engineering choices of ours, made to keep planning cheap and to let a fight finish inside an 8-step horizon. The enemy types' numbers (speeds, health, ranges) are ours too; the brute's four hit points were set so it can be shot down inside one plan.
- `surprise.scope.darkroom`: The dark room problem is real here. Without the habit and the "closer" preference, this agent found the most typical views it could, which are open rooms seen from the middle, and rocked forward and back there instead of passing through doors and corridors, whose views are rarer. The habit and the preference make it wander; they do not remove the problem. Friston, Thornton and Clark (2012) discuss it.
- `surprise.scope.forward`: The agent's forward model is the game's own rules, except that it holds only the enemies the agent knows of, where it believes they are, and runs each in the tactic it was last in. Real active inference agents have to learn how their actions change the world. Here that part is given.
- `surprise.scope.hidden`: The agent has no inferred hidden states. The alarm and the believed enemy positions are set by fixed rules, so the free-energy bound is tight and free energy equals surprise. The meter shows surprise, exactly.
- `surprise.scope.kinds`: The agent's senses do not tell the enemy kinds apart: an enemy is an enemy bit, whatever its kind. Its model and its comfort prior are the same on either roster; only its imagined copies of the world run each kind's rules.
- `surprise.scope.label`: SURPRISE · SCOPE
- `surprise.scope.shows`: It shows an agent that chooses moves by predicted surprise and a habit, with no reward, wandering a level and dealing with enemies, and that its behaviour depends on what its model counts as comfortable.
- `surprise.scope.title`: What it shows, and where it stops
- `surprise.scope.toy`: It is a toy. It is not a model of a brain and not a claim about how cells or animals work. The levels, the enemies' rules, the bits, the habit and every number in the prior were chosen by us.
- `surprise.settle.body`: The body (6 bits). hurt this step; walked forward this step; bumped a wall; fresh (stepped into a cell not stood in for 40 steps); closer (nearer the end of its route than before the step); alarm. The alarm is a belief bit: on while an enemy is seen or heard (within 2.5 cells) or the player is hurt, off when the agent sees the last enemy it knows of die, and it fades after 40 quiet steps. Being hit by a shot tells the agent where the shooter is.
- `surprise.settle.exact`: Surprise is the energy of what the agent sees plus one constant, ln Z. The pulls link each ray to its neighbours and the body to the centre ray, which makes a chain, so Z is summed exactly by a transfer matrix (8 states per ray, 64 body states). The surprise on the meter is exact.
- `surprise.settle.label`: SURPRISE · HOW IT MAPS ONTO SETTLE
- `surprise.settle.learning`: The learning rule (Boltzmann learning): move each lean and pull so that what was just seen becomes more expected. The averages ⟨·⟩ under the model are computed exactly on the chain. Each step is one gradient step on −ln p(o), so learning lowers the surprise of what is seen often.
- `surprise.settle.machine`: The model is a SETTLE machine over the {n} sense bits: every bit has a lean h, and linked pairs have a pull J. Comfortable arrangements have low energy.
- `surprise.settle.moves`: The moves. wait; turn left; turn right (22.5 degrees); forward; back; shoot (a shot hits an enemy inside the crosshair and in sight; two hits kill); explore (one step along the route); face (turn up to 67.5 degrees toward the nearest enemy it knows of); cover (one step toward the nearest cell that enemy cannot see from where the agent believes it is).
- `surprise.settle.pbit`: The p-bit rule that SETTLE uses to shake a machine is also each bit's own prediction of itself given the others. The "local surprise" row is that prediction's error, bit by bit. The "dreamed" row is the same rule running freely: the machine settling into what it expects.
- `surprise.settle.plan`: In this game the agent predicts each plan's observations ô by stepping a copy of the world that holds only the enemies it knows of, at the places it believes them to be. The predictions are certain, so the ambiguity term is zero and the risk term is the surprise of each predicted observation. The second term charges an alarm still on at the end of the plan as if it lasted {tail} more steps; without it, a fight that ends after the plan's eight steps earns nothing for ending it. The third term is ln E(π), the habit: {habit} nats for each step of the plan spent following the route. The second term is our engineering addition; the third has its place in active inference, and its size is our choice.
- `surprise.settle.prior`: The comfort prior. The body leans are set by hand and never learned in the default setting: the agent expects to walk (lean {walked}), to find fresh ground ({fresh}), to get closer to where it is going ({closer}), not to be hurt ({hurt}), not to bump ({bumped}) and not to be alarmed ({alarm}). These are Friston's prior preferences. Everything else, what comfortable views look like, is fitted by maximum likelihood to {steps} steps of wandering with no enemy on levels {levels}, which no measured run uses. The mean surprise on that walk is {mean} nats (the dashed line).
- `surprise.settle.senses`: The senses (36 bits). 12 rays across a 66 degree view. Each ray has three bits: an enemy in its direction, a wall nearer than 1.6 cells, a door panel as the first thing it hits.
- `surprise.settle.title`: The agent's model is a settling machine

- `surprise.view.aria`: The game view. Focus it and use the arrow keys or W A S D to move, space to shoot, E to follow the route, F to face the nearest known enemy, C to take cover.
- `surprise.view.canvas`: First-person view of a neon level of rooms and corridors. Surprise now {s} nats. {n} enemies in the level.
- `surprise.world.enemies`: Enemies and their tactics. Four kinds, six at a time; their rules are listed with the enemies. Every enemy sees across a 140 degree view; lost from sight, it goes to where it last saw the player and gives up after 80 steps. All of this is fixed rules, with no learning and no randomness inside a step, so the agent’s imagined copies of the world run exactly the same rules.
- `surprise.world.label`: SURPRISE · THE WORLD
- `surprise.world.level`: The level. A 44 by 32 grid. Up to nine rectangular rooms are placed at random; a minimum spanning tree over their centres, plus the two shortest extra edges, says which rooms are joined, so there are loops. Each joining corridor runs from a door on one room's wall to a door on the other's, carved by an A* search that may not cross a room, and is then widened to two cells. A level is rebuilt from the next seed until every floor cell can be reached. Doors are panels that slide open while anyone is within 1.6 cells.
- `surprise.world.outside`: The outside. Every pixel above the horizon is painted from the time of day. Eight keyframes, from dawn through noon and dusk to midnight, hold the colours of the sky, the sun, the clouds, the skyline and the fog, and the sky blends between the two around the moment. The sun runs from east to west along an arc, with stripes cut across its lower half; at night a moon takes the same arc and stars come out. Clouds are a noise map seen on a plane above, drifting with the wind and drawn in three flat tones with a bright rim. A skyline of rolling hills and seven clusters of towers stands on the horizon in every direction; their windows are lit by a fixed hash, so they never flicker. The fog takes a colour near the horizon's, so the far floor fades into the haze. By day the rows near the horizon shimmer sideways with the heat, at under one cycle a second. Rain is a field of slanted streaks and sparks are rising embers; both are closed formulas in time, so a frame drawn twice at the same moment is identical. The light on walls and floors follows the day.
- `surprise.world.pathfinding`: Pathfinding. A* over the grid with eight neighbours, cost 1 for a straight step and √2 for a diagonal, the octile distance as its heuristic, and no corner cutting. The tests check its path length against an independent Dijkstra search on 63 levels, and check that it reports no path on a map split by a wall.
- `surprise.world.picture`: The picture. A textured raycaster: one ray per picture column through the same grid the agent senses, walls and door panels with neon trim, the floor drawn row by row, light pooling under the lamps, distance fog that the neon shows through, and sprites sorted far to near. Beside each pixel's colour the renderer writes what the pixel shows (its class), which the settle can use to choose a light's colour. Every frame is written into one array of pixels and drawn at the chosen width. The figures under the view are this tab's own timings.
- `surprise.world.roof`: The open roof. No room and no corridor has a ceiling. The roof was taken off without a draw from the level's random number generator, so no wall, door, lamp or pickup moved, and the comfort prior still fits these levels exactly. The sky is only a picture: nothing the agent senses changed, and the test that re-runs a recorded seed still matches the measured table.
- `surprise.world.settle`: The picture drawn as a settle. In this mode the raycaster draws a small frame, one pixel per light (up to 128, 192 or 256 lights across). The frame is first brightened (g' = 1.5 g^0.8, capped at 1), because the dark neon scene would otherwise light only a few lights. Each light is a p-bit with the lean h = atanh(2g − 1) for its grey g, and a pull J to its four neighbours. With J = 0 a light says yes a fraction g of the time, so grey becomes a rate. By default there is one light per pixel: its grey is the pixel's brightness and a lit light shines in the pixel's own colour, so the settle decides how bright each light is and the frame decides its colour. The other option gives each pixel three lights, one per colour. Every frame the lights take a few Gibbs sweeps in checkerboard order, starting from where they ended the frame before, and the picture is drawn from each light's running average (the soft read) or from the raw bits. The lights keep fizzing because each is a coin. The caption reports the settle's own time and the PSNR of the soft read against the brightness it aims at.
- `surprise.world.title`: How the world is built
- `surprise.world.truetime`: True time. In this mode (the default) the game and the picture keep separate clocks. The game steps at its own rate and is filmed on a fixed grid, one frame every 500 ms unless the control says otherwise, into a ring of the last {ring} frames. The settle in front works toward the frame it was given, as many sweeps per animation frame as fit in {budget} ms. A frame counts as shown when 80% of the lights it asked to change agree with it: a light agrees when its soft read sits within 0.05 plus two standard deviations of a coin of its target rate, which is where a settled light stays. Counting only the lights a frame changed matters: frames half a second apart differ in a few percent of the lights, so a share of the whole frame would pass before anything had moved. When a frame is shown, the settle takes the frame the game is at at that moment, not the next one in order. A fast machine shows every frame and holds each, still fizzing, until the game moves on; a slow one skips frames and is never far behind. The clock is settle-see's TRUE TIME, so its frames turn on the page's one master beat.
- `surprise.world.wandering`: Wandering. The route: walk the A* path to a room, look round for six steps on arrival while strolling, then choose the next room, one of the three least recently entered, at random.

## sxl

- `sxl.about.label`: WHAT THIS PAGE EXPLORES
- `sxl.about.p1`: The first subject is the neocortex. Most of it has six layers. Some counts give five, because rodent work merges layers 2 and 3 into one layer 2/3; others give more, because primate V1 splits layer 4 into sublayers and layers 5 and 6 split into 5A, 5B, 6a and 6b. Inside each column the layers loop, and between areas they send feedforward and feedback connections.
- `sxl.about.p2`: The second subject is the cerebellar cortex and its Purkinje cells, the only output of that cortex. The third is Pentti Kanerva’s sparse distributed memory and his idea that the cerebellum is one.
- `sxl.about.p3`: Every panel is a live settle in your browser: yes/no things with leans and pulls, sampled until they settle. The cerebellum panels use a real Kanerva memory. One rule to keep in mind: a SETTLE pull works both ways. The brain’s connections have a direction; a pull does not. So a settle can show recurrence honestly and cannot show a one-way arrow. Each panel says how it puts direction back, or says that it does not.
- `sxl.about.p4`: Each panel carries two lists: faithful, what matches a measured fact, and cartoon, what is simplified or invented. Each fact carries its status: established, debated or hypothesis. Beside each live panel sit its program and its recorded outputs from the release binary; the browser sampler uses another random stream, so live rates agree with recorded ones to sampling noise, and exact values agree exactly.
- `sxl.about.title`: Three subjects, explored with one small language
- `sxl.areas.aria`: Two areas of six layers each. Feedforward runs from the lower area, layer 2/3, into the higher area, layer 4. Feedback runs from the higher area, layers 5 and 6, into the lower area, layers 1 and 6, and avoids layer 4.
- `sxl.areas.cap`: The layer depths are a schematic of a typical neocortex, not a measurement of any one area (settle-see CORTEX_LAYERS). The paths are drawn by hand from the laminar rules; they carry no data.
- `sxl.areas.fb`: feedback, into layers 1 and 6
- `sxl.areas.ff`: feedforward, into layer 4
- `sxl.areas.higher`: HIGHER AREA
- `sxl.areas.lower`: LOWER AREA
- `sxl.att.attention`: softmax attention
- `sxl.att.c1`: Binary random patterns, where attention uses learned and correlated vectors.
- `sxl.att.c2`: A cerebellar implementation of attention is a hypothesis.
- `sxl.att.counter`: Computed in this tab ({engine}); the attention read uses a fitted inverse temperature {b}.
- `sxl.att.f1`: The approximation of Bricken and Pehlevan (2021), computed under their stated conditions: normalised vectors and a fitted inverse temperature.
- `sxl.att.js`: the JavaScript copy
- `sxl.att.kernel`: the kernel read, infinitely many locations
- `sxl.att.noise`: address-noise
- `sxl.att.p1`: Give the hard locations a soft edge and the SDM read approaches softmax attention (Bricken and Pehlevan 2021). SETTLE computes three reads side by side: the sampled read of this machine, the read with infinitely many locations, and a fitted softmax attention read. In the recorded run at softness {s} they agree: {v} at {n}% noise for all three.
- `sxl.att.rec`: Recorded at softness {s} and this noise: all three reads say {v}.
- `sxl.att.sampled`: the sampled read of this machine
- `sxl.att.soft`: softness
- `sxl.att.softv`: softness {s}
- `sxl.bell.c1`: A round is not a millisecond, and the panel carries no Hz.
- `sxl.bell.c2`: The arrows live in the page loop, not in SETTLE: one SETTLE model cannot hold an E to I to E cycle.
- `sxl.bell.delay`: delay around the loop
- `sxl.bell.delayv`: delay {d}
- `sxl.bell.e`: E, excitatory
- `sxl.bell.f1`: Delayed negative feedback settles below unit loop gain and rings above it, with a period set by the delay.
- `sxl.bell.f2`: Rhythms from E-I loops, such as PING, exist in cortex (Buzsáki and Wang 2012).
- `sxl.bell.gain`: loop gain
- `sxl.bell.gainv`: gain {g}
- `sxl.bell.i`: I, inhibitory
- `sxl.bell.leak`: leak
- `sxl.bell.leakv`: leak {a}
- `sxl.bell.noleak`: no leak
- `sxl.bell.note`: The E population of the last round, as the script of the experiment writes it: its lean changes every round with what it hears from I. The arrows between E and I live in the loop, because a SETTLE pull is symmetric.
- `sxl.bell.p1`: A loop with a delay rings. E excites I, I inhibits E, and each hears the other one or more rounds late. Below unit loop gain the loop settles: at gain 0.5, E holds near {low}. Above it, it rings: at gain 1.5, E swings between about {hi} and {lo}, with a period of two rounds at delay 1 and six rounds at delay 3. A leak damps the short loop and leaves the long one ringing.
- `sxl.bell.run`: Round {k} of {n}, two settles of {s} samples a round, in this tab.
- `sxl.bell.still`: Still: all {n} rounds were run at once.
- `sxl.bell.trace.aria`: The E population mean, round by round, from -1 to +1: the live loop and the recorded one.
- `sxl.bell.trace.cap`: The live loop in rose, the recorded loop in mint. Each point is one round: the E population settled once, then I settled once.
- `sxl.carpet.again`: read again with fresh noise
- `sxl.carpet.aria`: Top: the read-address bits (mossy fibres). Middle: {M} hard locations (granule cells), {k} awake. Then the Purkinje columns, each lit by the sign of its summed counters. Bottom: the stored word the climbing fibres wrote.
- `sxl.carpet.c1`: The cerebellar names are a hypothesis with "little direct evidence" (Rogers 1988). Two thousand dots stand for tens of billions of granule cells.
- `sxl.carpet.c2`: Each dot checks all 256 address bits, where a granule cell has about four inputs (Billings et al. 2014); calling the share GOLGI follows Bricken et al. (2023), who call it the weakest part of their mapping.
- `sxl.carpet.c3`: SDM needs sparse granule firing, and in mice learning eyeblink conditioning about two thirds of imaged granule cells responded (Giovannucci et al. 2017). Debated.
- `sxl.carpet.crate`: Run by KANERVA itself, compiled to WebAssembly, in this tab.
- `sxl.carpet.e5`: Recorded in E5 at {n} words and this noise: {k} of {of} reads recalled the word.
- `sxl.carpet.f1`: The SDM arithmetic is Kanerva’s, run by KANERVA; iterated reading converges inside the critical distance and diverges outside it (Kanerva 1988).
- `sxl.carpet.f2`: The part-by-part mapping onto the cerebellum follows Kanerva (1989) and Bricken et al. (2023).
- `sxl.carpet.go`: read
- `sxl.carpet.golgi`: GOLGI: the share of granule cells a read wakes
- `sxl.carpet.js`: Run by the JavaScript copy of KANERVA while the crate loads.
- `sxl.carpet.l.climbing`: climbing fibres: the word that was written
- `sxl.carpet.l.granule`: granule cells: the hard locations, awake ones lit
- `sxl.carpet.l.mossy`: mossy fibres: the read-address
- `sxl.carpet.l.purkinje`: Purkinje columns: the vote, one per bit
- `sxl.carpet.noise`: address-noise
- `sxl.carpet.noisev`: {p}% noise
- `sxl.carpet.one`: one read
- `sxl.carpet.p1`: Kanerva read his sparse distributed memory as the cerebellum. Mossy fibres carry the address; granule cells are the hard locations, each waking when the address is near its own; the parallel fibre synapses onto a Purkinje cell are the counters; the climbing fibre says write; each Purkinje cell sums one column and votes one bit. In the recorded run a read woke about {k} of {M} locations and recalled :{w}; at {hn}% noise it woke {hk} and fell into :{hw}.
- `sxl.carpet.p2`: Feeding the read back as the next address cleans it up inside the critical distance and wanders outside it. With 50 words stored at 20% noise, one read recalled {a} of {n} and ten iterated reads {b}. With 100 words at 10% noise, one read recalled {c} and ten {d}.
- `sxl.carpet.reads`: reads
- `sxl.carpet.state`: Round {r}: {k} of {M} hard locations awake. Overlap with :{w} {o}. Closest: {c}. {v}.
- `sxl.carpet.stored`: stored words
- `sxl.carpet.storedv`: {n} words
- `sxl.carpet.ten`: up to ten iterated reads
- `sxl.carpet.v.none`: nothing clear yet
- `sxl.carpet.v.word`: landed on :{w}

- `sxl.chip.recorded`: recorded outputs from the release binary
- `sxl.chip.sections14`: 14 live sections

- `sxl.counter.run`: Settling: {n} of {total} samples, live in this tab.
- `sxl.counter.still`: Still: the whole settle of {n} samples was run at once, because your system asks for reduced motion.
- `sxl.ctx.both`: the input and the context
- `sxl.ctx.cap`: An input, two competing explanations and a context above them
- `sxl.ctx.context`: the context alone
- `sxl.ctx.input`: the input alone
- `sxl.ctx.modes`: what is held
- `sxl.ctx.p1`: Feedback as context. With the input alone, explanation b wins at {b}. Hold the context above and explanation a rises to {a} while b falls to {b2}: the two explanations compete, and the context tips them.
- `sxl.depth.aria`: Arm {arm}: the overlap with P, round by round, from -1 to +1, for the eight recorded sets, their mean and the live set.
- `sxl.depth.c1`: Twelve things and three stored patterns; the loop between rounds is the page’s script, not anatomy.
- `sxl.depth.c2`: The fresh layers differ only in their distractors; a real deep stack learns each layer.
- `sxl.depth.cap`: Faint lines: the eight recorded sets. Dashed mint: their mean. Rose: the set you chose, settling live in this tab. The score is the overlap with P, from -1 (the mirror image) to +1 (P itself).
- `sxl.depth.depth`: DEPTH: a fresh layer every round
- `sxl.depth.f1`: A residual stack with weights shared across layers is a recurrent network unrolled in time (Liao and Poggio 2016). An identity, stated by the authors.
- `sxl.depth.f2`: The climbing fibre as a teaching signal for the Purkinje cell (Marr 1969; Albus 1971; Ito). A classical theory with strong support, still debated.
- `sxl.depth.note`: The TIME arm’s layer for the round shown, as the script of the experiment writes it: the pulls store P and two distractors, and the leans are what the round before settled to.
- `sxl.depth.p1`: The navigator’s hypothesis, marked as a hypothesis: a residual layer does the work of individual feedback arcs, clusters of fibres, climbing fibres. What the literature supports: a residual stack whose layers share their weights is a shallow recurrent network unrolled in time (Liao and Poggio 2016), so one more residual add reads as one more pass round a recurrent arc, depth spent where the cortex spends time. What points elsewhere: the climbing fibre, one per Purkinje cell and about one complex spike a second, is read by Marr, Albus and Ito as a teaching or error signal, closer to a learning signal than to a residual pathway.
- `sxl.depth.p2`: The candidate experiment, run. A layer of {n} things stores a pattern P and two distractors as pulls. Round 1 leans each thing toward a cue, P with 4 of its {n} bits flipped; each later round leans on what the round before settled to. TIME settles the same layer {rounds} times; DEPTH settles {rounds} fresh layers, each storing P with its own two distractors. Every round in both arms is one settle of the same size.
- `sxl.depth.p3`: Over {sets} pattern sets the mean overlap with P after the last round is {t} for time and {d} for depth. Time cleaned up {tn} of {sets} sets and depth {dn}. They fail differently: the same layer can stay in the same wrong state round after round, and fresh layers can fall into the mirror image of P, which every layer also stores. On this toy, time stands in for depth about as well as depth does; {sets} sets cannot tell the two apart.
- `sxl.depth.run`: Round {k} of {n}, one settle of {s} samples per arm a round, in this tab.
- `sxl.depth.sets`: pattern set
- `sxl.depth.setv`: set {n}
- `sxl.depth.still`: Still: all {n} rounds of both arms were run at once.
- `sxl.depth.time`: TIME: the same layer, settled again
- `sxl.err.c1`: The prediction is held by hand, not computed. In a symmetric model the error things are readouts and do not drive the cause.
- `sxl.err.c2`: Laminar predictive coding is a hypothesis (Bastos et al. 2012), and its rhythm motif is disputed (Mendoza-Halliday et al. 2024; Mackey et al. 2025).
- `sxl.err.cap`: Inputs in layer 4, a prediction from the deep layers above, signed errors in layer 2/3
- `sxl.err.f1`: The four-condition truth table of signed errors (Keller and Mrsic-Flogel 2018) and the layer 2/3 subtraction measured in mouse V1 (Jordan and Keller 2020).
- `sxl.err.f2`: Activity in an input area with no bottom-up drive (Kok et al. 2016; Muckli et al. 2015).
- `sxl.err.inputs`: input and prediction
- `sxl.err.p.off`: prediction: absent
- `sxl.err.p.on`: prediction: present
- `sxl.err.p1`: Positive error things light when the input arrives unpredicted ({pos}); negative error things light when a predicted input is omitted ({neg}); when the input matches the prediction, both stay near {quiet}. The exact values are (1 + tanh(±2)) / 2.
- `sxl.err.surprise`: surprise: flip the input
- `sxl.err.x.off`: input absent
- `sxl.err.x.on`: input present
- `sxl.fb.c1`: Two areas stand for a hierarchy, and a binary label stands for a graded measure (Markov et al. 2014 measure SLN on a continuous scale).
- `sxl.fb.c2`: ARROWS samples no single distribution, and the E2 cartoon loop is an invented edge list, not a connectome.
- `sxl.fb.cap`: One column; the feedback thing pulls layers 2/3 and 5, never layer 4
- `sxl.fb.f1`: The laminar rule: feedforward ends in and around layer 4, feedback ends mainly in layers 1 and 6 and avoids layer 4 (Rockland and Pandya 1979; Felleman and Van Essen 1991). Established in macaque.
- `sxl.fb.f2`: SETTLE symmetry, shown as a measured fact: a pull carries influence both ways.
- `sxl.fb.held`: feedback held yes
- `sxl.fb.l4no`: feedback yes, layer 4 held no
- `sxl.fb.modes`: what is held
- `sxl.fb.nothing`: nothing held
- `sxl.fb.p1`: In cortex, feedback terminals avoid layer 4. A SETTLE pull has no direction, so the settle does not avoid it: in this column the feedback thing pulls only layers 2/3 and 5, and layer 4 still rises from {a} to {b} when feedback is held. With layer 4 held no as well, layer 2/3 sits at {c}, near a coin.
- `sxl.fill.cap`: One deep cause and four inputs
- `sxl.fill.cause`: hold only the deep cause
- `sxl.fill.modes`: what is held
- `sxl.fill.nothing`: hold nothing
- `sxl.fill.p1`: Hold only the deep cause and the inputs rise to {v} with no bottom-up drive at all, the shape of activity seen in an input area with nothing in front of the eye.
- `sxl.fill.three`: hold three inputs
- `sxl.gather.alone`: alone
- `sxl.gather.arms`: the two answers
- `sxl.gather.c1`: Two answers and six pieces of evidence, with no time: the settle gives where the network ends, not the climb to a bound.
- `sxl.gather.c2`: The push between the answers is symmetric; real mutual inhibition runs through inhibitory cells.
- `sxl.gather.cap`: Two answers and their evidence
- `sxl.gather.compete`: compete, push 2
- `sxl.gather.evidence`: evidence for :a
- `sxl.gather.f1`: Evidence integrated to a bound in decision making (Gold and Shadlen 2007), and two pools that inhibit each other until one wins (Wang 2002). Established as models; how cortex carries them out is debated.
- `sxl.gather.f2`: Exact rates by enumeration, and the release binary’s recorded rates, agree to sampling noise.
- `sxl.gather.kv`: {k} of 3
- `sxl.gather.p1`: Two answers, :a and :b, and three pieces of evidence for each; every piece pulls its answer by 0.4 and is held yes or no, so each answer is driven by the sum of its evidence. One piece for :b is yes. Alone, each answer follows its own evidence: as the evidence for :a goes from none to all three, :a climbs {a0}, {a1}, {a2}, {a3}, while :b stays near {b}.
- `sxl.gather.p2`: Let the two answers push each other by 2 and the network can hold only one of them. Now the evidence decides which: with no evidence for :a, :b commits at {cb0}; with all three, :a commits at {ca3} and :b is let go, down to {cb3}.
- `sxl.gather.p3`: The navigator’s image for this: each final thought is a leap that keeps one jewel and lets everything else go. It is an image over real mechanisms, evidence integrated to a bound and attractor dynamics, not a finding.
- `sxl.guess.blank`: a blank guess
- `sxl.guess.bot`: what is seen, settling
- `sxl.guess.c`: how hard the guess pulls
- `sxl.guess.c1`: The coupling is symmetric, so this is two layers inferring together, not a feedback pathway with layer-specific terminals.
- `sxl.guess.c2`: Five seeds and one picture.
- `sxl.guess.count`: Wrong pixels now: {live} of {n}. Recorded for this condition, mean of five seeds: {rec}.
- `sxl.guess.cv`: coupling {c}
- `sxl.guess.ev`: the evidence: a plus sign, a quarter of its pixels flipped
- `sxl.guess.f1`: Boltzmann clamping and explaining away, computed exactly.
- `sxl.guess.f2`: One coupling trades correction against hallucination, the shape of the proposal of Lee and Mumford (2003), a hypothesis for cortex.
- `sxl.guess.guess`: the guess
- `sxl.guess.none`: no guess layer
- `sxl.guess.note`: E4 writes its programs with this script; the page builds the same two grids and the same pulls.
- `sxl.guess.p1`: The same idea on a picture. Evidence alone leaves {ev} of 256 pixels wrong. A right guess pulling by 1 cuts that to {right}. A wrong guess makes it worse the harder it pulls: {w1} at 1, {w2} at 2. One coupling sets the trade between correction and hallucination.

- `sxl.guess.top`: the guess layer, settling

- `sxl.hier.c1`: Toy areas and labels, not the 305 reported pathways; integer levels where real SLN is fitted on a continuous scale.
- `sxl.hier.c2`: The weak-input effect comes from a flat sigmoid near its ceiling, not from the circuit of V1.
- `sxl.hier.contra`: distances that disagree
- `sxl.hier.count`: Visited every one of {n} arrangements in this tab: {k} tie at the calmest energy {e}.
- `sxl.hier.distance`: order and distance
- `sxl.hier.f1`: The constraint logic of Felleman and Van Essen (1991) and the indeterminacy of Hilgetag et al. (1996), in miniature.
- `sxl.hier.f2`: A graded measure adds distance (Barone et al. 2000; Markov et al. 2014); feedback effects are larger for low-salience stimuli (Hupé et al. 1998).
- `sxl.hier.held`: distance, V1 held at the bottom
- `sxl.hier.labels`: the labels between areas
- `sxl.hier.note`: Generated in this tab from four labels; a 0/1 penalty w on a pair is a push of w/4 and a lean of w/4 towards no on each.
- `sxl.hier.order`: order labels
- `sxl.hier.p1`: Felleman and Van Essen (1991) used the laminar rules to order 32 visual and visual-association areas into 10 levels. The order is not unique (Hilgetag et al. 1996). Here, in miniature: four areas, four order labels, sixteen one-hot things. Order labels alone leave {o} hierarchies tied at the calmest energy. Add a distance to each label, as SLN does, and {d} remain, the same hierarchy shifted one level. Hold V1 at the bottom and {h} remains.
- `sxl.hier.p2`: Distances that disagree leave no arrangement free of penalty: each calmest one breaks a label, the SETTLE picture of the pathways that do not fit cleanly.
- `sxl.hier.rec`: Recorded by `valleys`: {k} arrangements at the calmest energy {e}, of {n} visited.
- `sxl.hier.stack.aria`: Levels: a {a}, b {b}, c {c}, d {d}
- `sxl.honest.cartoon`: CARTOON
- `sxl.honest.faithful`: FAITHFUL
- `sxl.layers.GL`: granular layer: granule cells, the hard locations of Kanerva’s reading
- `sxl.layers.I`: I · molecular: tufts and long axons, almost no cell bodies
- `sxl.layers.II`: II · external granular
- `sxl.layers.III`: III · external pyramidal: pyramids that project to other areas
- `sxl.layers.IV`: IV · internal granular: where the core thalamus arrives
- `sxl.layers.ML`: molecular layer: parallel fibres cross the Purkinje fans
- `sxl.layers.PCL`: Purkinje cell layer: the only output of the cerebellar cortex
- `sxl.layers.V`: V · internal pyramidal: output to the brainstem and cord
- `sxl.layers.VI`: VI · multiform: back to the thalamus
- `sxl.layers.cb`: THE CEREBELLAR CORTEX · THREE LAYERS
- `sxl.layers.cb.aria`: The cerebellar cortex in its three layers, settling.
- `sxl.layers.cortex`: THE NEOCORTEX · SIX LAYERS
- `sxl.layers.cortex.aria`: The cerebral cortex in its six layers, settling.
- `sxl.layers.label`: THE TWO CORTICES
- `sxl.layers.lede`: Both drawn by settle-see, layer by layer. The layer depths are a schematic of a typical cortex, not a measurement of any one area.
- `sxl.layers.title`: Six layers on one side, three on the other
- `sxl.pass.c1`: A soft activation edge, binary Purkinje outputs, and no Golgi, basket or stellate cells.
- `sxl.pass.c2`: Purkinje cells do inhibit granule cells in some lobules (Guo et al. 2016); that real loop is inhibitory, not the symmetric pull drawn here.
- `sxl.pass.close`: The contrast the page ends on, an interpretation of the wiring: the neocortex settles inside itself, and the cerebellar cortex computes in one pass while its loops close outside it (Douglas and Martin 2007; Kelly and Strick 2003).
- `sxl.pass.f1`: Kanerva’s one-way mapping: mossy fibres to granule cells to Purkinje cells, whose targets are basket and Golgi cells, not granule cells (Kanerva 1993, via Bricken et al. 2023).
- `sxl.pass.f2`: The collapse under symmetric feedback is measured, not argued.
- `sxl.pass.final`: Closest after the last round: {c}.
- `sxl.pass.go`: read
- `sxl.pass.live`: the one-way pass, live: best overlap by round
- `sxl.pass.note`: mode: :settle lets the data things pull back on the hard locations, an arrow the anatomy lacks. The pass on the left runs in this tab; the settle on the right is the recorded run.
- `sxl.pass.p1`: The cerebellar cortex computes in one pass: granule cells drive Purkinje cells, which project out, not back to the granule cells. Let the outputs pull back and the memory breaks. In settle mode two different cues, :{a} and :{b}, ended on one blend ({o}), while the pass returned :{g} closest at {go}. At softness 0 both modes recalled :{h}.
- `sxl.pass.p2`: The measured counts: in E5b the pass recalled {p} of {pn} and the settle {s} of {sn}. In the SOFTSDM results, the settle read recalled {rs} of {all} read-addresses where the pass recalled {rp}.
- `sxl.pass.rec`: the settle, recorded: best overlap by round
- `sxl.pass.recfinal`: Recorded verdict: {v}.

- `sxl.rec.h`: RECORDED · settle 0.1.0, release binary, seed 1

- `sxl.ring.canonical`: cartoon loop
- `sxl.ring.cap`: Six layers of twelve things; each layer agreement with pattern P
- `sxl.ring.chain`: chain
- `sxl.ring.conflict`: and layer 1 held at Q
- `sxl.ring.input`: layer 4 held at P
- `sxl.ring.layer`: layer
- `sxl.ring.lights`: its twelve lights now
- `sxl.ring.mode`: what is held
- `sxl.ring.note`: E2 writes its programs with this script: twelve things a layer, thing i of one layer pulls thing i of a connected layer.
- `sxl.ring.p1`: Six layers held at once. In a chain, agreement with the held layer 4 falls with distance: {a}, {b}, {c} at one, two and three steps, matching (1 + tanh(W)^d) / 2 = {ea}, {eb}, {ec}. Hold layer 1 at another pattern and every layer follows the nearer held layer.

- `sxl.ring.pullv`: pull {w}
- `sxl.ring.ring`: ring
- `sxl.ring.wiring`: how the six layers are wired
- `sxl.rules.label`: THE FIVE DESIGN RULES
- `sxl.rules.r1`: Recurrent and interconnected, never residual layers. The cortex here is loops: layers lean on each other both ways, higher areas feed back into layer 1, and the answer is the state the whole network settles into. A settle is already this shape. Sections 1 and 5 show it.
- `sxl.rules.r2`: Timing decides. When a signal arrives matters, not only what it is. In section 9 the same loop with the same leak settles when the delay is one round and keeps ringing when it is three. Section 4 is the layer 5 coincidence window, without its clock.
- `sxl.rules.r3`: Gather, then commit. Evidence sums until the network commits to one answer and lets the others go, a settle cooling into one valley. Section 13.
- `sxl.rules.r4`: Settle first; KANERVA where a sparse distributed memory is the honest model. Every panel settles; sections 10 to 12 use KANERVA for the cerebellum.
- `sxl.rules.r5`: A hypothesis, marked as one: a residual layer does the work of individual feedback arcs, clusters of fibres, climbing fibres. Section 14 states it and runs the candidate experiment.
- `sxl.rules.title`: The navigator’s rules for this page, and where it keeps each
- `sxl.s1.label`: 1 · WEAK DOOR, LOUD ROOM
- `sxl.s1.lede`: Recurrence inside a column amplifies a weak input. Live: the thalamus held yes and held no, side by side.
- `sxl.s1.title`: A weak thalamic door into a loud room of layer 4 cells
- `sxl.s10.label`: 10 · THE GRANULE CARPET
- `sxl.s10.lede`: Mossy fibres, granule cells, Purkinje cells and climbing fibres, as Kanerva mapped them.
- `sxl.s10.title`: Kanerva’s cerebellum: a sparse distributed memory you can read
- `sxl.s11.label`: 11 · ATTENTION IS A SOFT GRANULE LAYER
- `sxl.s11.lede`: Softmax attention approximates the SDM read.
- `sxl.s11.title`: Three reads of a soft memory give one verdict
- `sxl.s12.label`: 12 · PASS OR SETTLE
- `sxl.s12.lede`: The honest warning: let the outputs pull back and the memory breaks.
- `sxl.s12.title`: Why the cerebellum computes in one pass
- `sxl.s13.label`: 13 · GATHER, THEN COMMIT
- `sxl.s13.lede`: The navigator’s third rule, run: gather the evidence, then commit to one valley.
- `sxl.s13.title`: Evidence sums until the network keeps one answer and lets the other go
- `sxl.s14.label`: 14 · TIME FOR DEPTH
- `sxl.s14.lede`: The navigator’s hypothesis about residual layers, marked as one, and the candidate experiment beside it.
- `sxl.s14.title`: Can time stand in for depth? One layer settled six times beside six fresh layers
- `sxl.s2.label`: 2 · SILENCE LAYER 4
- `sxl.s2.lede`: Two wirings, one button, opposite predictions.
- `sxl.s2.title`: Silence layer 4 and see whether layer 5 still hears the thalamus
- `sxl.s3.label`: 3 · THE DISINHIBITORY SWITCH
- `sxl.s3.lede`: The VIP to SST to pyramid chain, with one button that runs backwards on purpose.
- `sxl.s3.title`: Inhibit the inhibitor and the pyramid wakes
- `sxl.s4.label`: 4 · THE TUFT AND THE SOMA
- `sxl.s4.lede`: A coincidence detector, and the encoding trap that makes a silent inhibitor excite.
- `sxl.s4.title`: A layer 5 cell bursts only when its soma and its tuft agree
- `sxl.s5.label`: 5 · FEEDBACK AVOIDS LAYER 4
- `sxl.s5.lede`: The lead panel: a pull carries influence both ways, so feedback reaches layer 4 through the column.
- `sxl.s5.title`: Feedback avoids layer 4, and the settle does not

- `sxl.s6.lede`: The page visits every arrangement and draws every tied calmest hierarchy.
- `sxl.s6.title`: Order labels leave the hierarchy loose; distances tighten it
- `sxl.s7.label`: 7 · THE ERROR COLUMN
- `sxl.s7.lede`: Laminar predictive coding in miniature, with the prediction held by hand.
- `sxl.s7.title`: Signed errors in layer 2/3, and a deep cause that fills in its inputs
- `sxl.s8.label`: 8 · THE GUESS THAT SEES
- `sxl.s8.lede`: Context tips a competition between explanations; a guess grid corrects or hallucinates.
- `sxl.s8.title`: A guess from above corrects what is seen, or makes it up
- `sxl.s9.label`: 9 · THE BELL
- `sxl.s9.lede`: The arrows live in a loop outside SETTLE; below unit gain it settles, above it it rings.
- `sxl.s9.title`: A delayed loop between excitation and inhibition rings
- `sxl.sa.arrows`: ARROWS: a loop outside the settle
- `sxl.sa.counter`: Each round settles both columns, {n} samples each, in this tab; the loop carries the arrows.
- `sxl.sa.live.arrows`: live, ARROWS round {k} of {n}
- `sxl.sa.live.springs`: live, SPRINGS
- `sxl.sa.modes`: how the two areas are joined
- `sxl.sa.note`: ARROWS runs no single program: the script of the experiment writes one program per column per round, and this page runs the same loop.
- `sxl.sa.p1`: Two ways to join two areas. SPRINGS puts both in one settle, so every link pulls both ways. ARROWS runs each area as its own settle and carries the arrows in a loop outside them. With a weak input, the lower area layer 4 reads {none} with no feedback, {springs} with SPRINGS and {arrows} after the last ARROWS round. Feedback never touches layer 4 in either; it gets there through the symmetric pulls inside the column.
- `sxl.sa.p2`: ARROWS is not one distribution: two settles passing rates back and forth grow more confident than either alone, as E1 measured. Read its number as what the loop does, not as a probability.
- `sxl.sa.rec.arrows`: recorded, ARROWS round {k}
- `sxl.sa.rec.none`: recorded, no feedback
- `sxl.sa.rec.springs`: recorded, SPRINGS

- `sxl.sa.springs`: SPRINGS: one symmetric settle
